nodes.title: Capelli's theorem on the irreducibility of Xⁿ − a
nodes.statement: Let K be a field, n ≥ 1 and a ∈ K. Then Xⁿ − a is irreducible over K if and only if a ∉ K^p for every prime p dividing n, and a ∉ −4K⁴ when 4 | n.
hypotheses: K an arbitrary field, of any characteristic.
proofSteps: Necessity: if a = b^p with p | n then X^{n/p} − b divides Xⁿ − a; if 4 | n and a = −4b⁴ then Xⁿ − a = (X^{n/4})⁴ + 4b⁴ = (X^{n/2} + 2bX^{n/4} + 2b²)(X^{n/2} − 2bX^{n/4} + 2b²). (Mathlib pow_ne_of_irreducible_X_pow_sub_C covers the first.)
Sufficiency: write n = 2^k m with m odd. By Mathlib X_pow_sub_C_irreducible_of_odd, X^m − a is irreducible (a is not a p-th power for primes p | m).

With α a root of X^m − a and L = K(α) of degree m, Mathlib X_pow_mul_sub_C_irreducible reduces the claim to the irreducibility of X^{2^k} − α over L. The norm N_{L/K}(α) is a, because m is odd (Mathlib Algebra.PowerBasis.norm_gen_eq_coeff_zero_minpoly: N(α) = (−1)^m·(−a)). If α = γ² in L then a = N(γ)² is a square in K; if α = −4δ⁴ in L then a = (−4)^m N(δ)⁴ = −4·(2^{(m−1)/2} N(δ))⁴ ∈ −4K⁴. Both are excluded by the hypotheses (the second only matters when 4 | n, i.e. k ≥ 2).
Hence the hypotheses of CA.3/capelli-two-power-case hold for α over L, and X^{2^k} − α is irreducible.
acceptance: X⁴ + 4 is reducible over ℚ; X⁴ + 1 and X⁴ − 2 are irreducible.
X⁶ + 27 = X⁶ − (−3)³ is reducible (−27 is a cube).
For n odd the criterion is Mathlib's X_pow_sub_C_irreducible_iff_forall_prime_of_odd.

nodes.title: The analytic order of a complex polynomial is its root multiplicity
nodes.statement: For a nonzero p ∈ ℂ[X] and z ∈ ℂ, the order of vanishing at z of the entire function w ↦ p(w) equals the multiplicity of z as a root of p.
proofSteps: Write p = (X − z)^m q with m = rootMultiplicity z p and q(z) ≠ 0 (Mathlib Polynomial.exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd).
Then p(w) = (w − z)^m q(w) near z with q analytic and q(z) ≠ 0, which is the characterisation of analytic order m (Mathlib AnalyticAt.analyticOrderAt_eq_natCast).
acceptance: For p = (X − 1)² (X + 1) the order at 1 is 2 and at 0 is 0.
For p = X³ the order at 0 is 3.
Summing over a disc counts roots with multiplicity, which is how Rouché's theorem is applied to polynomials.

nodes.title: Root location under Perron's condition
nodes.statement: Let f = Xⁿ + a_{n−1}X^{n−1} + ⋯ + a_0 ∈ ℂ[X] be monic of degree n ≥ 2 with a_0 ≠ 0 and |a_{n−1}| > 1 + |a_{n−2}| + ⋯ + |a_0|. Then f has exactly one root (counted with multiplicity) with |z| ≥ 1, and n − 1 roots in the open unit disc.
hypotheses: Strict inequality; monic; n ≥ 2.
proofSteps: Tau Ceti TauCeti.rouche_add: f and v have the same number of zeros, counted by analytic order, in the open unit disc; by CA.3/analytic-order-of-a-polynomial these are root counts.

v has the root 0 of multiplicity n − 1 inside and the root −a_{n−1} with |a_{n−1}| > 1 outside, so f has n − 1 roots in the open disc; f has no root on the circle (|f| ≥ |v| − |f − v| > 0 there), so exactly one root has |z| ≥ 1.
acceptance: X³ + 5X² + X + 1: |5| > 1 + 1 + 1, so one root outside the disc and two inside.
The condition fails for X² + 2X + 1 (|2| = 1 + 1): two roots at −1.
Degree 1 is excluded by n ≥ 2.

nodes.title: Perron's irreducibility criterion
nodes.statement: Let f = Xⁿ + a_{n−1}X^{n−1} + ⋯ + a_0 ∈ ℤ[X] with n ≥ 2, a_0 ≠ 0 and |a_{n−1}| > 1 + |a_{n−2}| + ⋯ + |a_1| + |a_0|. Then f is irreducible in ℤ[X] (equivalently in ℚ[X]).
hypotheses: Monic with integer coefficients, nonzero constant term, strict inequality.
proofSteps: f is monic, hence primitive (Mathlib Polynomial.Monic.isPrimitive), so irreducibility in ℤ[X] and in ℚ[X] agree (Mathlib Polynomial.IsPrimitive.Int.irreducible_iff_irreducible_map_cast).
Suppose f = g h with g, h ∈ ℤ[X] monic of positive degree (a factorisation of a monic integer polynomial can be normalised to monic factors).
g(0) h(0) = a_0 ≠ 0, so |g(0)| ≥ 1 and |h(0)| ≥ 1; |g(0)| is the product of the absolute values of the roots of g, so g has a root with |z| ≥ 1, and so does h.
This gives two roots of f, with multiplicity, of absolute value at least 1, contradicting CA.3/perron-root-location.
acceptance: X³ + 5X² + X + 1 is irreducible over ℚ.
Xⁿ + 3X^{n−1} + 1 is irreducible for every n ≥ 2.
The hypothesis a_0 ≠ 0 is needed: X³ + 3X² = X²(X + 3).

nodes.title: A prime value far from the roots forces irreducibility
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ ℤ[X] and b ∈ ℤ with f(b) prime, f(b − 1) ≠ 0, and Re α < b − 1/2 for every complex root α of f. Then f is irreducible in ℤ[X].
hypotheses: f(b) is a prime (up to sign) of ℤ; f(b − 1) ≠ 0.
proofSteps: If deg f = 0 then f = f(b) is a prime constant, irreducible. Assume deg f ≥ 1 and f = g h with neither factor a unit.

Key inequality: for a nonconstant g ∈ ℤ[X] whose roots α satisfy Re α < b − 1/2, |g(b − 1/2 − t)| < |g(b − 1/2 + t)| for t > 0 (each linear factor satisfies |b − 1/2 − t − α| < |b − 1/2 + t − α|). At t = 1/2: |g(b − 1)| < |g(b)|; since g(b − 1) is a nonzero integer, |g(b)| ≥ 2.
A constant factor c with |c| ≥ 2 and a nonconstant cofactor g gives |f(b)| = |c||g(b)| ≥ 4 composite; two nonconstant factors give |f(b)| = |g(b)||h(b)| with both ≥ 2. Either contradicts primality.
acceptance: f = X² + 1, b = 2: f(2) = 5 prime, f(1) = 2 ≠ 0, roots ±i with real part 0 < 3/2: irreducible.
X³ − 9X² − 9X + 1 = (X + 1)(X² − 10X + 1) has the prime value 11 at 10 but a root 5 + √24 ≈ 9.9 with real part > 9.5: the root condition is essential.
f(b − 1) ≠ 0 is needed to get |g(b − 1)| ≥ 1.

nodes.title: The roots of a digit polynomial
nodes.statement: Let b ≥ 2 and let f = Σ a_k X^k ∈ ℤ[X] be nonzero with 0 ≤ a_k ≤ b − 1 for all k. Then every complex root α of f satisfies Re α < b − 1/2.
hypotheses: Digits: all coefficients in [0, b − 1]; f ≠ 0.
proofSteps: Degree 0 has no roots; degree 1: the root −a_0/a_1 ≤ 0 < b − 1/2.
Degree n ≥ 2: the leading digit a_n ≥ 1 and a_{n−1}, a_{n−2} ≥ 0, and m := max_{k≤n−2} |a_k|/a_n ≤ b − 1 ≤ B, where B = 1 for b = 2 and B = ⌊(2b − 1)(2b − 1 − √2)/2⌋ for b ≥ 3.

Theorem 3 of Brillhart–Filaseta–Odlyzko: all roots lie in Re z ≤ max(r_1/√2, r_2), where r_1 is the positive root of x² − x − m and r_2 that of x³ − x² − m (estimate |f(z)/zⁿ| from below on the two regions |z| > r_1, and |z| ≤ r_1 with |arg z| < π/4).
r_1 ≤ r_1*, r_2 ≤ r_2* for the roots with m replaced by B, and h(b − 1/2) = (2b − 1)(2b − 1 − √2)/2 − B > 0, g(b − 1/2) = (b − 1/2)²(b − 3/2) − B > 0 give b − 1/2 > max(r_1*/√2, r_2*).
acceptance: For b = 10 and f = 3X² + 9X + 7 (the digits of 397) the roots have real part −1.5 < 9.5.
For b = 2 the bound B = 1 equals b − 1.
Negative digits break it: X³ − 9X² − 9X + 1 has a root near 9.9.

nodes.title: Cohn's irreducibility criterion in every base
nodes.statement: Let b ≥ 2 and p a prime with base-b expansion p = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b^k, 0 ≤ a_k ≤ b − 1. Then Σ a_k X^k is irreducible in ℤ[X].

Every root has Re α < b − 1/2 (CA.3/digit-polynomial-root-location).

nodes.title: The sloped valuation of a polynomial over a valued field
nodes.statement: Let K be a field with an additive valuation v : K → ℝ ∪ {∞} (v(0) = ∞, v(xy) = v(x) + v(y), v(x + y) ≥ min(v(x), v(y))). For r ∈ ℝ and f = Σ a_i X^i ∈ K[X], the sloped valuation is v_r(f) = min_{i : a_i ≠ 0} (v(a_i) + r i), and v_r(0) = ∞. It is the intercept of the supporting line of slope r of the Newton polygon.
hypotheses: Valuation with values in ℝ ∪ {∞} (Mathlib AddValuation K (WithTop ℝ)); the minimum over the support of f.
proofSteps: Define v_r(f) as the infimum over the support of f in WithTop ℝ (Finset.inf), so v_r(0) = ⊤.
Monomial: v_r(c X^n) = v(c) + r n.
Each term bounds it: v_r(f) ≤ v(a_i) + r i.
Ultrametric: v_r(f + g) ≥ min(v_r(f), v_r(g)).
r = 0 gives the Gauss valuation min_i v(a_i).
acceptance: v_r(X) = r.
v_r(X − c) = min(v(c), r) for c ≠ 0.

nodes.title: Gauss's lemma for sloped valuations
nodes.statement: For f, g ∈ K[X] and r ∈ ℝ, v_r(f g) = v_r(f) + v_r(g).
hypotheses: K a field with an additive valuation to ℝ ∪ {∞}.
proofSteps: If f or g is 0 both sides are ∞. Otherwise the coefficient of X^k in f g is Σ_{i+j=k} a_i b_j (Mathlib Polynomial.coeff_mul), each term of value v(a_i) + v(b_j) (AddValuation.map_mul), so v_r(f g) ≥ v_r(f) + v_r(g) by the ultrametric inequality (AddValuation.map_add).

Let i_0, j_0 be the least indices minimising v(a_i) + r i and v(b_j) + r j. In the coefficient of X^{i_0 + j_0} the term a_{i_0} b_{j_0} has value exactly v_r(f) + v_r(g) − r(i_0 + j_0), and every other term (i < i_0 or j < j_0) has strictly larger value; so the coefficient has that exact value and v_r(f g) ≤ v_r(f) + v_r(g).
acceptance: v_r((X − c)(X − c′)) = min(v c, r) + min(v c′, r).

nodes.title: The Newton polygon, by slope multiplicities
nodes.statement: For a nonzero f = Σ a_i X^i ∈ K[X] and r ∈ ℝ, let S_r be the set of indices i with a_i ≠ 0 attaining v_r(f) = v(a_i) + r i. The multiplicity of r as a slope of f is m_r(f) = max S_r − min S_r (the width of the edge of slope r of the Newton polygon, in the orientation in which a linear factor X − c has the single slope v(c)); m_r(0) = 0. Only finitely many r have m_r(f) > 0, and Σ_r m_r(f) = deg f − ord_0 f.
hypotheses: Orientation pinned: slopes are valuations of roots (the lower convex hull of the points (−i, v(a_i))); in the usual picture with points (i, v(a_i)) this is the negative of the geometric slope.
proofSteps: Define S_r by filtering the support of f and m_r as the difference of its largest and least element (0 if S_r is empty, i.e. f = 0).
Linear factor: for X − c with c ≠ 0 both indices attain v_r exactly when v(c) = r, so m_r = 1 if r = v(c) and 0 otherwise.
Scaling by c ≠ 0 shifts every term by v(c) and does not change S_r.
Finiteness: m_r(f) > 0 needs two indices i < i′ with v(a_i) + r i = v(a_{i′}) + r i′, which determines r; there are finitely many pairs.
Sum of widths: as r increases, the minimising index set moves from the largest to the least index of the support, and the widths of the edges add up to the length of the support interval.
acceptance: If v(π) = 1 then X² − π has m_{1/2} = 2.
m_{−1/2}(X² − π) = 0 (orientation check).
A monomial has no slopes.

nodes.title: Dumas's theorem: Newton polygons multiply
nodes.statement: For nonzero f, g ∈ K[X] and every r ∈ ℝ, m_r(f g) = m_r(f) + m_r(g): the multiset of slopes of the Newton polygon of f g is the union of those of f and g.
hypotheses: K a field with an additive valuation to ℝ ∪ {∞}; f, g ≠ 0; no completeness or splitting hypothesis.
proofSteps: By CA.3/sloped-valuation-mul the least minimising index of f g for v_r is i_0 + j_0, the sum of the least minimising indices of f and g (the proof of that lemma exhibits the term a_{i_0} b_{j_0} as the unique term of least value in its coefficient, and no smaller index attains the minimum).
Symmetrically (largest indices, same argument with the largest minimising indices) the largest minimising index of f g is the sum of the largest ones.
Subtracting: the width m_r(f g) is m_r(f) + m_r(g).

nodes.title: The Eisenstein–Dumas irreducibility criterion
nodes.statement: Let K be a field with a discrete valuation v : K → ℤ ∪ {∞} and f = Σ_{i=0}^n a_i X^i ∈ K[X] of degree n ≥ 1 with a_0 ≠ 0. Suppose gcd(v(a_0) − v(a_n), n) = 1 and n v(a_i) ≥ (n − i) v(a_0) + i v(a_n) for every i with a_i ≠ 0 (the Newton polygon is the single segment joining its endpoints). Then f is irreducible over K. Eisenstein's criterion is the case v(a_n) = 0, v(a_i) ≥ 1 for i < n, v(a_0) = 1.
hypotheses: Discrete (ℤ-valued) valuation; a_0 a_n ≠ 0; the coprimality and the lower-bound conditions (D1), (D2).
proofSteps: View v as real-valued. By (D2) the only slope of f is λ = (v(a_0) − v(a_n))/n, with m_λ(f) = n.

Suppose f = g h with deg g = k, 0 < k < n. By CA.3/dumas-theorem, g has the single slope λ with multiplicity k, so its extreme coefficients satisfy v(g_0) − v(g_k) = k λ (the edge from index 0 to k has slope λ).
v(g_0) − v(g_k) is an integer, so n divides k (v(a_0) − v(a_n)); as gcd(v(a_0) − v(a_n), n) = 1, n | k, contradicting 0 < k < n.
acceptance: X² − p over ℚ with the p-adic valuation: v(a_0) − v(a_2) = 1, coprime to 2: irreducible.
X⁴ − p²: the difference 2 is not coprime to 4 and indeed X⁴ − p² = (X² − p)(X² + p).
Eisenstein's criterion for X^n − p is the case of one segment from (0, 1) to (n, 0).

nodes.title: Integer linear systems and the parametrisation of their solutions
nodes.statement: Let A be an integer matrix with n rows and m columns and b ∈ ℤⁿ. Let P ∈ GL_n(ℤ) and Q ∈ GL_m(ℤ) be unimodular matrices with PAQ = D rectangular diagonal, D_{ii} = d_i for i < min(n, m) and all other entries 0 (a Smith normal form in the sense of CA.3, or any diagonalisation by unimodular matrices; the d_i may be 0). Write c = Pb. The integer solution set Sol(A, b) = {x ∈ ℤᵐ : Ax = b} is nonempty if and only if d_i divides c_i for every i < min(n, m) (for d_i = 0 this means c_i = 0) and c_i = 0 for every i ≥ m. When it is nonempty, Sol(A, b) = x₀ + ker(A), where x₀ = Q y₀ with (y₀)_i = c_i/d_i when d_i ≠ 0 and 0 otherwise, and ker(A) = {x ∈ ℤᵐ : Ax = 0} is the free abelian group with basis the columns Q e_j for the indices j < m with j ≥ n or d_j = 0; its rank is m − s where s is the number of nonzero d_i.
hypotheses: A and b have integer entries; no rank, squareness or nonsingularity hypothesis is made.
P and Q are invertible over ℤ (determinant ±1), not merely over ℚ; the statement is about the full solution set in ℤᵐ, not over ℚ.
The d_i need not form a divisibility chain for this statement; the Smith normal form of CA.3 is one admissible choice of (P, D, Q).
proofSteps: Substitute x = Q y. Since Q is unimodular, x ↦ Q⁻¹x is a bijection ℤᵐ → ℤᵐ, and Ax = b is equivalent to D y = c with c = P b, because P is unimodular.
Solve D y = c coordinatewise: for i < min(n, m) the equation is d_i y_i = c_i; for min(n, m) ≤ i < n it reads 0 = c_i; the coordinates y_j with j ≥ n or d_j = 0 do not occur.
Read off the solvability criterion: each d_i y_i = c_i is solvable in ℤ exactly when d_i divides c_i (with 0 ∣ c meaning c = 0), and the remaining rows force c_i = 0.
A particular solution is y₀ as in the statement; every solution is y₀ plus a vector supported on the free coordinates, so Sol(A, b) = Q y₀ + Q·(ℤ-span of e_j, j free).

The kernel is the case b = 0 of the same description, so ker(A) = Q·span{e_j : j free}, and since Q is unimodular the vectors Q e_j (j free) are linearly independent: they form a basis of ker(A), of rank m − s.

Specialise to one equation a x + b y = n (A = (a b)): with g = gcd(a, b) the criterion is g ∣ n, which is Mathlib's Int.gcd_dvd_iff, and for (a, b) ≠ (0, 0) the solution set is (x₀, y₀) + ℤ·(b/g, −a/g).
acceptance: Both halves are stated and needed: the divisibility criterion and the coset parametrisation. Mathlib proves only solvability of one equation in two unknowns (Int.gcd_dvd_iff) and neither the general criterion nor any parametrisation.
The kernel is free of rank m − s, so the solution set is a coset of a free group of that rank, not a single solution.
For 6x + 10y = 4: g = 2 divides 4, and the solutions are (−1 + 5t, 1 − 3t), t ∈ ℤ.
For 6x + 10y = 3 there is no integer solution although there is a rational one, so a criterion over ℚ is the wrong one.

nodes.title: The descent step for x⁴ − y⁴ = z² with z odd
nodes.statement: If x, y, z are pairwise coprime positive integers with x⁴ − y⁴ = z² and z odd, then there are pairwise coprime positive integers x′, y′, z′ with x′⁴ − y′⁴ = z′², z′ odd and x′ < x.
hypotheses: x, y, z > 0 and pairwise coprime; z odd.
proofSteps: Since z is odd and z² + y⁴ = x⁴, y is even (otherwise z² + y⁴ ≡ 2 mod 4), so (z, y², x²) is a primitive Pythagorean triple with even middle term: by Mathlib's PythagoreanTriple.coprime_classification' there are coprime k > ℓ > 0 of opposite parity with z = k² − ℓ², y² = 2kℓ, x² = k² + ℓ².

Then (k, ℓ, x) is again a primitive Pythagorean triple. If k is odd, apply the classification with k odd: k = a² − b², ℓ = 2ab, x = a² + b²; if ℓ is odd, ℓ = a² − b², k = 2ab, x = a² + b²; in both cases a > b > 0 are coprime of opposite parity.
In both cases y² = 2kℓ = 4ab(a² − b²), so (y/2)² = ab(a² − b²) with the three factors positive and pairwise coprime (from gcd(a, b) = 1 and opposite parity).
A product of pairwise coprime positive integers that is a square has every factor a square (Mathlib's Int.sq_of_gcd_eq_one applied twice): a = x′², b = y′², a² − b² = z′² with x′, y′, z′ > 0.
Then x′⁴ − y′⁴ = z′², gcd(x′, y′) = 1 because gcd(a, b) = 1, z′² = a² − b² is odd because a and b have opposite parity, and x′ ≤ x′² = a < a² + b² = x.
acceptance: The new solution again has z′ odd, so the step can be iterated; this is what makes the case split of the theorem close.
Remark 3.11 of the source gives x = x′⁴ + y′⁴ and y = 2x′y′z′, which a formalisation can use as an alternative size measure.

nodes.title: Fermat's right-triangle theorem: x⁴ − y⁴ = z² has no solution in positive integers
nodes.statement: There are no positive integers x, y, z with x⁴ − y⁴ = z². Equivalently, every integer solution of x⁴ − y⁴ = z² has y = 0 or z = 0.
hypotheses: x, y, z positive integers (for the equivalent integral form: x, y, z ∈ ℤ, conclusion y = 0 or z = 0).
proofSteps: Reduce to pairwise coprime solutions: a common prime factor p of x and y gives p⁴ ∣ z², so p² ∣ z, and (x/p, y/p, z/p²) is a smaller solution; a common factor of x and z (or y and z) is a common factor of x and y by the equation.
Case z odd: by strong induction on x, using the descent step (fermat-right-triangle-descent-step), which produces a solution with z′ odd and x′ < x; there is no minimal such solution.

Case z even: y⁴ + z² = x⁴ makes (y², z, x²) a primitive Pythagorean triple with z even, so y² = m² − n², x² = m² + n² with coprime m, n > 0 (Mathlib's PythagoreanTriple.coprime_classification'); multiplying, (xy)² = m⁴ − n⁴ with xy odd, which is a solution of Case z odd.
The integral form follows by taking absolute values: a solution with y ≠ 0 and z ≠ 0 has x ≠ 0 and gives a positive solution.
acceptance: No positive solution: (1, 1, 0) solves x⁴ − y⁴ = z² only with z = 0, and (5, 4, ?) does not solve it since 625 − 256 = 369 is not a square.
This is not Mathlib's not_fermat_42 (x⁴ + y⁴ = z²): the two equations belong to non-isomorphic elliptic curves, y² = x³ − x and y² = x³ + x, and neither theorem is a formal consequence of the other.
Consequence (Conrad, Corollary 3.12): no Pythagorean triple has a leg and the hypotenuse both squares.

sources.match: The theorem, verbatim.

sources.excerpt: Case 2: z is even. (This has no analogue in the proof of Theorem 3.1.) Since y4 + z2 = x4, we have a primitive Pythagorean triple (y2, z, x2) with even z.

nodes.title: The quartic descent T⁴ + V⁴ = 2U²
nodes.statement: If T, V, U are positive integers with gcd(T, V, U) = 1 and T⁴ + V⁴ = 2U², then T = V = U = 1. Equivalently (Conrad, Corollary 3.17), every integer solution of x⁴ + y⁴ = 2z² is (x, ±x, ±x²).
hypotheses: T, V, U > 0 and gcd(T, V, U) = 1. Under the equation this is equivalent to gcd(T, V) = 1: if g = gcd(T, V) then g⁴ ∣ 2U² forces g² ∣ U.
proofSteps: From gcd(T, V, U) = 1 and the equation, gcd(T, V) = 1 (the hypothesis remark); then T and V are both odd, since T⁴ + V⁴ is even and they are not both even.
Square the equation and subtract 4T⁴V⁴: (T⁴ − V⁴)² = (T⁴ + V⁴)² − 4T⁴V⁴ = 4(U⁴ − (TV)⁴). Hence T⁴ − V⁴ is even and W = (T⁴ − V⁴)/2 is an integer with U⁴ − (TV)⁴ = W².
Since U > 0 and TV > 0, the integral form of fermat-right-triangle-theorem gives W = 0.
So T⁴ = V⁴, hence T = V by positivity, hence T = V = 1 by coprimality, and U² = 1 gives U = 1.
The integral form of Corollary 3.17 follows by dividing by the fourth power of gcd(x, y) and tracking signs; y = 0 forces x = z = 0 because 2 is not a rational square.
acceptance: (1, 1, 1) is a solution, and (2, 2, 4) is a solution with gcd(T, V, U) = 2, which is why the coprimality hypothesis is needed.
Bennett–Siksek use this at the end of Case II of the proof of Proposition 6.1, where it forces λ = 1/2 and the curve to have complex multiplication by ℤ[i].
The statement is not Fermat's equation x⁴ + y⁴ = z⁴ and does not follow from Mathlib's x⁴ + y⁴ = z² theorem: the source's 'classical descent argument' is the reduction to x⁴ − y⁴ = z² given here.

nodes.title: The Markoff surface X(R) and its nonzero locus X*(R)
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, X(R) = {x = (x₀, x₁, x₂) ∈ R³ : x₀² + x₁² + x₂² = 3x₀x₁x₂}, and X*(R) = X(R) ∖ {(0, 0, 0)}. Triples are indexed by Fin 3, so that coordinate permutations are precompositions. 'Nonzero' refers to the whole triple: individual coordinates of an element of X*(R) may vanish.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring; no field, characteristic or finiteness hypothesis.
The coefficient is 3 (the coefficient-one equation x² + y² + z² = xyz is a different surface, related by scaling by 3 only when 3 is invertible).
proofSteps: Define X(R) as the zero set of Φ(x) = x₀² + x₁² + x₂² − 3x₀x₁x₂ in R³ and X*(R) as its complement of the origin.
Functoriality: a ring homomorphism f : R → S satisfies Φ(f ∘ x) = f(Φ(x)), so f ∘ x ∈ X(S) when x ∈ X(R).
Permutation invariance: Φ is a symmetric polynomial, so x ∈ X(R) iff x ∘ σ⁻¹ ∈ X(R) for σ ∈ S₃.
acceptance: (1, 1, 1), (1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 5) and (2, 5, 29) lie in X(ℤ); (3, 3, 3) does not (it solves the coefficient-one equation).
Over 𝔽₃ the equation becomes x₀² + x₁² + x₂² = 0, and X*(𝔽₃) is the eight triples in {±1}³ (the regression case recorded by the review of the Martin extraction).

sources.locator: §1, equation (1.1), arXiv v1 p. 1 (published version p. 623)
sources.excerpt: Integer solutions to the equation x₁² + x₂² + x₃² = 3x₁x₂x₃ (1.1) are known as Markoff triples.

nodes.title: The Vieta moves R₀, R₁, R₂ and the integer Markoff graph
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R and i ∈ Fin 3, R_i : R³ → R³ replaces the i-th coordinate by 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2} − x_i and keeps the other two (indices mod 3). The integer Markoff graph is the simple graph on M in which x and y are adjacent iff x ≠ y and y = R_i x for some i.
hypotheses: R commutative; the moves are defined on all of R³, not only on X(R).
Indices are taken in Fin 3 (the source's R₁, R₂, R₃ are R₀, R₁, R₂ here).
proofSteps: Define R_i x = Function.update x i (3 · x(i + 1) · x(i + 2) − x i).
Evaluation: (R_i x)_i = 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2} − x_i and (R_i x)_j = x_j for j ≠ i; hence (R_i x)_i + x_i = 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2}, the sum of the two roots of the quadratic in the i-th variable.
Naturality: for a ring homomorphism f, f ∘ R_i x = R_i (f ∘ x), because R_i is given by an integer polynomial.
The graph: adjacency is the symmetrisation of y = R_i x on M, which is symmetric already by involutivity (markoff-vieta-involutive); M is preserved by markoff-vieta-preserves-positivity.
acceptance: R_i(0) = 0 in every ring.
The graph has no loops, since adjacency requires x ≠ y; that no move fixes a vertex of M is shown in markoff-tree.

nodes.title: The Vieta moves are involutions
nodes.statement: For every commutative ring R, every i ∈ Fin 3 and every x ∈ R³, R_i(R_i x) = x.
hypotheses: R commutative; no hypothesis on x.
proofSteps: Only the i-th coordinate changes, and the other two coordinates of R_i x are those of x; so (R_i(R_i x))_i = 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2} − (3x_{i+1}x_{i+2} − x_i) = x_i.
acceptance: In particular R_i is a bijection of R³ with inverse itself, with no field assumption.

nodes.title: The Vieta moves preserve the Markoff equation
nodes.statement: For every commutative ring R, i ∈ Fin 3 and x ∈ R³: Φ(R_i x) = Φ(x), where Φ(x) = x₀² + x₁² + x₂² − 3x₀x₁x₂. In particular x ∈ X(R) ↔ R_i x ∈ X(R).
hypotheses: R commutative.
proofSteps: Write u = x_i and c = x_{i+1}x_{i+2}; then Φ(x) = u² − 3cu + (x_{i+1}² + x_{i+2}²) and Φ(R_i x) is the same expression at u′ = 3c − u; the quadratic t² − 3ct + e takes equal values at u and 3c − u (a polynomial identity).
acceptance: The polynomial identity holds before imposing Φ = 0, which is why it is valid over every ring.

nodes.title: The Vieta moves permute X*(R)
nodes.statement: For every commutative ring R and i ∈ Fin 3, R_i restricts to a bijection X*(R) → X*(R), equal to its own inverse.
hypotheses: R commutative; no assumption that the coordinates of x are nonzero.
proofSteps: R_i maps X(R) into X(R) (markoff-vieta-preserves-equation).
R_i(0) = 0 and R_i is injective (markoff-vieta-involutive), so R_i x = 0 only for x = 0; hence R_i maps X*(R) into X*(R).
Involutivity gives the inverse.
acceptance: Over 𝔽₅, R₀ maps (0, 1, 2) ∈ X*(𝔽₅) to (1, 1, 2), which is again in X*(𝔽₅).

nodes.title: Coordinate permutations normalise the Vieta moves
nodes.statement: For σ ∈ S₃ let P_σ x = x ∘ σ⁻¹, so that (P_σ x)_{σ(i)} = x_i. Then P_σ preserves X(R), X*(R) and M, and P_σ ∘ R_i = R_{σ(i)} ∘ P_σ for every i.
hypotheses: R commutative; the convention (P_σ x)_{σ(i)} = x_i is pinned.
proofSteps: Φ is symmetric, so P_σ preserves X(R); P_σ fixes 0 and is bijective, so it preserves X*(R); it preserves positivity of all coordinates, so it preserves M.

Both sides of P_σ R_i x = R_{σ(i)} P_σ x agree at σ(i): the left gives (R_i x)_i = 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2} − x_i, and the right gives 3·x_{σ⁻¹(σ(i)+1)}x_{σ⁻¹(σ(i)+2)} − x_i, where {σ⁻¹(σ(i)+1), σ⁻¹(σ(i)+2)} = {i+1, i+2}.
At the other two coordinates both sides agree with P_σ x.
acceptance: For the transposition σ = (0 2): P_σ R₀ = R₂ P_σ, and P_σ(1, 1, 2) = (2, 1, 1).
The relation is the one needed to compare the Vieta group with the Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak group Γ generated by the moves and the permutations.

nodes.title: The other root is positive: the moves preserve M
nodes.statement: If x ∈ M and i ∈ Fin 3, then R_i x ∈ M; moreover (R_i x)_i · x_i = x_{i+1}² + x_{i+2}² > 0.
hypotheses: x ∈ M.
proofSteps: The i-th coordinate of R_i x and x_i are the two roots of t² − 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2}t + (x_{i+1}² + x_{i+2}²), so their product is x_{i+1}² + x_{i+2}² by Vieta's formulas (equivalently, by expanding with the equation).
Since x_i > 0 and the product is positive, (R_i x)_i > 0; the other coordinates are unchanged, and R_i x ∈ X(ℤ) by markoff-vieta-preserves-equation.
acceptance: The statement fails for signed solutions only through the sign pattern: R_i preserves the sign pattern of x.

sources.excerpt: we have c + c′ = 3ab and cc′ = a² + b². Thus c′ = 3ab − c is a positive integer and (a, b, c′) is another solution triple to (1) in positive integers, that is, a Markoff triple.
sources.match: Positivity of the other root.

nodes.title: The descent inequality for positive Markoff triples
nodes.statement: Let 1 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ c be integers with a² + b² + c² = 3abc and (a, b, c) ≠ (1, 1, 1). Then c′ = 3ab − c satisfies 0 < c′ ≤ b and c′ < c, with c′ = b only for (a, b, c) = (1, 1, 2). Moreover b < c, so c is the unique largest coordinate, and the other two moves strictly increase the largest coordinate: 3bc − a > c and 3ac − b > c.
hypotheses: (a, b, c) ordered increasingly, positive, not (1, 1, 1).
proofSteps: Let q(t) = t² − 3abt + a² + b², whose roots are c and c′ = 3ab − c; c′ > 0 by markoff-vieta-preserves-positivity.
q(b) = a² + (2 − 3a)b² ≤ a² − b² ≤ 0, with equality iff a = b = 1; in that case c² − 3c + 2 = 0 gives c ∈ {1, 2}, so (a, b, c) = (1, 1, 2), c′ = 1 = b.
Otherwise q(b) < 0, so b lies strictly between the roots; as c ≥ b, c is the larger root and c′ < b < c.
If b = c then q(b) = 0, which forces (1, 1, 1) or c = 2 ≠ b; hence b < c in all cases considered.
For the other moves: 3bc − a ≥ 3c − a > c and 3ac − b ≥ 3c − b > c, since a, b < 2c.
acceptance: Every nonroot ordered positive triple therefore has exactly one descending move, in its unique largest coordinate (item 9 of the paper extraction).

nodes.title: Markoff's theorem: every positive Markoff triple comes from (1, 1, 1)
nodes.statement: Every x ∈ M is obtained from (1, 1, 1) by a finite word in the moves R₀, R₁, R₂: there are i₁, …, i_k ∈ Fin 3 with x = R_{i₁} ⋯ R_{i_k}(1, 1, 1). No coordinate permutation is needed.
hypotheses: x ∈ M.
proofSteps: Strong induction on the largest coordinate max(x).
If x = (1, 1, 1) take the empty word.

Otherwise let i be the position of the unique largest coordinate (markoff-descent-inequality applied to the increasing rearrangement of x); R_i x ∈ M has smaller largest coordinate, so R_i x is a word applied to (1, 1, 1), and x = R_i(R_i x) by markoff-vieta-involutive.
acceptance: Consequently M is the orbit of (1, 1, 1) under the group generated by the moves, and a fortiori under Γ (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak).

nodes.title: The positive Markoff graph is a tree rooted at (1, 1, 1)
nodes.statement: The integer Markoff graph (vertices M, x adjacent to y iff x ≠ y and y = R_i x for some i) is a tree. Every vertex has degree exactly 3, and every vertex other than (1, 1, 1) has exactly one neighbour with smaller largest coordinate.
hypotheses: Vertices are ordered positive triples; the statement is false for the signed nonzero integer solutions, whose graph is a disjoint union of four copies of this tree (one for each sign pattern with product +1).
proofSteps: Connected: by markoff-root-generation every vertex is joined to (1, 1, 1) by the path of successive words.

Degree 3: the three moves change three different coordinates, and no move fixes a vertex of M ((R_i x)_i = x_i would give 2x_i = 3x_{i+1}x_{i+2} and x_i² = x_{i+1}² + x_{i+2}², hence 9x_{i+1}²x_{i+2}² = 4(x_{i+1}² + x_{i+2}²), impossible for positive integers).

Height function h(x) = max(x): along every edge h changes (a move changes one coordinate to a different value and the descent inequality compares the maxima), and every vertex x ≠ (1, 1, 1) has exactly one neighbour with smaller h (markoff-descent-inequality: the move in the unique largest coordinate decreases h, the other two increase it; for the permutations of (1, 1, 2) the descending neighbour is (1, 1, 1)).

Acyclic: in a cycle, a vertex of maximal h has two distinct neighbours on the cycle with smaller h, contradicting uniqueness of the descending neighbour; so the graph is a tree (Mathlib's SimpleGraph.IsTree: connected and acyclic).
acceptance: This is the positive-triple form of the statement the source attributes to Markoff; the finite-field graphs G_p of the Part II are not trees.

nodes.title: The coordinates of a positive Markoff triple are pairwise coprime
nodes.statement: If (a, b, c) ∈ M then gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, c) = gcd(a, c) = 1.
hypotheses: (a, b, c) ∈ M.
proofSteps: From the equation, gcd(a, b) divides c², and in fact gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, c) = gcd(c, a) = gcd(a, b, c) (a prime dividing two coordinates divides the square of the third and hence the third).
gcd(a, b, c) is invariant under each move, since gcd(a, b, 3ab − c) = gcd(a, b, c); by markoff-root-generation it equals gcd(1, 1, 1) = 1.
acceptance: Consequently no prime divides all three coordinates, so the reduction of x ∈ M modulo a prime p is never (0, 0, 0).

nodes.title: Reduction of Markoff triples modulo p
nodes.statement: For a natural number p, red_p : ℤ³ → (ℤ/pℤ)³ is coordinatewise reduction. It maps X(ℤ) into X(ℤ/pℤ), commutes with every move R_i and every coordinate permutation P_σ, sends (1, 1, 1) to (1, 1, 1), and for p prime it maps M into X*(𝔽_p).
hypotheses: p ≥ 2 for the last clause (for p = 1 the ring is trivial and X*(ℤ/1ℤ) is empty); the first clauses hold for every p.
proofSteps: red_p = (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p)) ∘ −; the first clause is functoriality of X (markoff-triples), the commutation with moves is naturality of R_i (markoff-vieta-involution), and the commutation with permutations is immediate.

Nonzero image for p prime: by markoff-triple-coordinates-coprime no prime divides all coordinates of x ∈ M, so red_p x ≠ 0; alternatively, by markoff-root-generation x is a word applied to (1, 1, 1), red_p x is the same word applied to (1, 1, 1) ∈ X*(𝔽_p), and the moves preserve X*(𝔽_p) (markoff-vieta-permutes-nonzero-locus).
Reduction may collapse an edge: distinct neighbours in M can reduce to the same triple, and R_i may fix a triple modulo p.

nodes.title: Strong approximation for positive Markoff triples at a prime
nodes.statement: For a prime p, strong approximation holds at p if the reduction red_p : M → X*(𝔽_p) is surjective: every nonzero solution of x₀² + x₁² + x₂² = 3x₀x₁x₂ over 𝔽_p lifts to a positive Markoff triple. Only the definition is planned here; the theorems about it (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, Chen, Martin) belong to the ArithmeticDynamics Part II.
hypotheses: p prime; the target is X*(𝔽_p), not X(𝔽_p): the origin is never the reduction of an element of M.
proofSteps: Define the predicate as surjectivity of red_p from M onto X*(𝔽_p) (Set.SurjOn).

Equivalent orbit form: by markoff-root-generation and the commutation of red_p with the moves, the image of M is the orbit of (1, 1, 1) under the group generated by the moves acting on X*(𝔽_p); so strong approximation at p holds iff that orbit is all of X*(𝔽_p).
acceptance: Strong approximation holds at p = 2 and p = 3 (by the lifts in the tests).
Surjectivity onto X(𝔽_p) always fails, since (0, 0, 0) is not a reduction of M.

nodes.title: Integers of the form 4ᵃ(8b + 7) are not sums of three squares
nodes.statement: If n = 4ᵃ(8b + 7) with a, b ∈ ℕ, then there are no integers x, y, z with x² + y² + z² = n.
hypotheses: a, b ∈ ℕ.
proofSteps: Squares are ≡ 0, 1 or 4 (mod 8), so a sum of three squares is never ≡ 7 (mod 8): this is the case a = 0.
Squares are ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4), so x² + y² + z² ≡ 0 (mod 4) forces x, y, z all even; then (x/2)² + (y/2)² + (z/2)² = 4^{a−1}(8b + 7), and induction on a finishes.
acceptance: 7, 15, 23, 28 = 4·7 and 60 = 4·15 are not sums of three squares; 12 = 4·3 is (2² + 2² + 2²).

nodes.title: Reduction of the three-square theorem to squarefree m ≢ 7 (mod 8)
nodes.statement: If n ≥ 1 is not of the form 4ᵃ(8b + 7), then n = 4ᵃ k² m with a ∈ ℕ, k odd and m squarefree with m mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}. Consequently, if every squarefree m with m mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6} is a sum of three squares, so is every such n.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1 not of the form 4ᵃ(8b + 7).
proofSteps: Write n = 4ᵃ n′ with 4 ∤ n′; then n′ is not ≡ 7 (mod 8).
Write n′ = k² m with m squarefree (Mathlib's Nat.sq_mul_squarefree_of_pos). If k were even, 4 would divide n′; so k is odd, k² ≡ 1 (mod 8) and m ≡ n′ (mod 8).
m is squarefree, so 4 ∤ m, and m ≢ 7 (mod 8): hence m mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}.
A representation m = x² + y² + z² gives n = (2ᵃkx)² + (2ᵃky)² + (2ᵃkz)².
acceptance: n = 28 is excluded; n = 44 = 4·11 gives m = 11 ≡ 3 (mod 8).

nodes.title: Ankeny's auxiliary prime
nodes.statement: Let m be a squarefree positive integer with m mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}. Then there is a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) such that: (a) if m ≡ 3 (mod 8), the Jacobi symbol (−2q/p) = 1 for every prime p ∣ m; (b) otherwise (−q/p) = 1 for every odd prime p ∣ m, and, if m = 2m₁ is even, (−2/q) = (−1)^{(m₁−1)/2}. In both cases the Jacobi symbol (−m/q) = 1, so −m is a quadratic residue modulo q.
hypotheses: m squarefree, m ≥ 1, m mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}.
proofSteps: Each condition on q is a condition on q modulo 4 or 8 and modulo the odd primes p ∣ m, and each is satisfied by a nonempty set of residue classes prime to p (half of the nonzero classes modulo p satisfy (−2r/p) = 1, respectively (−r/p) = 1, and (−2/q) is fixed by q mod 8); by the Chinese remainder theorem these conditions define a nonempty set of unit residue classes modulo 8m.
Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions (Mathlib's Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_eq_mod) gives a prime q in such a class, which may be taken larger than m so that q ∤ m.

Case (a): 1 = ∏_{p∣m}(−2q/p) = (−2/m)∏(q/p) = (−2/m)∏(p/q) = (−2/m)(m/q) = (−2/m)(−m/q) = (−m/q), using quadratic reciprocity for q ≡ 1 (mod 4) (Mathlib's jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity_one_mod_four), (−1/q) = 1, and (−2/m) = 1 for m ≡ 3 (mod 8) (jacobiSym.at_neg_two).

Case (b): (q/p) = (−1/p) for odd p ∣ m, so ∏_{p odd}(p/q) = (−1/m_odd) = (−1)^{(m_odd−1)/2} by reciprocity and jacobiSym.at_neg_one; for m odd this gives (−m/q) = (m/q) = (−1)^{(m−1)/2} = 1 as m ≡ 1 (mod 4); for m = 2m₁ it gives (−m/q) = (2/q)(−1)^{(m₁−1)/2} = 1 because (2/q) = (−2/q) for q ≡ 1 (mod 4).
acceptance: m = 3: the conditions say q ≡ 1 (mod 12). q = 13 works, and (−3/13) = 1 since 6² ≡ −3 (mod 13); q = 5 fails, since (−10/3) = (2/3) = −1.
m = 1: the conditions are vacuous apart from q ≡ 1 (mod 4), and (−1/q) = 1.

nodes.title: The Minkowski step in Ankeny's proof
nodes.statement: Let m and q be as in three-squares-auxiliary-prime. (a) If m ≡ 3 (mod 8), there are integers b (odd) and h with b² − 4qh = −m, and integers R, x, y such that R² + 2v = m for v = qx² + bxy + hy²; moreover 4qv = (2qx + by)² + my². (b) Otherwise there are integers b, h with b² − qh = −m and integers R, x, y such that R² + v = m for v = qx² + 2bxy + hy²; moreover qv = (qx + by)² + my². In both cases v ≥ 0.
hypotheses: m, q as in the auxiliary prime lemma.
proofSteps: Choose b with b² ≡ −m (mod q) (possible since (−m/q) = 1), odd in case (a); set h₁ = (b² + m)/q. In case (a), reducing modulo 4 with b odd, q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and m ≡ 3 (mod 8) gives 4 ∣ h₁; put h = h₁/4. In case (b) put h = h₁.
Choose t with t² ≡ −1/(2q) (mod m) in case (a) (possible by (−2q/p) = 1 for p ∣ m and the Chinese remainder theorem), respectively t odd with t² ≡ −1/q (mod p) for odd p ∣ m in case (b).

Case (a): R = 2tqx + tby + mz, S = (2q)^{1/2}x + b(2q)^{−1/2}y, T = m^{1/2}(2q)^{−1/2}y. This linear map ℤ³ → ℝ³ has determinant m^{3/2}; the ball R² + S² + T² < 2m has volume (4π/3)(2m)^{3/2}, so its preimage is a convex symmetric body of volume (4π/3)·2^{3/2} > 8. By Minkowski's convex body theorem (Mathlib's MeasureTheory.exists_ne_zero_mem_lattice_of_measure_mul_two_pow_lt_measure, with the volume from InnerProductSpace.volume_ball and MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_image_linearMap) there is a nonzero (x, y, z) ∈ ℤ³ with R² + S² + T² < 2m. Case (b): the same with R = tqx + tby + mz, S = q^{1/2}x + bq^{−1/2}y, T = m^{1/2}q^{−1/2}y.
Algebra: S² + T² = 2v in case (a) and = v in case (b), because b² + m = 4qh (resp. qh); and 4qv = (2qx + by)² + my² (resp. qv = (qx + by)² + my²).

Congruence: R ≡ t(2qx + by) (mod m) gives R² + 2v ≡ −(2qx + by)²/(2q) + (2qx + by)²/(2q) ≡ 0 (mod m) in case (a); in case (b) the same computation modulo each odd p ∣ m, and modulo 2 when m is even: with t odd, R² + v ≡ 0 (mod 2) whether b is odd or even.
So m ∣ R² + 2v (resp. R² + v); this number is positive because the triangular transformation is nondegenerate and (x, y, z) ≠ 0, and it is less than 2m; hence it equals m.
acceptance: For m = 3, q = 13: b = 7 (odd, 49 + 3 = 52 = 4·13·1, so h = 1) and t = 1 (t² ≡ −1/26 ≡ 1 mod 3); the lattice point (x, y, z) = (0, 1, −2) gives R = 1, v = 13·0 + 7·0 + 1 = 1 and R² + S² + T² = 3 < 6, so R² + 2v = 3 = m.
The body has volume (4π/3)2^{3/2} ≈ 11.85 > 8 = 2³, the Minkowski threshold in dimension 3.

sources.excerpt: In the (R, S, T) space (7) defines a convex, symmetric (about the origin) body of volume 4/3π(2m)^{3/2}. The determinant of the transformations (8) is m^{3/2}. Hence, in the (x, y, z) space, (7) represents a convex symmetric body of volume 1/3(2^{7/2}π), and certainly 1/3(2^{7/2}π) > 8.

sources.excerpt: We note that R₁ is a rational integer and by (9), (10), and (11) that m | R₁² + 2v, but by (7) R₁² + 2v < 2m. Furthermore R₁² + 2v ≠ 0, by the nondegenerate triangular transformation (8) and the fact that not all x₁, y₁, z₁ equal zero. Hence, (12) R₁² + 2v = m.

nodes.title: The remainder in Ankeny's proof is a sum of two squares
nodes.statement: In the situation of three-squares-lattice-point, every odd prime p that divides v to an odd power satisfies p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Hence 2v (case m ≡ 3 mod 8), respectively v (other cases), is a sum of two squares of integers.
hypotheses: m, q, b, h, R, x, y as in three-squares-lattice-point.
proofSteps: Let p be odd with v_p(v) odd. If p ∤ m: from R² + 2v = m (resp. R² + v = m), R² ≡ m (mod p), so (m/p) = 1.

Still p ∤ m: if p = q, then (−m/q) = 1 by the choice of b. If p ≠ q, p divides X² + mY² = 4qv (resp. qv) to an odd power, with X = 2qx + by (resp. qx + by), Y = y; dividing out p² while p divides both X and Y (then p² divides the sum) leaves p ∤ Y with p ∣ X² + mY², so (−m/p) = 1.

If p ∣ m: from R² + 2v = m, p ∣ R, and dividing R² + (1/2q)((2qx + by)² + my²) = m (resp. R² + (1/q)((qx + by)² + my²) = m) shows p ∣ 2qx + by (resp. qx + by); since m is squarefree, dividing by p gives y² ≡ 2q (mod p) (resp. y² ≡ q), so (2q/p) = 1 (resp. (q/p) = 1) unless p ∣ y, which would force p ∣ q; combined with (−2q/p) = 1 (resp. (−q/p) = 1) this gives (−1/p) = 1.
So the exponent of every prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) in v (and in 2v) is even, and Mathlib's Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff gives the representation as a sum of two squares.
acceptance: In the example m = 3, q = 13 of the previous lemma, 2v = 2 = 1² + 1², and 3 = 1² + 1² + 1².
The argument never needs p = 2, which is harmless for sums of two squares.

nodes.title: Legendre's three-square theorem
nodes.statement: A natural number n is a sum of three squares of integers if and only if n is not of the form 4ᵃ(8b + 7) with a, b ∈ ℕ.
hypotheses: n ∈ ℕ; squares of integers (equivalently of natural numbers).
proofSteps: Only if: three-squares-necessary-condition.
If: n = 0 is 0² + 0² + 0²; for n ≥ 1, three-squares-squarefree-reduction reduces to squarefree m with m mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}, which is three-squares-squarefree-case.
acceptance: 7, 15, 23, 28, 31, 39, 47, 55, 60, 63 are the numbers below 64 that are not sums of three squares.
Every n ≡ 3 (mod 8) is a sum of three odd squares (a consequence of the theorem and the parity of squares), e.g. 11 = 9 + 1 + 1.
The theorem is not in Mathlib or Tau Ceti; Mathlib has the two-square characterisation (Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff) and the four-square theorem (Nat.sum_four_squares).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. If m is a positive integer not of the form 4ᵃ(8w+7), then m is the sum of three squares.

sources.excerpt: Three-Square-Theorem (Legendre, 1797; Gauss, 1801). n ∈ N = {0, 1, 2, . . . } can be written as the sum of three squares if and only if it is not of the form 4ᵏ(8l + 7) with k, l ∈ N.

nodes.title: The representation numbers r_k(n)
nodes.statement: For k, n ∈ ℕ, r_k(n) is the number of x ∈ ℤᵏ with x₁² + ⋯ + x_k² = n, counting order and signs. It is finite, since every coordinate satisfies |x_i| ≤ √n.
hypotheses: Ordered representations with signs, including zero coordinates.
proofSteps: Define r_k(n) = Nat.card {x : Fin k → ℤ // ∑ x_i² = n}; the set is contained in the finite box |x_i| ≤ n.
Convolution: splitting ℤ^{k+l} = ℤᵏ × ℤˡ gives r_{k+l}(n) = Σ_{a+b=n} r_k(a) r_l(b); equivalently the generating function Σ_n r_k(n)xⁿ is θ(x)ᵏ with θ(x) = Σ_{m∈ℤ} x^{m²}.

nodes.title: The number of Gaussian integers of norm n, divided by 4, is multiplicative
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 let ρ(n) = r₂(n)/4. Then r₂(n) = #{α ∈ ℤ[i] : N(α) = n} is divisible by 4, ρ(n) is the number of associate classes of Gaussian integers of norm n, and ρ is multiplicative: ρ(mn) = ρ(m)ρ(n) for coprime m, n.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; m, n coprime for multiplicativity.
proofSteps: (x, y) ↦ x + yi identifies the representations of n with the Gaussian integers of norm n (Mathlib's Zsqrtd.norm for d = −1).
The unit group {±1, ±i} acts freely on the nonzero Gaussian integers and preserves the norm, so r₂(n) = 4ρ(n) with ρ(n) the number of associate classes.

ℤ[i] is a Euclidean domain, hence a unique factorisation domain (Mathlib's GaussianInt instances). For coprime m, n, every α of norm mn factors, uniquely up to units, as α = βγ with N(β) = m and N(γ) = n: group the prime factors of α according to whether the rational prime below them divides m or n.
Hence (β, γ) ↦ βγ induces a bijection between pairs of associate classes of norms m and n and associate classes of norm mn.
acceptance: ρ is not completely multiplicative: ρ(25) = 3 ≠ 4 = ρ(5)².

sources.excerpt: By unique factorisation in Z[i], the latter sum has an Euler product expansion: Σ_{0≠α∈Z[i]} 1/N(α)ˢ = 4 ∏_{π∈Pi} 1/(1 − N(π)⁻ˢ), where the product is over all prime elements π of Z[i], choosing one from each set of four associate primes, and the factor of 4 allows for the unit factor

nodes.title: The number of associate classes of Gaussian integers of prime-power norm
nodes.statement: With ρ as in gaussian-norm-count-multiplicative and k ≥ 0: ρ(2ᵏ) = 1; ρ(pᵏ) = k + 1 for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4); ρ(qᵏ) = 1 if k is even and 0 if k is odd, for primes q ≡ 3 (mod 4). In every case ρ(pᵏ) = Σ_{j=0}^{k} χ₄(p)ʲ, where χ₄ is the nontrivial character modulo 4 (χ₄(2) = 0).
hypotheses: p prime, k ∈ ℕ.
proofSteps: Classification of Gaussian primes (Wuthrich, Proposition 5.7): 1 + i is the unique prime of norm 2 up to units; for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) there are exactly two non-associate primes π, π̄ of norm p (Mathlib's Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq gives p = a² + b²); for q ≡ 3 (mod 4), q is prime in ℤ[i] (Mathlib's GaussianInt.prime_iff_mod_four_eq_three_of_nat_prime), of norm q².

An element of norm pᵏ is, up to units, a product of primes above p with norms multiplying to pᵏ: (1 + i)ᵏ for p = 2; π^j π̄^{k−j} for j = 0, …, k when p ≡ 1 (mod 4); q^{k/2} when q ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k even, and none when k is odd.
Compare with Σ_{j≤k} χ₄(p)ʲ, which is 1 for p = 2, k + 1 for χ₄(p) = 1, and (1 + (−1)ᵏ)/2 for χ₄(p) = −1.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 5.7. Up to associates, the Gaussian primes are the following : • 1 + i is a Gaussian prime of norm 2. • For each prime number p ≡ 1 (mod 4) there are exactly two Gaussian primes π and π̄ of norm p. • Each prime number q ≡ 3 (mod 4) is a Gaussian prime of norm q².

nodes.title: Jacobi's two-square theorem
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1, r₂(n) = 4 Σ_{d∣n} χ₄(d) = 4(d₁(n) − d₃(n)), where χ₄ is the nontrivial Dirichlet character modulo 4 and d_j(n) is the number of divisors of n congruent to j modulo 4.
proofSteps: Both n ↦ r₂(n)/4 (gaussian-norm-count-multiplicative) and n ↦ Σ_{d∣n} χ₄(d) (a Dirichlet convolution of multiplicative functions, Mathlib's ArithmeticFunction.IsMultiplicative.mul) are multiplicative.
They agree on prime powers by gaussian-norm-count-prime-power, since Σ_{d∣pᵏ} χ₄(d) = Σ_{j≤k} χ₄(p)ʲ.
Mathlib's ArithmeticFunction.IsMultiplicative.eq_iff_eq_on_prime_powers concludes.
acceptance: Consequence: d₁(n) ≥ d₃(n) for every n ≥ 1, and for a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) the representation p = a² + b² with 0 < a < b is unique.

nodes.title: Hirschhorn's coalescence identity for ∏(1 − xⁿ)⁶
hypotheses: Identity of formal power series; each coefficient on the right is a finite sum and an integer.
proofSteps: Square Jacobi's identity ∏(1 − xⁿ)³ = ½ Σ_{n∈ℤ} (−1)ⁿ(2n + 1)x^{(n²+n)/2} (supplied by QSeriesPartitionsAndMockModularForms:QM.0) to get ¼ Σ_{m,n}(−1)^{m+n}(2m + 1)(2n + 1)x^{(m²+n²+m+n)/2}.

Split according to the parity of m + n. For m ≡ n put r = (m + n)/2, s = (m − n)/2; for m ≢ n put r = (m − n − 1)/2, s = (m + n + 1)/2. Each substitution is a bijection onto ℤ², the exponent becomes r² + r + s², and the signed coefficient becomes (2r + 1)² − (2s)² in both cases.
The two sums coalesce into twice the same sum, giving the factor ½.
acceptance: Constant coefficient: the pairs with r² + r + s² = 0 are (0, 0) and (−1, 0), each contributing 1, so the right side has constant term ½·2 = 1.
Coefficient of x: pairs (0, ±1), (−1, ±1) give ½·4·(1 − 4) = −6, matching (1 − x)⁶ = 1 − 6x + ⋯.

sources.excerpt: In the first sum, set r = ½(m + n), s = ½(m − n), and in the second set r = ½(m − n − 1), s = ½(m + n + 1), and, remarkably, the two sums coalesce to give ∏(1 − xⁿ)⁶ = ½ Σ_{r,s=−∞}^{∞} ((2r + 1)² − (2s)²)x^{r²+s²+r}.
sources.match: The identity and its proof.

nodes.title: Hirschhorn's product-rule identity
hypotheses: Identity of formal power series; x^{j}/(1 + x^{j}) denotes the power series Σ_{t≥1}(−1)^{t−1}x^{jt}.
proofSteps: Split the right side of hirschhorn-sixth-power-identity as ½(Σ_s x^{s²} · (1 + 4x d/dx)Σ_r x^{r²+r} − Σ_r x^{r²+r} · 4x d/dx Σ_s x^{s²}), using (2r + 1)²x^{r²+r} = (1 + 4x d/dx)x^{r²+r} and (2s)²x^{s²} = 4x d/dx x^{s²}.
Substitute the product forms Σ_s x^{s²} = ∏(1 + x^{2n−1})²(1 − x^{2n}) and Σ_r x^{r²+r} = 2∏(1 + x^{2n})²(1 − x^{2n}) (both consequences of the Jacobi triple product identity, supplied by QM.0).

Apply the product rule in logarithmic-derivative form, x d/dx log ∏(1 + x^j)^{e} = e Σ j x^j/(1 + x^j) and x d/dx log ∏(1 − x^j)^{e} = −e Σ j x^j/(1 − x^j), and collect terms: the Σ 2n x^{2n}/(1 − x^{2n}) terms cancel.
acceptance: Both sides have constant term 1 and coefficient of x equal to −6: on the right, 1 − 8·1 contributes −8 and the product contributes 2 (from (1 + x)²).

sources.excerpt: Making use of the triple-product identity, we obtain ∏(1 − xⁿ)⁶ = ½{∏(1 + x^{2n−1})²(1 − x^{2n}) × (1 + 4x d/dx)2∏(1 + x^{2n})²(1 − x^{2n}) − 2∏(1 + x^{2n})²(1 − x^{2n}) × 4x d/dx ∏(1 + x^{2n−1})²(1 − x^{2n})}.
