nodes.title: θ(x)⁴ as a Lambert series
hypotheses: Identity of formal power series; nxⁿ/(1 − xⁿ) = Σ_{t≥1} n x^{nt}.
proofSteps: Divide hirschhorn-logarithmic-derivative-identity by ∏(1 + xⁿ)⁴(1 − xⁿ)² = ∏(1 + x^{2n−1})²(1 + x^{2n})²(1 − x^{2n})² to get ∏((1 − xⁿ)/(1 + xⁿ))⁴ = 1 − 8Σ((2n − 1)x^{2n−1}/(1 + x^{2n−1}) − 2nx^{2n}/(1 + x^{2n})).
Use Gauss's identity ∏(1 − xⁿ)/(1 + xⁿ) = Σ_{n∈ℤ}(−1)ⁿx^{n²} (a consequence of the triple product identity, supplied by QM.0) and substitute −x for x.
The difference Σ nxⁿ/(1 − xⁿ) − Σ 4nx^{4n}/(1 − x^{4n}) is Σ_{4∤n} nxⁿ/(1 − xⁿ).
acceptance: Coefficient of x: 8·1 = 8 = r₄(1). Coefficient of x⁴: 8(1 + 2) = 24 = r₄(4) (the divisor 4 is excluded).

sources.excerpt: Now, it is a simple consequence of the triple-product identity that ∏((1 − xⁿ)/(1 + xⁿ)) = Σ_{−∞}^{∞}(−1)ⁿx^{n²}
sources.match: The identity used in the second proof step.

sources.excerpt: or, (Σ_{−∞}^{∞} x^{n²})⁴ = 1 + 8 Σ_{4∤n} nxⁿ/(1 − xⁿ) from which Theorem 1 follows directly.
sources.match: The statement of the lemma.

nodes.title: Jacobi's four-square theorem
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1, r₄(n) = 8 Σ_{d∣n, 4∤d} d. Equivalently r₄(n) = 8σ(n) for n odd and r₄(n) = 24σ(n_odd) for n even, where n_odd is the odd part of n.
proofSteps: The generating function Σ_n r₄(n)xⁿ is θ(x)⁴ with θ(x) = Σ_{m∈ℤ} x^{m²} (sumSquaresCount_add of sum-of-squares-representation-count).
The coefficient of xⁿ in Σ_{4∤m} m x^m/(1 − x^m) is Σ_{m∣n, 4∤m} m.
Compare coefficients in theta-fourth-power-lambert-series.
acceptance: It implies Lagrange's four-square theorem (r₄(n) ≥ 8 > 0), which Mathlib already has as Nat.sum_four_squares.
The two forms of the formula agree: for n = 12, 8(1 + 2 + 3 + 6) = 96 = 24σ(3).

sources.excerpt: The number r₄(n) of representations of the positive integer n as a sum of four squares is given by r₄(n) = 8 Σ_{d|n, 4∤d} d.
sources.match: The theorem, verbatim.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 5.14 (Jacobi). Let n ⩾ 1 be an integer. Let Aₙ be the number of solutions x, y, z, w ∈ Z to the equation x² + y² + z² + w² = n.
sources.match: The equivalent odd/even form of the formula, stated without proof in this source.

nodes.title: The solution set of the generalised Pell equation x² − dy² = n
nodes.statement: For d, n ∈ ℤ, S(d, n) = {z ∈ ℤ[√d] : N(z) = n}, where ℤ[√d] is Mathlib's Zsqrtd d and N(x + y√d) = x² − dy² is Zsqrtd.norm. Its elements are identified with the integer solutions (x, y) of x² − dy² = n. The group of solutions of the Pell equation (Mathlib's Pell.Solution₁ d, the elements of norm 1) acts on S(d, n) by multiplication; an orbit is a class of 'Pell multiples'.
hypotheses: d, n ∈ ℤ arbitrary in the definition; the finiteness theorems assume d > 0 not a square and n ≠ 0.
proofSteps: Define S(d, n) as the fibre of the multiplicative map Zsqrtd.norm over n.

Multiplicativity of the norm (Mathlib's Zsqrtd.norm_mul) gives S(d, n)·S(d, n′) ⊆ S(d, nn′) and the action of S(d, 1) = Pell.Solution₁ d on S(d, n) (the identification S(d, 1) = unitary elements is Zsqrtd.norm_eq_one_iff_mem_unitary).
Conjugation x + y√d ↦ x − y√d and negation preserve S(d, n).
acceptance: S(3, −1) is empty (reduce mod 3), S(34, −1) is empty although x² − 34y² = −1 has rational solutions such as (5/3, 1/3).

uses.where: Conrad, Pell's equation II, Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.5
uses.how: every element of S(d, n) is a Pell multiple of one in an explicit box
S(d, −1) ∪ S(d, 1) is a cyclic group up to sign when S(d, −1) is nonempty
positive elements of S(d, n) with |n| < √d come from convergents of √d
Pell-type equations x² − (a² − 1)y² = 1 and their norm-n variants enter the Diophantine definition of exponentiation

tests.name: pellNormSet_three_neg_one
tests.statement: S(3, −1) = ∅: x² ≡ −1 (mod 3) is impossible.

tests.name: pellNormSet_one_compat
tests.statement: z ∈ S(d, 1) ↔ z ∈ unitary (ℤ√d), the carrier of Mathlib's Pell.Solution₁ d.

api.name: pellNormSet
api.statement: S(d, n) = {z : ℤ√d | Zsqrtd.norm z = n}.

api.name: mem_pellNormSet_iff
api.statement: ⟨x, y⟩ ∈ S(d, n) ↔ x² − d·y² = n.

api.name: pellNormSet.mul_mem
api.statement: z ∈ S(d, n) → w ∈ S(d, n′) → z·w ∈ S(d, n·n′).

api.name: pellNormSet.solution_mul_mem
api.statement: For a : Pell.Solution₁ d and z ∈ S(d, n), a·z ∈ S(d, n); this is a MulAction of Pell.Solution₁ d on S(d, n).

api.name: pellNormSet.star_mem
api.statement: z ∈ S(d, n) → conj(z) ∈ S(d, n), and −z ∈ S(d, n).

api.name: pellNormSet_one
api.statement: S(d, 1) is the set of elements of Mathlib's unitary submonoid, i.e. the image of Pell.Solution₁ d.

api.name: pellNormSet_zero
api.statement: For d not a square, S(d, 0) = {0}.

sources.excerpt: The key algebraic idea is that solutions to x² − dy² = n remain solutions when multiplied by solutions of x² − dy² = 1: if a² − db² = 1 and x² − dy² = n then the coefficients of the product x′ + y′√d := (a + b√d)(x + y√d) satisfy x′² − dy′² = n
sources.match: The set S(d, n) and the action of the Pell solutions.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 7.1. If x² − dy² = n and x′² − dy′² = n′ then the coefficients of (x + y√d)(x′ + y′√d) are a solution of X² − dY² = nn′.
sources.match: The multiplicativity API item.

nodes.title: Positive solutions of x² − dy² = −1 are ordered by either coordinate
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be a nonsquare. (a) If x² − dy² = −1 with x, y ∈ ℤ and x + y√d > 1, then x ≥ 1 and y ≥ 1. (b) If x² − dy² = −1 and a² − db² = −1 with x, y, a, b ≥ 1, then a + b√d < x + y√d ⇔ (a < x and b < y) ⇔ (a < x or b < y).
hypotheses: d > 0 not a square; solutions in integers.
proofSteps: (a): 1/(x + y√d) = −(x − y√d) = −x + y√d, so x + y√d > 1 > −x + y√d > 0; adding gives x > 0, and then y√d > x > 0.

(b): if x + y√d > a + b√d ≥ 1 + √d > 1, taking reciprocals gives −x + y√d < −a + b√d; adding the two inequalities gives a < x; then db² = 1 + a² < 1 + x² = dy² gives b < y. The remaining equivalences are the same monotonicity.
acceptance: For d = 2: (1, 1) < (7, 5) < (41, 29) in both coordinates.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 7.3. If x² − dy² = −1 in Z and x + y√d > 1 then x ≥ 1 and y ≥ 1.
sources.match: Part (a).

sources.excerpt: Lemma 7.4. Suppose x² − dy² = −1 and a² − db² = −1 in Z where x, y, a, b ≥ 1. Then a + b√d < x + y√d ⇐⇒ a < x and b < y ⇐⇒ a < x or b < y.
sources.match: Part (b).

nodes.title: The square of the least negative Pell solution is the fundamental Pell solution
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be a nonsquare such that x² − dy² = −1 has a solution in positive integers, and let (x₁, y₁) be the one with least y₁. Then (x₁ + y₁√d)² = X₁ + Y₁√d, where (X₁, Y₁) = (x₁² + dy₁², 2x₁y₁) is the fundamental solution of x² − dy² = 1 in the sense of Mathlib's Pell.IsFundamental.
hypotheses: d > 0 nonsquare; a positive solution of the negative equation exists.
proofSteps: (x₁ + y₁√d)² has norm 1 and positive coordinates, so by Mathlib's Pell.IsFundamental.eq_zpow_or_neg_zpow and positivity it is u^k for the fundamental solution u = X₁ + Y₁√d and some k ≥ 1.
If k = 2ℓ were even, x₁ + y₁√d = ±u^ℓ would have norm 1, not −1; so k = 2ℓ + 1.
Then u = (x₁ + y₁√d)²u^{−2ℓ} = (a + b√d)² with a + b√d = (x₁ + y₁√d)u^{−ℓ} of norm −1; 2ab = Y₁ > 0, so a, b may be taken positive.
If ℓ > 0 then (x₁ + y₁√d)² = u^{2ℓ+1} > u = (a + b√d)² > 1, so x₁ + y₁√d > a + b√d and y₁ > b by negative-pell-solution-ordering, contradicting minimality; hence ℓ = 0 and (x₁ + y₁√d)² = u.
acceptance: d = 2: (1 + √2)² = 3 + 2√2, the fundamental solution of x² − 2y² = 1.

sources.excerpt: We will show X₁ + Y₁√d = (x₁ + y₁√d)².
sources.match: The lemma is the first half of the source's proof of Theorem 7.5.

nodes.title: Classification of the solutions of x² − dy² = ±1 when the negative equation is solvable
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be a nonsquare such that x² − dy² = −1 has a solution in positive integers, and let (x₁, y₁) be the one with least y₁; put ε = x₁ + y₁√d, a unit of ℤ[√d] of norm −1. Then the integer solutions of x² − dy² = ±1 are exactly the x + y√d = ±ε^k with k ∈ ℤ; those of x² − dy² = −1 have k odd and those of x² − dy² = 1 have k even.
hypotheses: d > 0 nonsquare; S(d, −1) contains an element with positive coordinates. (No solvability criterion is asserted: whether S(d, −1) is nonempty is decided by generalised-pell-finite-classes-and-bounded-search, and necessary local conditions are negative-pell-local-obstruction.)
proofSteps: ±ε^k has norm (−1)^k (multiplicativity of the norm).

A positive solution of norm 1 is a positive power of the fundamental solution ε² (negative-pell-least-solution-squares-to-fundamental and Mathlib's Pell.IsFundamental.eq_zpow_or_neg_zpow), hence an even power of ε.
A positive solution α of norm −1: α² has norm 1 and is ε^{2k}, so α = ε^k by taking positive square roots, and k is odd because the norm is −1.

Solutions that are not positive: by negative-pell-solution-ordering(a), α ∉ (1, ∞); if α ≠ ±1 then exactly one of α⁻¹, −α⁻¹, −α lies in (1, ∞) and has coordinates equal to those of α up to sign, so it is ε^K for some K ≥ 1.
acceptance: d = 2, ε = 1 + √2: the solutions of x² − 2y² = −1 in positive integers are (1, 1), (7, 5), (41, 29), from ε, ε³, ε⁵.
The statement complements Mathlib's Pell.IsFundamental.eq_zpow_or_neg_zpow, which classifies only the norm-one solutions.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 7.5. Assume x² − dy² = −1 has a solution in positive integers and let (x₁, y₁) be that solution where y₁ is minimal. The integral solutions to both equations x² − dy² = ±1 are, up to sign, generated from (x₁, y₁) by taking integral powers of x₁ + y₁√d
sources.match: The theorem, verbatim.

nodes.title: Congruence obstructions to x² − dy² = −1
nodes.statement: Let d ∈ ℤ. If 4 ∣ d, or if some prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) divides d, then x² − dy² = −1 has no integer solution. (More generally, x² − dy² = n has no solution when x² ≡ n has no solution modulo some p dividing d with p ∤ n.)
hypotheses: d ∈ ℤ; no nonsquare hypothesis is needed.
proofSteps: A solution gives x² ≡ −1 (mod p) for every p ∣ d; for p ≡ 3 (mod 4) this is impossible by Mathlib's ZMod.mod_four_ne_three_of_sq_eq_neg_one.
If 4 ∣ d, x² ≡ −1 (mod 4) is impossible because squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4.
acceptance: x² − 3y² = −1 and x² − 21y² = −1 have no solution; x² − 34y² = −1 passes these tests but has no solution (so the condition is necessary, not sufficient).
The generalised form rules out x² − 5y² = 2 (2 is not a square mod 5).

sources.excerpt: Remark 3.6. For the negative Pell equation x² − dy² = −1, with squarefree d, the existence of a solution in Z requires no prime factor of d to be 3 mod 4.
sources.match: The obstruction at primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), stated in the source without proof; the node drops the squarefree hypothesis and adds the obstruction at 4.

sources.excerpt: Example 6.1. If integers x and y satisfy x² − 3y² = −1 then reduce both sides mod 3 to get x² ≡ −1 mod 3. This congruence has no solution: the only squares mod 3 are 0 and 1.
sources.match: The generalised congruence form and the example d = 3; Remark 6.4 supplies d = 34 as the non-sufficiency example.

nodes.title: Chebyshev's bound for the generalised Pell equation
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be a nonsquare, and u = a + b√d with a, b positive integers and a² − db² = 1. For every n ≠ 0, every integer solution of x² − dy² = n is (x′ + y′√d)u^k for some k ∈ ℤ and some solution (x′, y′) of x′² − dy′² = n with |x′| ≤ √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/2 and |y′| ≤ √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/(2√d). If n > 0 one may take |y′| ≤ √n(√u − 1/√u)/(2√d).
hypotheses: d > 0 nonsquare; u > 1 a Pell solution with positive coordinates (for instance the fundamental one, which exists by Mathlib's Pell.exists_of_not_isSquare); n ≠ 0.
proofSteps: For α = x + y√d with norm n put L(α) = (log|x + y√d|, log|x − y√d|) ∈ ℝ²; L is multiplicative-to-additive, and L(u) = (log u)(1, −1) because |a − b√d| = 1/u.
Write L(α) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂L(u); adding coordinates gives c₁ = (log|n|)/2. Choose k ∈ ℤ with |c₂ − k| ≤ 1/2 and set α′ = αu^{−k} = x′ + y′√d, which has integer coordinates and norm n.
Then {|x′ + y′√d|, |x′ − y′√d|} = {s, |n|/s} with √|n| ≤ s ≤ √(|n|u), and |x′| ≤ (s + |n|/s)/2, |y′| ≤ (s + |n|/s)/(2√d); t ↦ t + |n|/t is increasing for t ≥ √|n|, which gives the bounds.
For n > 0 the two conjugates have the same sign, so |y′| = |s − n/s|/(2√d) ≤ (√(nu) − √(n/u))/(2√d).
acceptance: x² − 6y² = 3 with u = 5 + 2√6: the bounds give |y′| ≤ 1 and the fundamental solutions (±3, ±1).
x² − 37y² = 11 with u = 73 + 12√37: no solution inside the box, hence none at all (Conrad, Example 4.5).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 3.3. Fix u = a + b√d where a² − db² = 1 with a and b in Z⁺. For each n ∈ Z − {0}, every integral solution of x² − dy² = n is (x′ + y′√d)u^k where x′² − dy′² = n, k ∈ Z, and
sources.match: The theorem; the displayed bounds (3.1) and the refinement for n > 0 follow on the same page.

sources.excerpt: the bounds in Theorem 3.3 were found by Chebyshev in 1851 [2, pp. 260, 262].
sources.match: The attribution in the node's title.

nodes.title: Finitely many classes of solutions, and the complete bounded search
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be a nonsquare, n ≠ 0, and u = a + b√d as in chebyshev-bound-generalised-pell. (a) There is a finite set F ⊆ S(d, n) such that every element of S(d, n) is a Pell multiple ±f·u^k of an element of F; one may take F = S(d, n) ∩ B with B the box |x| ≤ √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/2, |y| ≤ √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/(2√d). (b) Consequently x² − dy² = n has an integer solution if and only if it has one in B, which is a finite check: the generalised Pell equation, and in particular the negative Pell equation, is decidable once a nontrivial Pell solution u is known.
hypotheses: d > 0 nonsquare; n ≠ 0; u a Pell solution with positive coordinates.
proofSteps: (a) is chebyshev-bound-generalised-pell together with finiteness of the integer points of B.
(b): a solution outside B is a Pell multiple of one inside B; conversely a solution in B is a solution.
Mathlib's Pell.exists_of_not_isSquare provides u, so the bound is effective in d and n once u is computed.
acceptance: x² − 194y² = −1 has no solution: the box for n = −1 contains no solution (Conrad, Example 4.6), although 194 = 2·97 passes the congruence test of negative-pell-local-obstruction.
The search is complete only because of the proved bound, as the stage's acceptance requires.

sources.excerpt: Corollary 3.5. For a generalized Pell equation x² − dy² = n with n ≠ 0 there is a finite set of solutions such that every solution is a Pell multiple of one of these solutions.
sources.match: Part (a).

sources.excerpt: Proof #1: Each solution is a Pell multiple of a solution with |x| ≤ √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/2 and |y| ≤ √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/(2√d) by Theorem 3.3, so x and y have finitely many choices.
sources.match: Part (b): the source uses the same box to prove nonexistence in Examples 4.5–4.7.

nodes.title: Solutions of x² − dy² = n with |n| < √d come from convergents of √d
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be a nonsquare and n an integer with 0 < |n| < √d. If x, y are positive integers with x² − dy² = n, then the rational number x/y is a convergent of the regular continued fraction of √d: x/y = Real.convergent (√d) k for some k.
hypotheses: d > 0 nonsquare, 0 < |n| < √d, x, y > 0.
proofSteps: By Legendre's theorem (Mathlib's Real.exists_rat_eq_convergent), it suffices to show |ξ − q| < 1/(2 den(q)²) for the relevant ξ and q.
If n > 0 then x > y√d, and |x/y − √d| = |n|/(y²(x/y + √d)) < 1/(2y²) since x/y + √d > 2√d > 2|n|; as den(x/y) ≤ y this gives the hypothesis.

If n < 0 then x < y√d, and the same computation gives |y/x − 1/√d| < 1/(2x²), so y/x is a convergent of 1/√d; since 0 < 1/√d < 1, Mathlib's Real.convergent_succ gives Real.convergent (1/√d) (k + 1) = (Real.convergent (√d) k)⁻¹, so x/y is a convergent of √d.
acceptance: d = 13: the only n with 0 < |n| < √13 for which x² − 13y² = n is solvable are ±1 and ±3 (Conrad, Example 5.4).
Only the equality x/y = p_k/q_k of rationals is asserted: for non-squarefree n, (x, y) can be a multiple (gp_k, gq_k) with g² ∣ n.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 5.1. If positive integers x and y satisfy x² − dy² = n with |n| < √d then x/y is a convergent to the continued fraction of √d.
sources.match: The theorem, verbatim; the source's proof is the one in the proof steps.

nodes.title: Positive solutions of x² − dy² = ±1 are numerators and denominators of convergents
nodes.statement: Let d > 1 be a nonsquare. If x, y are positive integers with x² − dy² = ±1, then there is k with Real.convergent (√d) k = x/y in lowest terms, i.e. x and y are the numerator and denominator of that convergent.
hypotheses: d > 1 nonsquare (so that 1 < √d), x, y > 0.
proofSteps: Apply small-norm-solutions-are-convergents with n = ±1 (|n| = 1 < √d).
x² − dy² = ±1 forces gcd(x, y) = 1, so x/y is already in lowest terms and its numerator and denominator are x and y.
acceptance: d = 2: (1, 1), (3, 2), (7, 5), (17, 12) are the numerators and denominators of the convergents 1, 3/2, 7/5, 17/12 of √2.

sources.excerpt: Corollary 5.2. For each positive solution to x² − dy² = ±1, there is a convergent p/q to √d such that x = p and y = q.
sources.match: The statement, verbatim.

nodes.title: The continued-fraction decision procedure for x² − dy² = n with |n| < √d
nodes.statement: Let d > 1 be a nonsquare, 0 < |n| < √d, and u = a + b√d a Pell solution with positive coordinates; let Y = √|n|(√u + 1/√u)/(2√d). Then x² − dy² = n has a solution in positive integers if and only if either n is a perfect square, or there are k, g ∈ ℕ with g ≥ 1, g² ∣ n, g·q_k ≤ Y and p_k² − dq_k² = n/g², where p_k/q_k is the k-th convergent Real.convergent (√d) k in lowest terms. Only the finitely many k with q_k ≤ Y need to be checked, since q_k ≥ F_{k+1} (Fibonacci numbers).
hypotheses: d > 1 nonsquare, 0 < |n| < √d, u as in chebyshev-bound-generalised-pell.
proofSteps: If n = g² is a perfect square, (ga, gb) is a positive solution. If k, g are as in the statement, (gp_k, gq_k) is a positive solution (p_k ≥ 1 because √d > 1).

Conversely, let a positive solution exist and n not be a square. By generalised-pell-finite-classes-and-bounded-search there is a solution (x′, y′) in the box B; y′ ≠ 0 because n is not a square, and x′ ≠ 0 because |n| < d; so (|x′|, |y′|) is a positive solution with |y′| ≤ Y.
By small-norm-solutions-are-convergents, |x′|/|y′| = p_k/q_k for some k; with g = gcd(x′, y′), |x′| = gp_k, |y′| = gq_k, g² ∣ n, p_k² − dq_k² = n/g² and gq_k ≤ Y.

Finiteness: the denominators of the convergents satisfy q_k ≥ F_{k+1} (Mathlib's GenContFract.succ_nth_fib_le_of_nth_den, transported to Real.convergent by Real.convs_eq_convergent, with p_k, q_k coprime by SimpContFract.determinant).
acceptance: d = 13, n = 2: no convergent up to the bound gives norm 2 or 2/g², so x² − 13y² = 2 has no solution.
This decides the negative Pell equation (n = −1) without the periodicity of the continued fraction of √d.

sources.excerpt: Not only is the continued fraction of √d periodic, but so is x² − dy² when x/y runs through the convergents to √d. All distinct values of x² − dy² when x/y is a convergent to √d occur before the last term in the second period of the continued fraction.
sources.match: The source's decision procedure uses the periodicity of the continued fraction of √d, which it states without proof; the node replaces periodicity by the proved bound of Theorem 3.3, so that only finitely many convergents are checked.

sources.excerpt: If positive integers x and y satisfy x² − dy² = n with |n| < √d then x/y is a convergent to the continued fraction of √d.
sources.match: The link used in the second proof step.

nodes.title: ℤ[(1 + √−7)/2] is norm-Euclidean
nodes.statement: Let R = ℤ[θ] with θ = (1 + √−7)/2, realised as Mathlib's QuadraticAlgebra ℤ (−2) 1 (θ² = θ − 2); θ′ = 1 − θ; norm N(x + yθ) = x² + xy + 2y² (Mathlib's QuadraticAlgebra.norm). For all α, β ∈ R with β ≠ 0 there are q, r ∈ R with α = βq + r and N(r) < N(β). Consequently R is a Euclidean domain, hence a principal ideal domain and a unique factorisation domain.
hypotheses: The norm is the one of Mathlib's QuadraticAlgebra.norm for a = −2, b = 1.
proofSteps: Write γ = α/β = ξ + η√−7 with ξ, η ∈ ℚ; it suffices to find q ∈ R with N(γ − q) < 1, since N is multiplicative (N(α − βq) = N(β)N(γ − q)).
Elements of R are (j + k√−7)/2 with j ≡ k (mod 2). Choose k ∈ ℤ nearest to 2η (|η − k/2| ≤ 1/4) and j ≡ k (mod 2) nearest to 2ξ (|ξ − j/2| ≤ 1/2).
A Euclidean domain is a principal ideal domain and a unique factorisation monoid (Mathlib's instances from EuclideanDomain).
acceptance: Rounding both coordinates of ℤ[√−7] would only give N ≤ 2: the half-integers are essential.
The same computation fails for ℤ[√−5], whose class number is 2.

sources.excerpt: Hence N is a Euclidean function on R , so R is a Euclidean domain, and therefore a principal ideal domain (PID) and a unique factorization domain (UFD).
sources.match: The conclusion; the rounding argument precedes it on p. 3.

nodes.title: Units and the primes above 2 in ℤ[(1 + √−7)/2]
nodes.statement: In R (as in ramanujan-nagell-ring-norm-euclidean): the units are ±1; θθ′ = 2, θ + θ′ = 1 and (θ − θ′)² = −7; θ and θ′ are prime elements of norm 2 and are not associates.
hypotheses: R as above.
proofSteps: 4N(x + yθ) = (2x + y)² + 7y², so N = 1 forces y = 0 and x = ±1; units have norm 1.
N(θ) = N(θ′) = 2 is a rational prime, so θ, θ′ are irreducible, hence prime in the UFD R.
θ/θ′ is not in R (its norm is 1 but it is not ±1), so θ and θ′ are not associates; the identities are direct computations with θ² = θ − 2.
acceptance: θ′ = 1 − θ; θ − θ′ = 2θ − 1 squares to 4θ² − 4θ + 1 = −7.

sources.excerpt: The units of R are precisely ±1 : a unit has norm 1 , and 1/4((2x + y)² + 7y²) = 1 forces y = 0 and x = ±1 . Finally, N(θ) = N(θ′) = 2 is prime in Z , so θ and θ′ are irreducible, hence prime; and they are not associates, since their ratio is not a unit.
sources.match: The lemma, verbatim in substance.

nodes.title: The Ramanujan–Nagell equation with even exponent
nodes.statement: If x ∈ ℤ, n ∈ ℕ is even and x² + 7 = 2ⁿ, then n = 4 and x = ±3.
hypotheses: n even.
proofSteps: (2^{n/2} + |x|)(2^{n/2} − |x|) = 7 with both factors positive integers, so 2^{n/2} + |x| = 7 and 2^{n/2} − |x| = 1; adding, 2^{n/2+1} = 8, so n = 4 and |x| = 3.
acceptance: n = 0 and n = 2 give x² = −6 and x² = −3, impossible.

sources.excerpt: If n is even, then x² + 7 = 2ⁿ gives a factorization of integers (2^{n/2} + x)(2^{n/2} − x) = 7 . Since 7 is prime, we must have 2^{n/2} + x = 7 and 2^{n/2} − x = 1 , giving 2^{1+n/2} = 8 , hence n = 4 and x = 3 .
sources.match: The lemma, with the sign of x restored.

nodes.title: Factorisation of x² + 7 = 2ⁿ in ℤ[(1 + √−7)/2]
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 5 be odd, m = n − 2, and x a positive odd integer with x² + 7 = 2ⁿ; write x = 2k + 1. Then α = k + θ = (x + √−7)/2 and β = k + θ′ = (x − √−7)/2 satisfy αβ = 2^m = θ^mθ′^m and α − β = θ − θ′ = √−7, and α ∈ {±θ^m, ±θ′^m}. Consequently θ^m − θ′^m = ±(θ − θ′).
hypotheses: n odd, n ≥ 5 (so m ≥ 3 odd); x > 0 (x is odd because 2ⁿ − 7 is odd).
proofSteps: x² + 7 = 4(k² + k + 2), so αβ = k² + k + 2 = 2^m = (θθ′)^m.
A common prime factor of α and β divides α − β = θ − θ′, of norm 7, and divides 2^m, so it is θ or θ′ (ramanujan-nagell-ring-units-and-primes) of norm 2; 2 ∤ 7, so α and β are coprime.
By unique factorisation (ramanujan-nagell-ring-norm-euclidean) and units ±1, α = ±θ^m or α = ±θ′^m.
Taking conjugates (θ ↔ θ′) gives β, and subtracting gives θ − θ′ = α − β = ±(θ^m − θ′^m).
acceptance: x = 5, n = 5, m = 3, k = 2: θ³ = −θ − 2 and θ′³ = θ − 3, so α = 2 + θ = −θ³ and θ³ − θ′³ = −(2θ − 1) = −(θ − θ′).

sources.excerpt: Since R is a unique factorization domain with units ±1 , comparing the two factorizations of θ^mθ′^m forces (x + √−7)/2 = ± θ^m or ± θ′^m.
sources.match: The factorisation conclusion; §2.5 opens with the consequence θ^m − θ′^m = ±√−7.

nodes.title: The sign in θ^m − θ′^m = ±(θ − θ′)
nodes.statement: If m ≥ 3 is odd and θ^m − θ′^m = ±(θ − θ′) in R, then the sign is negative: θ^m − θ′^m = −(θ − θ′).
hypotheses: m odd, m ≥ 3 (for m = 1 the positive sign holds trivially).
proofSteps: Suppose θ^m − θ′^m = θ − θ′. Modulo θ′² (using θθ′ = 2 and θ = 1 − θ′), θ² = (1 − θ′)² ≡ 1, so θ^m ≡ θ as m is odd, and θ′^m ≡ 0 as m ≥ 2.
Then θ − θ′ ≡ θ^m − θ′^m ≡ θ (mod θ′²), so θ′ ≡ 0 (mod θ′²), impossible since θ′ is not a unit.
acceptance: m = 3: θ³ − θ′³ = (−θ − 2) − (−θ′ − 2) = −(θ − θ′), the negative sign.

sources.excerpt: We claim that the positive sign cannot occur. For, if it does, then we have θ^m−θ′^m = θ−θ′ , and working modulo θ′² and using θθ′ = 2 and θ = 1 −θ′ , we have θ² = (1 −θ′)² ≡ 1 (mod θ′²)
sources.match: The lemma and its proof.

nodes.title: The exponent lies in three classes modulo 42
nodes.statement: If m is odd and θ^m − θ′^m = −(θ − θ′), then −2^{m−1} ≡ m (mod 7), and hence m ≡ 3, 5 or 13 (mod 42).
hypotheses: m odd.
proofSteps: Binomial expansion of ((1 + √−7)/2)^m − ((1 − √−7)/2)^m gives 2^{1−m}√−7(C(m,1) − 7C(m,3) + 7²C(m,5) − ⋯); comparing with −√−7 and multiplying by 2^{m−1} gives −2^{m−1} = C(m,1) − 7C(m,3) + ⋯, so −2^{m−1} ≡ m (mod 7).
2 has order 3 modulo 7, so −2^{m−1} mod 7 depends on m mod 3; together with m mod 7 and m odd this is a condition on m mod 42, and a direct check of the 21 odd residues gives exactly 3, 5, 13.

sources.excerpt: A direct check shows that the only solutions to (4) modulo 42 are m ≡ 3, 5, or 13 (mod 42).
sources.match: The conclusion; congruence (4) is −2^{m−1} ≡ m (mod 7), derived just before by the binomial expansion.

nodes.title: At most one exponent in each class modulo 42
nodes.statement: There are no odd m < m′ with m ≡ m′ (mod 42) such that both satisfy θ^m − θ′^m = −(θ − θ′) = θ^{m′} − θ′^{m′}.
hypotheses: m, m′ odd; the identity for both.
proofSteps: Let d = m′ − m, so 42 ∣ d; let l = v₇(d) ≥ 1; work modulo 7^{l+1} in R.
Binomial expansion: (1 + √−7)^d ≡ 1 + d√−7 (mod 7^{l+1}), because every term with j ≥ 1 has 7-adic valuation at least j + l − v₇(k) ≥ l + 1 (using k·C(d,k) = d·C(d−1,k−1)).
Lifting the exponent (Mathlib's Int.emultiplicity_pow_sub_pow with 8 − 1 = 7 and d/3): v₇(2^d − 1) = v₇(8^{d/3} − 1) = 1 + l, so 2^d ≡ 1 (mod 7^{l+1}) and θ^d ≡ 1 + d√−7, θ′^d ≡ 1 − d√−7.
Then θ^{m′} − θ′^{m′} ≡ (θ^m − θ′^m) + d√−7(θ^m + θ′^m), so d√−7·P ≡ 0 with P = θ^m + θ′^m.

P_k = θ^k + θ′^k satisfies P_{k+2} = P_{k+1} − 2P_k with P₀ = 2, P₁ = 1, and modulo 7 it cycles 2, 1, 4, never 0; so P is invertible modulo 7^{l+1} and d√−7 ≡ 0, i.e. the coordinates (−d, 2d) of d(2θ − 1) are divisible by 7^{l+1}, contradicting v₇(d) = l.
acceptance: The three classes contain m = 3, 5, 13 respectively, so these are the only odd m ≥ 3 with the negative-sign identity.

sources.excerpt: It remains to show that each class in (5) contains at most one value of m . Suppose, for contradiction, that two solutions give exponents m < m′ with m ≡ m′ (mod 42) .
sources.match: The lemma; the proof steps follow the source's (6)–(9).

nodes.title: The Ramanujan–Nagell theorem
nodes.statement: The integer solutions (x, n) ∈ ℤ × ℕ of x² + 7 = 2ⁿ are exactly (±1, 3), (±3, 4), (±5, 5), (±11, 7) and (±181, 15).
hypotheses: x ∈ ℤ, n ∈ ℕ.
proofSteps: The listed pairs are solutions (direct computation).
n even: ramanujan-nagell-even-case gives (±3, 4).

n odd: n ≤ 3 gives only n = 3, x = ±1; for n ≥ 5, ramanujan-nagell-factorisation and ramanujan-nagell-sign give θ^m − θ′^m = −(θ − θ′) with m = n − 2; ramanujan-nagell-residues-mod-42 and ramanujan-nagell-one-per-class leave m ∈ {3, 5, 13}, i.e. n ∈ {5, 7, 15}, with x = ±5, ±11, ±181.
acceptance: A complete Lean 4 formalisation against Mathlib, with no unfinished proofs, exists outside Tau Ceti (Banwait, arXiv:2604.09808); the roadmap cites it as prior work for coordination.

sources.excerpt: the only integer solutions to the Diophantine equation x² + 7 = 2ⁿ are (n, x) ∈ {(3, ±1), (4, ±3), (5, ±5), (7, ±11), (15, ±181)} .
sources.match: The theorem, verbatim.

sources.excerpt: By (5) and the uniqueness just proved, each of the residue classes m ≡ 3, 5, 13 (mod 42) contributes at most one value of m from a solution, and these are realised by m = 3, 5, 13 , that is n = 5, 7, 15 , with x = 5, 11, 181 respectively
sources.match: The assembly of the proof.

nodes.title: Levi ben Gershon's theorem: powers of 2 and 3 differing by 1
nodes.statement: The solutions (a, b) ∈ ℕ² of |2ᵃ − 3ᵇ| = 1 are (1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 1) and (3, 2); that is, the only pairs (2ᵃ, 3ᵇ) of consecutive integers are (2, 1), (2, 3), (4, 3) and (8, 9).
hypotheses: a, b ∈ ℕ (exponent 0 allowed).
proofSteps: 3ᵇ − 2ᵃ = 1: if a = 0 then 3ᵇ = 2, impossible; if a = 1 then b = 1. If a ≥ 2 then 3ᵇ ≡ 1 (mod 4), so b is even, b = 2c, and (3ᶜ − 1)(3ᶜ + 1) = 2ᵃ; the factors are powers of 2 differing by 2, so 3ᶜ − 1 = 2, c = 1, b = 2, a = 3.
2ᵃ − 3ᵇ = 1: if b = 0 then a = 1. If b ≥ 1 then 2ᵃ ≡ 1 (mod 3), so a is even, a = 2c, and (2ᶜ − 1)(2ᶜ + 1) = 3ᵇ; the factors are powers of 3 differing by 2, so 2ᶜ − 1 = 1, c = 1, a = 2, b = 1.
Levi's own argument works modulo 8: 3ᵇ ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8) according to the parity of b, while 2ᵃ ≡ 0 (mod 8) for a ≥ 3; the only surviving infinite case is 3^{2k} − 1 = 2ᵃ, treated as above.
acceptance: This is the case {x, y} = {2, 3} of Catalan's equation xᵖ − y^q = 1, which (with exponents ≥ 2) has only 3² − 2³ = 1; Catalan–Mihăilescu in general is not planned here (see the gaps).
The equation 2ᵃ − 3ᵇ = −1 with a = 3, b = 2 is the only solution with both exponents at least 2.

sources.locator: the section on Levi's harmonic numbers, pp. 7–8
sources.excerpt: An elementary proof that the only pairs of harmonic numbers (numbers in the form 2ⁿ3ᵐ) that differ by 1 are the pairs (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4) and (8, 9).
sources.match: The statement; the source sketches Levi's mod-8 argument, reproduced in the third proof step.

sources.excerpt: The history of the problem dates back to at least Levi ben Gerson (also known as Gersonides), who considered in 1343 the Diophantine equations 2ᵖ − 3^q = 1 and 3ᵖ − 2^q = 1.
sources.match: The same equations in the context of Catalan's conjecture.

nodes.title: Numerical semigroups, their gaps, genus and Frobenius number
nodes.statement: A numerical semigroup is an additive submonoid S of ℕ whose complement G(S) = ℕ ∖ S (the gaps) is finite; equivalently the subgroup of ℤ generated by S contains 1 (Assi–García-Sánchez, Proposition 1). Its genus is g(S) = #G(S), its Frobenius number is F(S) = max G(S) ∈ ℤ with the convention F(ℕ) = −1, its conductor is C(S) = F(S) + 1, and its multiplicity m(S) is the least positive element of S.
hypotheses: S is an AddSubmonoid of ℕ (so 0 ∈ S and S is closed under addition).
The Frobenius number is integer-valued so that S = ℕ is covered (F = −1, g = 0).
proofSteps: Define the predicate 'the complement of S is finite' on Mathlib's AddSubmonoid ℕ, and the invariants g, F, C, m from the finite set of gaps.

Proposition 1 (finite complement ⟺ gcd 1): if G(S) is finite, some s and s + 1 lie in S; conversely, if the elements of S have gcd 1, all large integers lie in S, which is Mathlib's Nat.exists_mem_closure_of_ge applied to S (a submonoid is the closure of itself).
Every x > F(S) lies in S, and F(S) ∉ S when S ≠ ℕ; the conductor is the least c with c + ℕ ⊆ S.
For S = ⟨s⟩ the submonoid generated by a set s, F(S) is the Frobenius number of Mathlib's FrobeniusNumber predicate whenever S ≠ ℕ.
acceptance: ⟨5, 7, 9⟩: F = 13, g = 8 (the source's GAP example 15).
⟨2, 4⟩ is a submonoid but not a numerical semigroup (all odd numbers are gaps).

uses.how: Apéry sets, Selmer's formulas and symmetry are statements about these invariants
extends Mathlib's Frobenius number of two coprime generators to arbitrary numerical semigroups and adds genus and gaps
⟨a₁, …, a_k⟩ is the set of right-hand sides b for which a₁x₁ + ⋯ + a_kx_k = b has a solution in nonnegative integers (the source's Introduction)
semigroups of values of plane curve branches are numerical semigroups (context for the invariant conductor)

sources.match: The definition; Proposition 1 gives the equivalent finite-complement form used here.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 1. Let S be a submonoid of N. Then S is a numerical semigroup if and only if N \ S is a finite set.
sources.match: The characterisation taken as the definition.

sources.locator: §1, p. 5, the definitions of Frobenius number and conductor
sources.excerpt: We set F(S) = max(N \ S) and we call it the Frobenius number of S. We set C(S) = F(S) + 1 and we call it the conductor of S.
sources.match: The Frobenius number and the conductor; the convention F(ℕ) = −1 pins the empty maximum.

nodes.title: The Apéry set of a numerical semigroup
nodes.statement: For a numerical semigroup S and n ∈ S ∖ {0}, Ap(S, n) = {s ∈ S : s − n ∉ S} (with s − n computed in ℤ, so every s < n in S belongs to it). It has exactly n elements, one in each residue class modulo n: Ap(S, n) = {w(0) = 0, w(1), …, w(n − 1)}, where w(i) is the least element of S congruent to i modulo n (Lemma 4).
hypotheses: S a numerical semigroup; n ∈ S, n > 0.
proofSteps: Define Ap(S, n) as a subset of ℕ.
Each w(i) exists because S contains all large integers; w(i) ∈ Ap(S, n) since w(i) − n is smaller and congruent to i.
Two elements of Ap(S, n) are never congruent modulo n (the larger minus a multiple of n would lie in S), so Ap(S, n) = {w(0), …, w(n − 1)} and #Ap(S, n) = n.
acceptance: For n ∉ S the same formula gives a set of a different size: for S = ⟨5, 9, 21⟩ and n = 6 it has 9 elements.

uses.how: F(S) and g(S) are computed from Ap(S, n)
symmetry is the pairing a_i + a_{n−1−i} = a_{n−1} on the sorted Apéry set
S is generated by n and Ap(S, n) ∖ {0}, so every numerical semigroup is finitely generated

sources.excerpt: We define the Apéry set of S with respect to n, denoted Ap(S, n), to be the set Ap(S, n) = {s ∈ S | s − n ∉ S}.
sources.match: The definition.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 4. Let S be a numerical semigroup and let n ∈ S∗. For all i ∈ {1, . . . , n}, let w(i) be the smallest element of S such that w(i) ≡ i mod n. Then Ap(S, n) = {0, w(1), . . . , w(n − 1)}.
sources.match: The description by least representatives, from which #Ap(S, n) = n.

nodes.title: Unique decomposition through the Apéry set
nodes.statement: Let S be a numerical semigroup and n ∈ S ∖ {0}. Every s ∈ S can be written uniquely as s = kn + w with k ∈ ℕ and w ∈ Ap(S, n). Consequently S is generated by n and Ap(S, n) ∖ {0}, and is finitely generated.
hypotheses: S numerical, n ∈ S, n > 0.
proofSteps: Existence: subtract n while the result stays in S; the process stops at an element of Ap(S, n).
Uniqueness: two decompositions give two elements of Ap(S, n) congruent modulo n, which are equal (apery-set).

sources.excerpt: Proposition 6. Let S be a numerical semigroup and let n ∈ S∗. For all s ∈ S, there exists a unique (k, w) ∈ N × Ap(S, n) such that s = kn + w.
sources.match: The lemma; Corollary 7 is the finite generation.

nodes.title: Selmer's formula for the Frobenius number
nodes.statement: Let S be a numerical semigroup and n ∈ S ∖ {0}. Then F(S) = max Ap(S, n) − n.
hypotheses: S numerical, n ∈ S, n > 0 (for S = ℕ and n = 1: max Ap = 0 and F = −1).
proofSteps: max Ap(S, n) − n ∉ S by definition of Ap.
If x > max Ap(S, n) − n, write x + n = qn + i and let w(i) ∈ Ap(S, n) be the least element of S in the class i; x + n > w(i), so x + n = kn + w(i) with k ≥ 1 and x = (k − 1)n + w(i) ∈ S.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 12 (Selmer’s formulas). Let S be a numerical semigroup and let n ∈ S∗. We have the following: (i) F(S) = max(Ap(S, n)) − n,
sources.match: Part (i), with the source's proof.

nodes.title: Selmer's formula for the genus
nodes.statement: Let S be a numerical semigroup and n ∈ S ∖ {0}. Then g(S) = (1/n)Σ_{w∈Ap(S,n)} w − (n − 1)/2; equivalently 2n·g(S) = 2Σ_{w∈Ap(S,n)} w − n(n − 1).
hypotheses: S numerical, n ∈ S, n > 0.
proofSteps: Write the element of Ap(S, n) in the class i as w(i) = k_i n + i (0 ≤ i < n, k₀ = 0).
An integer x ≡ i (mod n), x ≥ 0, lies in S iff x ≥ w(i); so the gaps in the class i are i, i + n, …, i + (k_i − 1)n, k_i of them.

sources.match: Part (ii), with the source's proof.

nodes.title: Sylvester's formulas for two generators
nodes.statement: Let a, b ≥ 1 be coprime and S = ⟨a, b⟩. Then Ap(S, a) = {0, b, 2b, …, (a − 1)b}, F(S) = ab − a − b and g(S) = (a − 1)(b − 1)/2 = (F(S) + 1)/2.
hypotheses: a, b ≥ 1, gcd(a, b) = 1 (for a = 1 or b = 1, S = ℕ, F = −1 and g = 0, consistently with the formulas).
proofSteps: The multiples jb, 0 ≤ j < a, are pairwise incongruent modulo a (gcd(a, b) = 1), and jb − a ∉ S because a representation jb − a = ua + vb with u, v ≥ 0 would force vb < jb, so 0 ≤ v < j < a, together with v ≡ j (mod a), which is impossible. So Ap(S, a) = {jb : 0 ≤ j < a}.
selmer-frobenius-formula gives F(S) = (a − 1)b − a.
selmer-genus-formula gives g(S) = (1/a)·b·a(a − 1)/2 − (a − 1)/2 = (a − 1)(b − 1)/2.
acceptance: F agrees with Mathlib's frobeniusNumber_pair; the gap count g = (a − 1)(b − 1)/2 is new.

sources.excerpt: Example 13. Let S = ⟨a, b⟩ be a numerical semigroup. We have Ap(S, a) = {0, b, 2b, . . . , (a − 1)b}. Hence (i) F(S) = (a − 1)b − a = ab − a − b.
sources.match: The Apéry set and the Frobenius number; part (ii), the genus, is printed with a misprint recorded as sourceIssue ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E504.

nodes.title: The genus is at least half the conductor
nodes.statement: For every numerical semigroup S, 2g(S) ≥ F(S) + 1. More precisely n(S) + g(S) = F(S) + 1 and n(S) ≤ g(S), where n(S) = #{s ∈ S : s ≤ F(S)}.
hypotheses: S numerical (for S = ℕ both sides are 0).
proofSteps: {0, …, F(S)} is the disjoint union of the gaps and the elements of S below F(S), so n(S) + g(S) = F(S) + 1.
s ↦ F(S) − s maps {s ∈ S : s ≤ F(S)} injectively into the gaps, because s, F(S) − s ∈ S would give F(S) ∈ S.
acceptance: ⟨3, 5⟩: 2·4 = 8 = F + 1 (equality: symmetric).

sources.excerpt: Lemma 14. Let S be a numerical semigroup. We have g(S) ≥ (F(S)+1)/2 . Proof. Let s ∈ N. If s ∈ S, then F(S) − s ∉ S. Thus g(S) is greater than or equal to n(S). But n(S) + g(S) = F(S) + 1.
sources.match: The lemma with its proof.

nodes.title: Symmetric numerical semigroups
nodes.statement: A numerical semigroup S is symmetric if for every x ∈ ℤ with x ∉ S (negative integers are never in S) one has F(S) − x ∈ S. Equivalently, for 0 ≤ x ≤ F(S) exactly one of x and F(S) − x lies in S.
hypotheses: S numerical; ℕ counts as symmetric (F = −1). The source defines symmetric as 'irreducible with F(S) odd' and proves the equivalence with this condition in Proposition 43(i); the condition is taken as the definition here.
proofSteps: Define the predicate on the numerical semigroup S, testing x ∈ ℤ against (S : Set ℕ) through the cast.
For x < 0 the condition says F(S) − x ∈ S, which holds as F(S) − x > F(S); for x > F(S) it is vacuous; so only 0 ≤ x ≤ F(S) matters, and there at most one of x, F(S) − x is in S (else F(S) ∈ S).
A symmetric S ≠ ℕ has F(S) odd: if F(S) = 2y, then y ∉ S and F(S) − y = y ∉ S.

uses.how: symmetric semigroups are those of least genus for their Frobenius number
two-generator and free semigroups (in particular semigroups of plane branches, §3) are symmetric
the Apéry-set test for symmetry

nodes.title: Symmetric semigroups are those of least genus
nodes.statement: A numerical semigroup S is symmetric if and only if 2g(S) = F(S) + 1.
hypotheses: S numerical.
proofSteps: By genus-frobenius-inequality, s ↦ F(S) − s is an injection from {s ∈ S : s ≤ F(S)} into the gaps, and n(S) + g(S) = F(S) + 1.
S is symmetric iff this injection is onto the gaps (a gap x has F(S) − x ∈ S, and F(S) − x ≤ F(S) as x ≥ 0), iff n(S) = g(S), iff 2g(S) = F(S) + 1.
acceptance: The source proves this through irreducibility (Theorem 40, Proposition 43); with the classical definition the proof is the counting argument above.

nodes.title: Apéry sets are closed under summands
nodes.statement: Let S be a numerical semigroup and n ∈ S ∖ {0}. If x, y ∈ S and x + y ∈ Ap(S, n), then x, y ∈ Ap(S, n).
hypotheses: S numerical, n ∈ S, n > 0.
proofSteps: If y − n ∈ S then x + y − n ∈ S, so x + y ∉ Ap(S, n); similarly for x.

nodes.title: The Apéry-set criterion for symmetry
nodes.statement: Let S be a numerical semigroup, n ∈ S ∖ {0}, and Ap(S, n) = {0 = a₀ < a₁ < ⋯ < a_{n−1}}. Then S is symmetric if and only if a_i + a_{n−1−i} = a_{n−1} for all i.
hypotheses: S numerical, n ∈ S, n > 0.
proofSteps: If S is symmetric: F(S) = a_{n−1} − n (selmer-frobenius-formula); a_i − n ∉ S gives a_{n−1} − a_i = F(S) − (a_i − n) ∈ S, and apery-set-summand-closed puts it in Ap(S, n); the map a_i ↦ a_{n−1} − a_i is an order-reversing bijection of Ap(S, n), so it sends a_i to a_{n−1−i}.

Conversely, if the pairing holds, every w ∈ Ap(S, n) satisfies a_{n−1} − w ∈ S. For a gap x, choose w ∈ Ap(S, n) with w ≡ x (mod n); then x = w − kn with k ≥ 1 and F(S) − x = (a_{n−1} − w) + (k − 1)n ∈ S. So S is symmetric.
acceptance: ⟨3, 4, 5⟩, n = 3: Ap = {0, 4, 5} and 4 + 4 ≠ 5, so it is not symmetric.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 47. Let S be a numerical semigroup and let n ∈ S∗. Let Ap(S, n) = {0 = a₀ < a₁ < · · · < a_{n−1}}. Then S is symmetric if and only if a_i + a_{n−1−i} = a_{n−1} for all i ∈ {0, . . . , n − 1}.

nodes.title: Egyptian fraction expansions
nodes.statement: An Egyptian fraction expansion of a rational number r is a finite set D of positive integers with Σ_{d∈D} 1/d = r. (The denominators are distinct because D is a set; a representation with repetitions is not an Egyptian expansion.)
hypotheses: D a finite set of positive integers; r ∈ ℚ.
proofSteps: Define the predicate on (r, D) with D a Finset ℕ not containing 0.

Basic calculus: the empty set expands 0 and only 0; {n} expands 1/n; a disjoint union of expansions of r and s expands r + s; the splitting identity 1/n = 1/(n + 1) + 1/(n(n + 1)) replaces one denominator by two larger ones.

nodes.title: The greedy step decreases the numerator
nodes.statement: Let r = m/n with 0 < m < n coprime, and c = ⌈n/m⌉ ≥ 2. Then r − 1/c = m′/(nc) with m′ = (−n) mod m, so 0 ≤ m′ < m; and if m′ > 0, then ⌈nc/m′⌉ > c, i.e. the next greedy denominator is strictly larger.
hypotheses: 0 < m < n, gcd(m, n) = 1 (the lowest-terms numerator of r − 1/c is at most m′).
proofSteps: mc − n = m⌈n/m⌉ − n = (−n) mod m ∈ [0, m), and r − 1/c = (mc − n)/(nc).
Since c − 1 < n/m, r − 1/c < 1/(c − 1) − 1/c = 1/(c(c − 1)) ≤ 1/c, so the next greedy denominator ⌈1/(r − 1/c)⌉ exceeds c(c − 1) ≥ c.
acceptance: 2/(2k + 1): c = k + 1 and the remainder is 1/((k + 1)(2k + 1)), a unit fraction.

sources.excerpt: 0 < −n (mod m) < m. So, the numerator of the second fraction in the expansion continues to decrease until it reaches 1.

nodes.title: The Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy algorithm
nodes.statement: For a rational 0 < r ≤ 1, the greedy expansion is the list c₁ < c₂ < ⋯ < c_k defined by c₁ = ⌈1/r⌉ and c_{j+1} = ⌈1/(r − Σ_{i≤j} 1/c_i)⌉ as long as the remainder is positive. It terminates after k ≤ num(r) steps (num(r) the numerator in lowest terms), its denominators are strictly increasing, and Σ_{i≤k} 1/c_i = r; so {c₁, …, c_k} is an Egyptian expansion of r.
hypotheses: 0 < r ≤ 1 rational (r = 1 gives the one-term list [1]).
proofSteps: Define the list by well-founded recursion on the numerator of the remainder, which strictly decreases by greedy-egyptian-step.
Termination with at most num(r) terms follows from the strict decrease; the sum is r by telescoping; the denominators increase strictly by greedy-egyptian-step.
acceptance: The greedy expansion need not be the shortest: 5/31 = 1/7 + 1/62 + 1/434 has three terms.

the variant with strict inequality is the greedy underapproximation, whose value at θ = 1 is Sylvester's sequence

nodes.title: Every positive rational number is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions
nodes.statement: For every rational r > 0 there is a finite set D of positive integers with Σ_{d∈D} 1/d = r.
proofSteps: The harmonic series diverges (Mathlib's Real.tendsto_sum_range_one_div_nat_succ_atTop), so there is a largest N ≥ 0 with H_N = Σ_{d=1}^{N} 1/d ≤ r.

If H_N = r, take D = {1, …, N}. Otherwise 0 < s = r − H_N < 1/(N + 1), so the greedy expansion of s (greedy-egyptian-algorithm) has first denominator ⌈1/s⌉ > N + 1 and increasing denominators, all larger than N.
D = {1, …, N} ∪ egyptianGreedy s is a disjoint union, and its reciprocal sum is r.

sources.excerpt: It is elementary to prove that such a decomposition is always possible, for instance by using a greedy algorithm.

nodes.title: Sylvester's sequence
nodes.statement: Sylvester's sequence is s₀ = 2, s_{k+1} = s_k² − s_k + 1; equivalently s_{k+1} = s₀s₁⋯s_k + 1. Its terms are 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, 3263443, ….
hypotheses: Indexing from 0 (Nathanson indexes from 1).
proofSteps: Define s by recursion; the product form follows by induction from s_{k+1} − 1 = s_k(s_k − 1) = s_k(s₀⋯s_{k−1}).
Growth: s_{k+1} − 1 = s_k(s_k − 1) ≥ (s_k − 1)², so s_k − 1 ≥ 2^{2^{k−1}} for k ≥ 1 (doubly exponential growth).
acceptance: The terms are pairwise coprime (s_{k+1} ≡ 1 modulo every earlier term).

nodes.title: The Egyptian fraction identity of Sylvester's sequence
nodes.statement: For every k ≥ 0, Σ_{j<k} 1/s_j = 1 − 1/(s_k − 1). Consequently Σ_j 1/s_j = 1, and s_k is the greedy underapproximation choice for the remainder: s_k = ⌊1/(1 − Σ_{j<k} 1/s_j)⌋ + 1.

proofSteps: 1/s_k = 1/(s_k − 1) − 1/(s_{k+1} − 1), because s_{k+1} − 1 = s_k(s_k − 1); sum telescopically from 1/(s₀ − 1) = 1.
The remainder 1 − Σ_{j<k} 1/s_j = 1/(s_k − 1), and ⌊s_k − 1⌋ + 1 = s_k.

nodes.title: Primitive integer zeros of a form
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[x₀, …, x_n] be homogeneous of degree e ≥ 1. A primitive zero of F is x ∈ ℤ^{n+1} with F(x) = 0 and gcd(x₀, …, x_n) = 1.
hypotheses: F homogeneous of degree ≥ 1 (for the scaling API); the definition itself makes sense for any F.
proofSteps: Define the predicate F(x) = 0 ∧ gcd = 1 on ℤ^{n+1}, with the gcd of Mathlib's Finset.gcd over the coordinates.

Homogeneity gives F(λx) = λᵉF(x), so every nonzero integer zero is g·x for a primitive zero x and g = gcd ≥ 1, and every nonzero rational zero is a rational multiple of a primitive zero (clear denominators, then divide by the gcd); −x is primitive when x is.
acceptance: (3, 4, 5) is a primitive zero of x² + y² − z²; (6, 8, 10) is a zero but not primitive; (0, 0, 0) is not primitive.

nodes.title: Primitive zeros are the rational points of the projective hypersurface, up to sign
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[x₀, …, x_n] be homogeneous of degree ≥ 1 and V(F) ⊆ ℙⁿ_ℚ its zero set. The map x ↦ [x] from primitive zeros of F to ℚ-points of V(F) (Mathlib's Projectivization of ℚ^{n+1}) is surjective, and [x] = [y] iff y = ±x.
hypotheses: F homogeneous of degree ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Well defined: F(x) = 0 is invariant under scaling by homogeneity, so the zero set in ℙⁿ(ℚ) is defined through any representative.
Surjective: a point [ξ] with ξ ∈ ℚ^{n+1} ∖ 0 has a primitive integral representative (exists_isPrimitiveZero_of_rat of primitive-zero-of-a-form).
Fibres: [x] = [y] means y = λx with λ ∈ ℚ^×; primitivity of both forces λ = ±1 (write λ = a/b in lowest terms; a divides every coordinate of y and b every coordinate of x).
acceptance: For x² + y² − z²: the rational points of the conic correspond to the primitive Pythagorean triples up to sign.
The correspondence is the interface through which an equation of genus ≥ 1 is handed to the rational-point owners without losing primitivity.

nodes.title: A primitive zero is locally soluble everywhere
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[x₀, …, x_n] and let x be a primitive zero of F. Then for every prime p and every k ≥ 1, the reduction of x modulo pᵏ is a zero of F modulo pᵏ with some coordinate not divisible by p; x is a zero of F in ℤ_p^{n+1} with a unit coordinate for every p; and x is a nonzero real zero. Contrapositively, if for some p and k every zero of F modulo pᵏ has all coordinates divisible by p, then F has no primitive zero.
hypotheses: F with integer coefficients; x primitive.
proofSteps: Reduction is a ring homomorphism, so F(x) = 0 gives F(x mod pᵏ) = 0; gcd(x) = 1 gives a coordinate prime to p.
The inclusion ℤ → ℤ_p and ℤ → ℝ are ring homomorphisms; a coordinate prime to p is a unit in ℤ_p.
acceptance: x² − 5y² = 6z² (the homogenised x² − 5y² = 6): modulo 3, x² ≡ 2y² forces x ≡ y ≡ 0, and then 9 ∣ 6z² forces z ≡ 0 (mod 3); so there is no primitive zero, and x² − 5y² = 6 has no rational solution (Conrad, Example 6.3 and Remark 6.4).
x² − 34y² = −z² has primitive zeros (5, 1, 3) over ℤ, although x² − 34y² = −1 has no integer solution: local and rational solubility do not give integral solutions of the dehomogenised equation.

nodes.title: Routing example: the rational points of y² = x³ + x
nodes.statement: Let E be the Weierstrass curve y² = x³ + x over ℚ (Mathlib's WeierstrassCurve with a₁ = a₂ = a₃ = a₆ = 0, a₄ = 1). Its only affine rational point is (0, 0); so E(ℚ) = {O, (0, 0)}. Conversely, this statement implies that x⁴ + y⁴ = z² has no solution in positive integers.
hypotheses: Rational points in the sense of Mathlib's WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Equation over ℚ.
proofSteps: Let (x, y) be a rational point with x ≠ 0; then y ≠ 0 and x > 0. Write x = a/b, y = c/d in lowest terms; b³c² = d²(a³ + ab²) forces b = t², d = t³ (the primitive representative of the point of weighted projective space).
Then c² = a(a² + t⁴) with a, a² + t⁴ coprime and positive, so a = u² and a² + t⁴ = v², i.e. u⁴ + t⁴ = v² with t ≠ 0.
Mathlib's x⁴ + y⁴ = z² theorem (Fermat42.exists_pos_odd_minimal and Fermat42.not_minimal) forces u = 0, so x = 0, a contradiction.
Conversely a positive solution of x⁴ + y⁴ = z² gives the rational point ((x/y)², xz/y³) with x-coordinate ≠ 0.
acceptance: The analogous statement for y² = x³ − x (points O, (0, 0), (±1, 0)) is the routing of fermat-right-triangle-theorem (Conrad, Corollary 3.19).

This compares a CA.4 descent statement with Mathlib's Weierstrass-curve points, the carrier used by the elliptic-curve and rational-point owners (Tau Ceti's Mordell–Weil theorem WeierstrassCurve.Affine.fg_point_of_numberField is stated for these points).

nodes.title: The class group is generated by the primes of norm at most the Minkowski bound
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree n with r_2 complex places and discriminant d_K, and M_K = (4/π)^{r_2} · n!/nⁿ · √|d_K| (Mathlib's Minkowski bound, a local notation M K in Mathlib.NumberTheory.NumberField.ClassNumber). The classes of the nonzero prime ideals P of 𝓞_K with N(P) ≤ M_K generate the class group Cl(K).
hypotheses: K any number field; the bound is Minkowski's, in the form Mathlib states it.
proofSteps: Let C be a class. Mathlib NumberField.exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le gives a nonzero integral ideal I in C with N(I) ≤ M_K.
Every prime P dividing I has N(P) ≤ N(I) ≤ M_K: I ⊆ P gives N(P) | N(I) (Mathlib Ideal.absNorm_dvd_absNorm_of_le).

So the multiplicities of I vanish at every prime outside T = {P : N(P) ≤ M_K}; Tau Ceti ClassGroup.mk0_mem_closure_of_count_eq (with x = 1) puts the class of I in the subgroup generated by the classes IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.classGroupMk of the primes in T.
acceptance: K = ℚ(i): M_K = 4/π < 2, so no prime is needed and Cl(K) = 1 (Conrad Example 2.1).
K = ℚ(√−14): M_K ≈ 4.764, so the primes over 2 and 3 generate.
Compatibility: Mathlib RingOfIntegers.isPrincipalIdealRing_of_isPrincipal_of_norm_le_of_isPrime (all primes of norm ≤ M_K principal ⇒ PID) is the case in which every generator is trivial.

nodes.title: The class-group presentation by a family of ideals and its relation lattice
nodes.statement: Let I_1, …, I_N be nonzero ideals of 𝓞_K. The presentation map is φ_I : ℤ^N → Cl(K), e ↦ ∏ [I_i]^{e_i} (a group homomorphism from the additive group ℤ^N, written multiplicatively), and the relation lattice is Λ_I = ker φ_I ⊆ ℤ^N: for e ≥ 0, e ∈ Λ_I exactly when the ideal ∏ I_i^{e_i} is principal. If the classes [I_i] generate Cl(K), φ_I induces Cl(K) ≅ ℤ^N / Λ_I and Λ_I has index h_K.
hypotheses: The I_i are nonzero ideals (nonzero divisors of the ideal monoid); N ≥ 0.
Relations are recorded as column vectors (the lattice convention of CA.3).
proofSteps: Define φ_I(e) = ∏_i ClassGroup.mk0(I_i)^{e_i}; it is a homomorphism because Cl(K) is commutative.
Define Λ_I as the ℤ-submodule {e | φ_I(e) = 1}.
For e ≥ 0, φ_I(e) is the class of ∏ I_i^{e_i} (ClassGroup.mk0 is multiplicative), which is trivial iff that ideal is principal.
φ_I is surjective iff the [I_i] generate: its image is the subgroup they generate.
If surjective, the first isomorphism theorem (Mathlib QuotientGroup.quotientKerEquivOfSurjective) gives Cl(K) ≅ ℤ^N/Λ_I, and the index of Λ_I is |Cl(K)| = h_K (NumberField.classNumber).
acceptance: With no generators Λ = ℤ⁰ = everything.
In a field with h_K = 1 every vector is a relation.
For K = ℚ(√−14) and I = (p_2, p_3), Λ contains (2, 0) and (1, 2).

nodes.title: The class group from a complete relation matrix
nodes.statement: Let I_1, …, I_N be nonzero ideals whose classes generate Cl(K), and let A be an N × R integer matrix whose columns span the relation lattice Λ_I. For any Smith normal form certificate of A with invariant factors d_0 | ⋯ | d_{r−1}: r = N, Cl(K) ≅ ⊕_{i<N} ℤ/d_i ℤ, and h_K = ∏ d_i. The invariant factors > 1 are the invariant factors of Cl(K).
hypotheses: Generation: the [I_i] generate Cl(K) (for instance all primes of norm ≤ M_K, CA.5/class-group-generated-by-small-primes).
Completeness: the columns of A span Λ_I, not merely lie in it.
proofSteps: Cl(K) ≅ ℤ^N/Λ_I = ℤ^N/Aℤ^R (CA.5/class-group-presentation).
ℤ^N/Aℤ^R ≅ ⊕_{i<r} ℤ/d_i ⊕ ℤ^{N−r} (CA.3/cokernel-of-an-integer-matrix).
Cl(K) is finite, so N − r = 0; the order is ∏ d_i.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√−14), I = (p_2, p_3): Λ is spanned by (2, 0) and (1, 2); the Smith form of the matrix with these columns is diag(1, 4), so Cl ≅ ℤ/4.
K = ℚ(√−30), I = (p_2, p_3, p_5): Λ is spanned by 2e_1, 2e_2, 2e_3 and (1, 1, 1); invariant factors 1, 2, 2, so Cl ≅ (ℤ/2)², with the same class number 4 as ℚ(√−14).
Omitting the relation (1, 2) for ℚ(√−14) leaves a matrix of rank 1 < N: an incomplete relation set is detected by the rank before any class number is read off.

nodes.title: Found relations bound the class number from above
nodes.statement: Let I_1, …, I_N be nonzero ideals whose classes generate Cl(K), and A an N × N integer matrix with det A ≠ 0 whose columns are relations (lie in Λ_I). Then h_K · [Λ_I : Aℤ^N] = |det A|. In particular h_K divides |det A|, and h_K = |det A| exactly when the columns of A span Λ_I.
hypotheses: Generation of Cl(K) by the [I_i].
det A ≠ 0 (the found relations have full rank).
proofSteps: [ℤ^N : Aℤ^N] = |det A| (Mathlib AddSubgroup.index_eq_natAbs_det).
[ℤ^N : Λ_I] = h_K (ClassGroupPresentation.index_relationLattice).
Multiplicativity of the index along Aℤ^N ⊆ Λ_I ⊆ ℤ^N (Mathlib Subgroup.relIndex_mul_index, additively).
acceptance: K = ℚ(i) with I = ((1 + i)): the relation (2) gives |det| = 2, while (1 + i) is principal, so Λ = ℤ, h = 1 and [Λ : 2ℤ] = 2.
Found relations alone never prove completeness: a lower bound for h_K (or for h_K R_K) is needed (CA.5/class-number-regulator-certificate).

sources.excerpt: Indeed, it allows us to derive a bound h∗in polynomial time under GRH that satisfies h∗⩽hR < 2h∗(see [3]). If the tentative class number and regulator do not satisfy this inequality, we declare a failure (or in practice, collect more relations).
sources.match: The node is the fact behind the "tentative class number": the determinant of found relations is a multiple of h, equal to it only for a complete relation set.

nodes.title: A regulator lower bound certifies a fundamental system of units
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of unit rank r, u_1, …, u_r units whose logarithmic embeddings are linearly independent (Mathlib IsMaxRank), and L a real number with L ≤ R_K. If R(u) < 2L, where R(u) is the regulator of the family, then u_1, …, u_r together with the roots of unity generate 𝓞_K^×.
hypotheses: L is a certified lower bound for the regulator, supplied independently (analytically, or by an enumeration argument).
IsMaxRank u: the family has finite index.
proofSteps: Mathlib NumberField.Units.regOfFamily_div_regulator: R(u)/R_K = [𝓞_K^× : ⟨u⟩·μ_K] =: j, a positive integer (finite index by Mathlib isMaxRank_iff_closure_finiteIndex; R_K > 0 by regulator_pos).
j = R(u)/R_K ≤ R(u)/L < 2, so j = 1.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√5), u = (1 + √5)/2: R(u) = log((1 + √5)/2) ≈ 0.4812 = R_K; any certified L with R_K/2 < L ≤ R_K certifies u.
u = ((1 + √5)/2)² has R(u) = 2R_K ≥ 2L for every L ≤ R_K: a non-fundamental family is never certified.
Rank 0 (imaginary quadratic): the empty family has R = 1 = R_K, and any L ∈ (1/2, 1] certifies that μ_K is the whole unit group.

sources.excerpt: then certifying the result boils down to verifying that h∗⩽h′R′ < 2h∗.
sources.match: The unit half of the certificate: with the class group known, R′ < 2R_K bounds the index of the found units by 1. The node states it with an independent regulator bound L.

nodes.title: The class-number–regulator certificate
nodes.statement: Let I_1, …, I_N be nonzero ideals whose classes generate Cl(K), A an N × N integer matrix with det A ≠ 0 whose columns lie in Λ_I, u a family of r units with IsMaxRank, and h* a real number with h* ≤ h_K R_K. If |det A| · R(u) < 2h*, then the columns of A span Λ_I (so Cl(K) ≅ ℤ^N/Aℤ^N, read off from the Smith form of A) and u together with μ_K generates 𝓞_K^×; in particular h_K = |det A| and R_K = R(u).
hypotheses: h* is a certified lower bound for h_K R_K; in practice it comes from the analytic class number formula (the residue of ζ_K at 1), evaluated with error control, and is an input here.
The other hypotheses are those of CA.5/class-number-divides-relation-determinant and CA.5/fundamental-units-from-regulator-bound.
proofSteps: |det A| = h_K · j_1 with j_1 = [Λ_I : Aℤ^N] (CA.5/class-number-divides-relation-determinant).
R(u) = R_K · j_2 with j_2 = [𝓞_K^× : ⟨u⟩μ_K] (Mathlib regOfFamily_div_regulator).
|det A| R(u) = h_K R_K j_1 j_2 ≥ h* j_1 j_2; with |det A| R(u) < 2h* this gives j_1 j_2 < 2, so j_1 = j_2 = 1.
Then Cl(K) ≅ ℤ^N/Aℤ^N by CA.5/class-group-of-a-relation-matrix.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√−14): h = 4, R = 1; the relation matrix with columns (2, 0), (1, 2) and the empty unit family pass for any h* ∈ (2, 4].
With the incomplete matrix of columns (2, 0), (0, 4) (det 8) no h* ≤ 4 passes: the certificate refuses it.
The certificate checks the class group and the units together; neither index is certified from found relations or found units alone.

sources.excerpt: Indeed, it allows us to derive a bound h∗in polynomial time under GRH that satisfies h∗⩽hR < 2h∗(see [3]). If the tentative class number and regulator do not satisfy this inequality, we declare a failure (or in practice, collect more relations).

nodes.title: The Hermite matrix of an ideal in a fixed integral basis
nodes.statement: Fix a ℤ-basis ω = (ω_1, …, ω_n) of 𝓞_K. For a nonzero ideal I, the Hermite matrix H_ω(I) is the unique n × n integer matrix in Hermite normal form (CA.3 convention: columns, upper triangular, entries to the right of each pivot reduced) whose columns are the ω-coordinates of a ℤ-basis of I. I ↦ H_ω(I) is injective; H_ω(𝓞_K) = 1; H_ω((m)) = m·1 for m ∈ ℤ_{>0}; x ∈ I iff the coordinate vector of x lies in the column lattice of H_ω(I); and when ω_1 = 1, I ∩ ℤ = H_ω(I)_{1,1} ℤ.
hypotheses: ω is a ℤ-basis of 𝓞_K (for instance Mathlib NumberField.RingOfIntegers.basis); I ≠ 0, so its coordinate lattice has full rank n.
proofSteps: The coordinate map ω.equivFun identifies 𝓞_K with ℤ^n and I with a full-rank sublattice.
CA.3/hermite-basis-of-a-sublattice gives a unique Hermite basis of that sublattice; it is square because the rank is n. Define H_ω(I) as that matrix.
Injectivity and the characterisation "H = H_ω(I) iff H is in Hermite normal form and its columns span I" follow from uniqueness (CA.3/hermite-normal-form-unique).
Membership: x ∈ I iff ω.equivFun x lies in the column lattice.

Corner: with ω_1 = 1, the elements of I in ℤ = ℤω_1 are the lattice vectors with coordinates 2, …, n equal to 0; the upper triangular shape forces them to be multiples of the first column H_{1,1} e_1.
acceptance: In ℤ[i] with ω = (1, i), H_ω((1 + i)) has columns (2, 0) and (1, 1).

sources.excerpt: This matrix is often produced by building a Z-basis from larger generating sets, for instance when adding or multiplying ideals. An efficient way to do this is the HNF algorithm modulo a. It has the added benefit that the HNF representation is canonical, for a fixed (wi), with entries bounded by a.
sources.match: The node is the canonical HNF representation of the source, with the canonicity proved by CA.3. Transcribed from the page image.

sources.excerpt: Note that a ∩ Z is easily read off from A since w1 = 1, namely |a| is the upper left entry of the HNF matrix A.

nodes.title: The norm of an ideal is the product of its Hermite pivots
nodes.statement: For a nonzero ideal I of 𝓞_K and any ℤ-basis ω of 𝓞_K, N(I) = ∏_i H_ω(I)_{i,i}.
proofSteps: The columns of H = H_ω(I) are the ω-coordinates of a ℤ-basis of I, so the change-of-basis determinant from ω to that basis is det H.
Mathlib Ideal.natAbs_det_basis_change: |det| = N(I).
det H = ∏ H_{i,i} > 0 (CA.3: a square Hermite matrix is upper triangular with positive diagonal).
acceptance: N((m)) = mⁿ.

nodes.title: Which Hermite matrices are the matrices of ideals
nodes.statement: Let ω be a ℤ-basis of 𝓞_K and H an n × n integer matrix in Hermite normal form. Then H = H_ω(I) for some nonzero ideal I if and only if the column lattice L_ω(H) = Σ_j ℤ (Σ_i H_{i,j} ω_i) is stable under multiplication by every ω_k. Equivalently, for the multiplication matrices M_k of the ω_k (from the multiplication table of ω), each M_k H = H X_k for an integer matrix X_k.
hypotheses: H square in Hermite normal form (so det H > 0 and L_ω(H) has full rank).
proofSteps: If L_ω(H) is stable under each ω_k, it is stable under their ℤ-span 𝓞_K, so it is an ideal I; it is nonzero because it has full rank; H = H_ω(I) by IdealHermiteMatrix.eq_iff.
Conversely an ideal is stable under multiplication by 𝓞_K.
Matrix form: ω_k · (ω-coordinates x) = M_k x, and M_k H has columns in L_ω(H) iff M_k H = H X_k with X_k integral (H is invertible over ℚ, X_k = H⁻¹ M_k H).
acceptance: In ℤ[i] with ω = (1, i), diag(2, 1) is in Hermite normal form but its lattice 2ℤ + ℤi is not an ideal (i · i = −1 ∉ it).
The matrix with columns (2, 0), (1, 1) passes: it is H_ω((1 + i)).
The identity always passes (I = 𝓞_K).

nodes.title: The discriminant of a basis of a sublattice of 𝓞_K
nodes.statement: Let b_1, …, b_n ∈ 𝓞_K be linearly independent over ℤ, n = [K : ℚ], and L = Σ ℤ b_i. Then disc(b) = [𝓞_K : L]² · d_K. Consequently b is an integral basis iff disc(b) = d_K; if disc(b) is squarefree then b is an integral basis; and for an order O ⊆ 𝓞_K, disc(O) = [𝓞_K : O]² d_K.
hypotheses: n = [K : ℚ] and the b_i are ℤ-linearly independent (so L has finite index).
proofSteps: Let ω be an integral basis and C the integer matrix expressing b in ω (Mathlib Module.Basis.toMatrix), so b = ω·C.
Mathlib Algebra.discr_of_matrix_vecMul: disc(b) = det(C)² · disc(ω).
Tau Ceti NumberField.discr_eq_of_integralBasis: disc(ω) = d_K.
|det C| = [𝓞_K : L] (Mathlib Submodule.natAbs_det_basis_change).
If disc(b) is squarefree then [𝓞_K : L]² divides it, so the index is 1.
acceptance: ℤ[ζ_n] = 𝓞_{ℚ(ζ_n)}: disc(power basis) = d_K (Mathlib IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.discr is the computation of this discriminant).
Dedekind's cubic x³ + x² − 2x + 8: every order ℤ[α] has even index, so 4 | disc(α) for every α (Stein Example 6.2.7).

sources.excerpt: Proposition 6.2.6. Suppose O is an order in OK. Then Disc(O) = Disc(OK) · [OK : O]2.
sources.match: The node is the proposition for any full sublattice, with the source's proof (change-of-basis determinant).

nodes.title: The index of ℤ[√d] in the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)
nodes.statement: Let d ≠ 0, 1 be squarefree, K = ℚ(θ) with θ² = d (minpoly ℤ θ = X² − d). Then [𝓞_K : ℤ[θ]] = 2 if d ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 1 otherwise.

proofSteps: θ is an integral primitive element; Tau Ceti TauCeti.NumberField.IntegralPrimitiveElement.discr_minpoly_eq_index_sq_mul_discr gives disc(X² − d) = 4d = index(θ)² · d_K.
Tau Ceti NumberField.discr_eq_of_squarefree_of_mod_four_eq_one and NumberField.discr_eq_four_mul_of_mod_four_ne_one give d_K = d or 4d.
Hence index(θ)² = 4 or 1.

d = −3: ℤ[√−3] has index 2 in ℤ[(1 + √−3)/2], the ring containing the primitive cube roots of unity.

nodes.title: Dedekind–Kummer at every prime for a monogenic presentation
nodes.statement: Let θ ∈ 𝓞_K with ℤ[θ] = 𝓞_K and f = minpoly ℤ θ. For every rational prime p, the primes of 𝓞_K over p correspond bijectively to the monic irreducible factors Q of f mod p; the prime attached to Q is (p, Q(θ)), its residue degree is deg Q and its ramification index is the multiplicity of Q in f mod p. No prime is excluded.
hypotheses: ℤ[θ] = 𝓞_K (a monogenic presentation: quadratic fields with θ = √d or (1 + √d)/2, cyclotomic fields with θ = ζ).
proofSteps: ℤ[θ] = 𝓞_K is equivalent to exponent θ = 1 (Mathlib RingOfIntegers.exponent_eq_one_iff), so no prime divides the exponent.
Apply Mathlib NumberField.Ideal.primesOverSpanEquivMonicFactorsMod with that hypothesis, and its three companion lemmas for the span, the residue degree and the ramification index.
acceptance: ℤ[i], p = 3: X² + 1 is irreducible mod 3, one prime, inert.
ℤ[i], p = 5: X² + 1 ≡ (X − 2)(X + 2), two primes of degree 1.

ℤ[i], p = 2: X² + 1 ≡ (X + 1)², one prime with e = 2; the monogenic presentation covers the prime dividing the discriminant, which the general theorem with p ∤ exponent also covers but the hypothesis p ∤ disc f does not.

nodes.title: The ring ℤ√d inside the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)
nodes.statement: For d ∈ ℤ and θ ∈ 𝓞_K with θ² = d, the ring homomorphism φ : ℤ√d → 𝓞_K, x + y√d ↦ x + yθ (Mathlib Zsqrtd.lift). Its image is ℤ[θ]; it is injective when d is not a square; for squarefree d with K = ℚ(θ) it is an isomorphism iff d ≢ 1 (mod 4); and it carries the norm form x² − dy² of ℤ√d to the field norm N_{K/ℚ}.
hypotheses: θ² = d; for the bijectivity and norm statements, d squarefree and θ generating K.
proofSteps: φ is Zsqrtd.lift applied to (θ, θ² = d).
Image: generated by 1 and θ, i.e. ℤ[θ] (θ² = d).
Injective: x + yθ = 0 with y ≠ 0 would make θ rational, so d a square.
Bijective iff ℤ[θ] = 𝓞_K iff d ≢ 1 (mod 4) (Tau Ceti NumberField.adjoin_gen_eq_top_of_mod_four_ne_one; for d ≡ 1 the index is 2 by CA.5/index-of-the-order-z-sqrt-d).
Norm: N(x + yθ) = (x + yθ)(x − yθ) = x² − dy² (the conjugate of θ is −θ).
acceptance: d = −1: an isomorphism ℤ[i] ≅ 𝓞_{ℚ(i)}.
d = 5: not surjective, (1 + √5)/2 is missed.

nodes.title: Pell solutions are the units of norm one
nodes.statement: Let d > 1 be squarefree with d ≢ 1 (mod 4) and K = ℚ(√d), so that 𝓞_K = ℤ[√d]. The map (x, y) ↦ x + y√d is an isomorphism from Mathlib's group Pell.Solution₁ d of integer solutions of x² − dy² = 1 onto the kernel of the norm 𝓞_K^× → {±1}. This subgroup has index 1 or 2 in 𝓞_K^×, and the fundamental Pell solution generates it modulo ±1.
hypotheses: d > 1 squarefree, d ≢ 1 (mod 4); K = ℚ(θ) with θ² = d.
proofSteps: Pell.Solution₁ d is the unitary group of ℤ√d, the elements of norm 1 (Mathlib Pell.is_pell_solution_iff_mem_unitary); they are units (Zsqrtd.norm_eq_one_iff).
CA.5/zsqrtd-into-the-ring-of-integers: φ is a ring isomorphism ℤ√d ≅ 𝓞_K compatible with norms, so it restricts to an isomorphism of the norm-one units.
The norm is a homomorphism 𝓞_K^× → {±1} with kernel the norm-one units, so the index is 1 or 2.
Generation modulo ±1 by the fundamental solution: Mathlib Pell.IsFundamental.eq_zpow_or_neg_zpow.
acceptance: d = 2: the fundamental Pell solution 3 + 2√2 = (1 + √2)², where 1 + √2 has norm −1; index 2.
d = 3: 2 + √3 has norm 1 and generates the units modulo ±1; index 1.
For d ≡ 1 (mod 4) the solutions of x² − dy² = 1 are the norm-one units of the order ℤ[√d], of finite index but possibly not all norm-one units of 𝓞_K (d = 5: (1 + √5)/2 squared is not in ℤ[√5]).

sources.excerpt: Thus if (x, y) are integers such that x2 −dy2 = 1, then α = x + √ dy ∈OK has norm 1, so by Proposition 8.1.4 we have α ∈UK. The integer solutions to Pell’s equation thus form a finite-index subgroup of the group of units in the ring of integers of Q( √ d).
sources.match: The node makes the subgroup precise (the norm-one units, of index ≤ 2 when d ≢ 1 mod 4). The sentence that follows in the source misstates the cyclic group (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E601).

nodes.title: The negative Pell equation and units of norm −1
nodes.statement: Let d > 1 be squarefree with d ≢ 1 (mod 4) and K = ℚ(√d). The equation x² − dy² = −1 has an integer solution if and only if 𝓞_K has a unit of norm −1; in that case the norm-one units have index 2, and the least positive solution x_1 + y_1√d generates 𝓞_K^× modulo ±1.
hypotheses: d > 1 squarefree, d ≢ 1 (mod 4).
proofSteps: Under the isomorphism ℤ√d ≅ 𝓞_K (CA.5/zsqrtd-into-the-ring-of-integers), x + y√d has norm x² − dy²; an element of norm −1 is a unit (Zsqrtd.norm_eq_one_iff).
Conversely a unit of norm −1 of 𝓞_K = ℤ[√d] is x + y√d with x² − dy² = −1.
The index statement is CA.5/pell-solutions-are-norm-one-units with the norm surjective onto {±1}.

The last clause, that the least positive solution generates the units modulo ±1, is CA.4/negative-pell-classification read through the identification of ℤ[√d] with 𝓞_K (CA.5/zsqrtd-into-the-ring-of-integers); nothing is re-proved here.
acceptance: d = 2: 1² − 2·1² = −1, the unit 1 + √2 of norm −1.
d = 3: x² ≡ −1 (mod 3) has no solution, so no unit of norm −1; the fundamental unit 2 + √3 has norm 1.

nodes.title: The class group of ℚ(√−14) is cyclic of order 4
nodes.statement: For K = ℚ(√−14), Cl(K) ≅ ℤ/4ℤ.
proofSteps: M_K = (2/π)√56 ≈ 4.76, so Cl(K) is generated by the primes of norm ≤ 4, which lie over 2 and 3 (CA.5/class-group-generated-by-small-primes).
𝓞_K = ℤ[θ] since −14 ≡ 2 (mod 4); by CA.5/kummer-dedekind-for-a-monogenic-presentation, X² + 14 ≡ X² (mod 2) and ≡ (X − 1)(X + 1) (mod 3), so (2) = p_2² and (3) = p_3 p_3′, and p_3′ ∼ p_3^{−1}.

Relations: p_2² = (2); (2 + θ) has norm 18 = 2·3² and is not divisible by 3, so (2 + θ) = p_2 p_3² for the suitably named p_3. The relation lattice of (p_2, p_3) contains the columns (2, 0) and (1, 2).

Completeness: p_2 is not principal (a² + 14b² = 2 has no solution), so [p_2] has order 2; [p_3]² = [p_2]^{−1} ≠ 1, so [p_3] has order 4 and generates. Hence Λ is spanned by (2, 0), (1, 2), of index 4 = h.
The Smith form of the matrix with columns (2, 0), (1, 2) is diag(1, 4) (CA.3/smith-normal-form-of-an-integer-matrix); CA.5/class-group-of-a-relation-matrix gives Cl(K) ≅ ℤ/4.
acceptance: h = 4 = |det| of the relation matrix.
The class group is cyclic, unlike ℚ(√−30) of the same class number.
The generator is the class of a prime of norm 3.

sources.excerpt: Example 2.3. Let K = Q(√−14). We will show the class group is cyclic of order 4. Here n = 2, r2 = 1, and disc(K) = −56. The Minkowski bound is ≈4.764, so the class group is generated by primes dividing (2) and (3).

nodes.title: The class group of ℚ(√−30) is ℤ/2 × ℤ/2
nodes.statement: For K = ℚ(√−30), Cl(K) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ × ℤ/2ℤ.
proofSteps: M_K = (2/π)√120 ≈ 6.97, so the primes over 2, 3 and 5 generate.
Relations: 2e_1, 2e_2, 2e_3 and (θ) = p_2 p_3 p_5 (norm 30), i.e. the columns 2e_1, 2e_2, 2e_3, (1, 1, 1).

Completeness: a² + 30b² takes none of the values 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, so no nontrivial product p_2^{a} p_3^{b} p_5^{c} with exponents in {0, 1} other than p_2p_3p_5 is principal; the lattice spanned by the four columns has index 4 in ℤ³ and is the whole relation lattice.
The Smith form of the 3 × 4 matrix is diag(1, 2, 2) padded with a zero column; Cl(K) ≅ (ℤ/2)².
acceptance: h = 4 as for ℚ(√−14), but the invariant factors are (2, 2), not (4).
Every class has order dividing 2.
The relation (1, 1, 1) is what cuts (ℤ/2)³ down to (ℤ/2)².

nodes.title: Interpreting certified number-field outputs as intrinsic invariants
nodes.statement: For a number field K, the certified outputs of ComputationalNumberTheory:CN.2 are interpreted by the comparison theorems of this layer as follows. (1) A family b of n elements of 𝓞_K with a certificate disc(b) = d_K (or disc(b) squarefree) is an integral basis (CA.5/discriminant-of-a-sublattice-basis). (2) A matrix certified to be in Hermite normal form with an 𝓞_K-stable column lattice is the Hermite matrix of a unique ideal, of norm the product of its pivots (CA.5/hermite-matrix-of-an-ideal-criterion, CA.5/ideal-norm-eq-prod-hermite-diagonal). (3) A family of prime ideals containing all primes of norm ≤ M_K with a relation matrix and a completeness certificate determines Cl(K) ≅ ⊕ ℤ/d_i by the Smith form (CA.5/class-group-of-a-relation-matrix); without the completeness certificate it determines only a multiple of h_K (CA.5/class-number-divides-relation-determinant). (4) A unit family with IsMaxRank and a certified bound h* ≤ h_K R_K with |det A| R(u) < 2h* is a fundamental system (CA.5/class-number-regulator-certificate).
hypotheses: The certificates are those CN.2 produces; termination of a search alone is not a certificate of completeness.
proofSteps: Each clause is the application of the named comparison theorem to the output, whose hypotheses are exactly the certified properties.
The analytic bound h* and its error control are CN.2/CN.4 outputs and enter only as the hypothesis h* ≤ h_K R_K.
acceptance: The worked examples ℚ(√−14) and ℚ(√−30) are instances of clause (3) with hand-checked completeness.
A relation matrix of determinant 8 for ℚ(√−14) (h = 4) is an output without completeness certificate: clause (3) yields only 4 | 8.
For ℚ(√5) the unit (1 + √5)/2 with any certified L > R_K/2 is an instance of clause (4) with the class group trivial.

sources.excerpt: then certifying the result boils down to verifying that h∗⩽h′R′ < 2h∗.
sources.match: The certification step of a class group and unit computation; the node lists which intrinsic invariant each certified output determines.

nodes.title: Pisot numbers
nodes.statement: A Pisot number is a real number θ that is an algebraic integer (integral over ℤ), satisfies θ > 1, and all of whose other complex conjugates lie in the open unit disc: every complex root z ≠ θ of the minimal polynomial minpoly ℤ θ has |z| < 1. The conjugates are the complex roots of minpoly ℤ θ (Mathlib's aroots of the minimal polynomial over ℤ, which for an algebraic integer is the monic minimal polynomial over ℚ by Gauss's lemma). Convention (pinned): degree one is allowed, so the Pisot numbers of degree one are exactly the integers n ≥ 2; the inequality θ > 1 is strict, so 1 is not a Pisot number.
hypotheses: θ real; the definition is a predicate on ℝ, not on an abstract number field.
Strict inequalities: θ > 1 and |z| < 1 for every other conjugate z. A conjugate on the unit circle makes θ a Salem number (CA.6/salem-number) or neither, never a Pisot number.
Integrality is part of the definition: 3/2 has no other conjugate but is not a Pisot number.
proofSteps: Define IsPisot θ as the conjunction of IsIntegral ℤ θ, 1 < θ and the modulus condition on the roots of minpoly ℤ θ in ℂ other than θ.
Projections isIntegral, one_lt, norm_lt_one are the three conjuncts.
eq_of_one_le_norm: a root z with |z| ≥ 1 cannot be ≠ θ by the modulus condition.
isPisot_iff_minpoly_rat: for θ integral over ℤ, minpoly ℤ θ maps to minpoly ℚ θ (minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions'), so the two root multisets in ℂ agree.
isPisot_natCast_iff: minpoly ℤ n = X − n has the single root n, so the modulus condition is vacuous and IsPisot n ⟺ n > 1 ⟺ n ≥ 2.
acceptance: The golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 is a Pisot number (its conjugate −1/φ has modulus 0.618…).
2 is a Pisot number; 1, 3/2 and √2 are not.
M(φ) = φ, agreeing with Mathlib's Polynomial.mahlerMeasure of X² − X − 1.

nodes.title: Salem numbers
nodes.statement: A Salem number is a real number τ that is an algebraic integer, satisfies τ > 1, all of whose other complex conjugates lie in the closed unit disc (every complex root z ≠ τ of minpoly ℤ τ has |z| ≤ 1), and at least one of whose conjugates lies on the unit circle (some complex root z of minpoly ℤ τ has |z| = 1). This is Salem's form of the definition; by Salem's lemma (CA.6/salem-number-conjugates) it is equivalent to the form 'degree at least 4, conjugate to τ⁻¹, all conjugates other than τ^{±1} of modulus 1'. Convention (pinned): the reciprocal quadratic units (3 + √5)/2, … (sometimes called quadratic Salem numbers) are not Salem numbers.
hypotheses: τ real, τ > 1 strictly.
The existence of a conjugate on the circle is what excludes Pisot numbers; without it the definition would contain every Pisot number.
No degree bound is imposed: degree ≥ 4 is a consequence (CA.6/salem-number-conjugates).
proofSteps: Define IsSalem τ as the conjunction of IsIntegral ℤ τ, 1 < τ, |z| ≤ 1 for every complex root z ≠ τ of minpoly ℤ τ, and the existence of a complex root z with |z| = 1.
Projections are the four conjuncts.
not_isPisot: a root z with |z| = 1 is ≠ τ (as τ > 1), so the Pisot condition |z| < 1 fails for it.

isConjRoot_inv, four_le_natDegree, even_natDegree: read off from CA.6/salem-number-conjugates (τ⁻¹ is a conjugate; the conjugates other than τ^{±1} lie on the circle, are non-real and come in complex-conjugate pairs, so the degree is 2 + an even number ≥ 2).
acceptance: The largest real root 2.1537… of X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1 is a Salem number (Smyth's example).
Lehmer's number τ₁₀ = 1.17628… is a Salem number (CA.6/lehmer-number-is-salem).
2, φ and (3 + √5)/2 are not Salem numbers.

nodes.title: The classification of Pisot and Salem numbers by conjugate moduli
nodes.statement: Let τ be a real algebraic integer with τ > 1, and let r_> and r_= be the numbers of complex roots of minpoly ℤ τ (counted in the multiset of roots) of modulus > 1 and of modulus = 1. Then (a) τ is a Pisot number iff r_> = 1 and r_= = 0; (b) τ is a Salem number iff r_> = 1 and r_= ≥ 1. In particular every real algebraic integer τ > 1 whose other conjugates lie in the closed unit disc is exactly one of Pisot or Salem, and τ is neither iff r_> ≥ 2. In case (b) the number of roots of modulus < 1 is 1 and r_= = deg τ − 2 ≥ 2 (CA.6/salem-number-conjugates).
hypotheses: τ real, integral over ℤ, τ > 1; τ itself is always one of the r_> roots, so r_> ≥ 1.
The counts refer to the minimal polynomial; for a non-minimal polynomial P with root τ the certificate form is CA.6/pisot-certificate.
proofSteps: τ is a root of minpoly ℤ τ of modulus > 1, and the roots are simple (separability in characteristic 0), so r_> ≥ 1 with equality iff every root z ≠ τ has |z| ≤ 1.
(a) IsPisot τ ⟺ every root z ≠ τ has |z| < 1 ⟺ (r_> = 1 and no root of modulus 1), since |τ| > 1.
(b) IsSalem τ ⟺ every root z ≠ τ has |z| ≤ 1 and some root has modulus 1 ⟺ r_> = 1 and r_= ≥ 1.
Exclusivity and exhaustion follow from (a) and (b) as r_= = 0 or r_= ≥ 1.
acceptance: φ: r_> = 1, r_= = 0 (Pisot). Lehmer's number: r_> = 1, r_= = 8 (Salem).
1 + √3 (conjugate 1 − √3 = −0.73): Pisot. 3 + √2 (conjugate 3 − √2 = 1.59): r_> = 2, neither Pisot nor Salem.
