nodes.title: A root certificate for Pisot numbers
nodes.statement: Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic and θ > 1 a real root of P such that every complex root of P other than one copy of θ (the multiset of complex roots of P with one occurrence of θ removed) has modulus < 1. Then θ is a Pisot number. No irreducibility of P is needed.
hypotheses: P monic with integer coefficients; θ real, θ > 1, P(θ) = 0.
If θ were a multiple root of P the hypothesis would put θ itself inside the unit disc, which is false; so the hypothesis forces θ to be a simple root.
proofSteps: θ is integral over ℤ (root of the monic P).
minpoly ℤ θ divides P in ℤ[X] (Gauss: minpoly ℤ θ is primitive and minpoly ℚ θ ∣ P in ℚ[X]); hence the complex roots of minpoly ℤ θ form a sub-multiset of those of P.
A root z ≠ θ of minpoly ℤ θ is therefore a root of P different from θ, hence in the multiset with one copy of θ removed, so |z| < 1.
acceptance: X² − X − 1 certifies φ; X³ − X − 1 certifies θ₀ (its complex roots have |z|² = 1/θ₀ < 1 since the product of the three roots is 1); (X² − X − 1)(X² + X + 1)·… with any cyclotomic factor does not certify, the roots of modulus 1 violating the hypothesis.
P = (X − 2)(X² + 1) certifies nothing for 2's partner roots i, −i (modulus 1): the lemma does not apply, although 2 is Pisot (the certificate is sufficient, not necessary).

sources.locator: Section 2, Proposition 6 and its proof, p. 2
sources.excerpt: Every rational Pisot Number is an integer greater than 1. Proof: This directly follows from the polynomial P(x) having the requirement of having integer coeﬃcients and being monic.
sources.match: The source identifies Pisot numbers through a monic integer polynomial; the lemma is the form used to certify conjugate moduli from any monic multiple of the minimal polynomial.

sources.excerpt: Most constructions of families of Salem numbers produce a monic reciprocal integer polynomials having roots τ > 1, 1/τ < 1 and all other roots on the unit circle.
sources.match: Certification from a (possibly reducible) monic integer polynomial, the Pisot counterpart.

nodes.title: Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials
nodes.statement: Let α ≠ 0 be an algebraic integer in a field of characteristic 0, with minimal polynomial P = minpoly ℤ α of degree d, and let P* = X^d P(1/X) (Mathlib's Polynomial.reverse). Then α is conjugate to α⁻¹ over ℚ (IsConjRoot ℚ α α⁻¹) iff P* = P or P* = −P. In that case P(0) = ±1, so α is a unit.
hypotheses: α ≠ 0, so P(0) ≠ 0 and deg P* = deg P.
Sign convention: P* = −P occurs exactly for P = X − 1 (a reciprocal polynomial with the minus sign is divisible by X − 1, and P is irreducible).
proofSteps: (⇒) If α⁻¹ is a root of P then α is a root of P* (Polynomial.eval₂_reverse_mul_pow); P is irreducible, so P ∣ P* in ℚ[X]; both have degree d, so P* = c P with c = leading coefficient of P* = P(0) (Polynomial.coeff_zero_reverse, reverse_leadingCoeff).
Comparing constant terms: the constant term of P* is the leading coefficient 1 of P, so 1 = c·P(0) = P(0)²; hence P(0) = ±1 and P* = ±P.

(⇐) If P* = ±P then P*(α) = 0 gives P(α⁻¹) = 0 (Polynomial.eval₂_reverse_eq_zero_iff); P is irreducible and monic, so P = minpoly ℤ α⁻¹ and minpoly ℚ α = minpoly ℚ α⁻¹ (Gauss's lemma, minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions').
acceptance: α = 1: P = X − 1, P* = −P, and 1 is conjugate to 1⁻¹.
α = 2: P = X − 2, P* = 1 − 2X ≠ ±P, and 2 is not conjugate to 1/2.
Lehmer's polynomial L satisfies L* = L; X³ − X − 1 has reverse −X³ − X² + 1 ≠ ±(X³ − X − 1).

sources.excerpt: Recall that a polynomial P(z) of degree d is said to be reciprocal if it satisﬁes z^dP(1/z) = ±P(z).
sources.match: The polynomial side, with both signs.

sources.excerpt: Furthermore an algebraic number α is reciprocal if it is conjugate to α−1 (as then Pα is a reciprocal polynomial).
sources.match: The implication (⇒); the node adds the converse and the sign analysis.

nodes.title: Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number
nodes.statement: A real number τ is a Salem number iff τ is an algebraic integer, τ > 1, deg τ ≥ 4, τ is conjugate to τ⁻¹, and every complex conjugate z of τ other than τ and τ⁻¹ has |z| = 1. Consequently τ⁻¹ is the only conjugate of τ in the open unit disc, the conjugates on the circle are non-real and occur in pairs z, z̄ = z⁻¹, and deg τ is even.
hypotheses: τ real; conjugates are the complex roots of minpoly ℤ τ.
proofSteps: (⇐) The conditions give |z| ≤ 1 for z ≠ τ (τ⁻¹ < 1 and the others have modulus 1), and deg τ ≥ 4 provides a conjugate other than τ^{±1}, which has modulus 1.
(⇒) Let τ′ be a conjugate on |z| = 1. It is not ±1 (otherwise minpoly ℤ τ = X ∓ 1 and τ = ±1), so it is non-real and τ̄′ = τ′⁻¹ is also a conjugate (the minimal polynomial has real coefficients).

Hence the minimal polynomial P of τ and its reverse P* share the root τ′⁻¹; by irreducibility P ∣ P*, so the roots of P are closed under z ↦ z⁻¹ (CA.6/reciprocal-iff-reverse); in particular τ⁻¹ is a conjugate: IsConjRoot ℚ τ τ⁻¹. (Source: apply a Galois automorphism mapping τ′⁻¹ to any conjugate τ₁.)
τ is the only conjugate of modulus > 1, so by the pairing τ⁻¹ is the only one of modulus < 1, and all others have modulus 1.
Degree: τ, τ⁻¹, τ′ and τ̄′ are four distinct roots (τ^{±1} real ≠ ±1, τ′ non-real); the circle roots come in pairs z ≠ z̄, so deg τ = 2 + 2k with k ≥ 1.
acceptance: For Lehmer's number: deg 10, conjugates τ₁₀, τ₁₀⁻¹ and eight on the unit circle.
For the quartic example 2.1537…: conjugates τ, τ⁻¹ = 0.4643… and 0.19098 ± 0.98159i of modulus 1.

sources.locator: Lemma 1 and its proof, p. 2 (arXiv v3)
sources.excerpt: Taking τ′ to be a conjugate of τ on |z| = 1, we have that τ̄′ = τ′−1 is also a conjugate τ′′ say, so that τ′−1 = τ′′. For any other conjugate τ1 of τ we can apply a Galois automorphism mapping τ′′ ↦ τ1
sources.match: The implication (⇒) except the degree bound, which the proof does not address (sourceIssue ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E702).

sources.match: The right-hand side of the equivalence.

nodes.title: The minimal polynomial of a Salem number is reciprocal
nodes.statement: If τ is a Salem number with minimal polynomial P = minpoly ℤ τ of degree d, then X^d P(1/X) = P, i.e. Polynomial.reverse P = P (the plus sign).
hypotheses: τ a Salem number.
proofSteps: τ is conjugate to τ⁻¹ (CA.6/salem-number-conjugates), so reverse P = ±P (CA.6/reciprocal-iff-reverse).
The sign is + : reverse P = −P forces P = X − 1 (P(1) = 0 from P*(1) = P(1) = −P(1) and irreducibility), but deg P ≥ 4.
Equivalently: P(0) = (−1)^d ∏ roots = (+1)·τ·τ⁻¹·∏ z z̄ = 1 with d even.
acceptance: reverse L = L for Lehmer's polynomial; reverse (X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1) = X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1.

sources.excerpt: This holds for the minimal polynomial of every Salem number. It is simply a consequence of τ and τ−1 having the same minimal polynomial.

nodes.title: Powers of a Salem number
nodes.statement: If τ is a Salem number of degree d and n ≥ 1, then τⁿ is a Salem number of degree d.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1 (τ⁰ = 1 is not Salem).
proofSteps: The conjugates of τⁿ are the n-th powers of the conjugates of τ (a ℚ-embedding of ℚ(τ) sends τⁿ to σ(τ)ⁿ).
The degree of τⁿ is d unless two conjugates satisfy τ₁ⁿ = τ₂ⁿ with τ₁ ≠ τ₂; applying a Galois automorphism mapping τ₁ ↦ τ gives τⁿ = τ₃ⁿ with τ₃ ≠ τ a conjugate, impossible since |τⁿ| > 1 ≥ |τ₃ⁿ|.
τⁿ > 1 is an algebraic integer; its other conjugates σ(τ)ⁿ have modulus ≤ 1, and a conjugate on the circle stays on the circle.
acceptance: τ₁₀² is a Salem number of degree 10; the quartic example's square is a Salem number of degree 4.

sources.excerpt: If τ is a Salem number of degree d, then so is τ^n for all n ∈ N.
sources.match: Exactly the statement (ℕ = {1, 2, …} in the source).

sources.excerpt: But then, by applying a Galois automorphism mapping τ1 ↦ τ, we would have τ^n = τ3^n say, where τ3 ≠ τ is a conjugate of τ, giving |τ^n| > 1 while |τ3^n| ≤ 1, a contradiction.

nodes.title: Powers of a Pisot number
nodes.statement: If θ is a Pisot number and n ≥ 1, then θⁿ is a Pisot number.
proofSteps: The conjugates of θⁿ are among the n-th powers σ(θ)ⁿ of the conjugates of θ.
A conjugate σ(θ)ⁿ equal to θⁿ with σ(θ) ≠ θ is impossible (|σ(θ)ⁿ| < 1 < θⁿ); so every conjugate of θⁿ other than θⁿ is σ(θ)ⁿ with σ(θ) ≠ θ, of modulus < 1.
θⁿ > 1 is an algebraic integer.
acceptance: φ² = φ + 1 = 2.618… is a Pisot number (minimal polynomial X² − 3X + 1); θ₀³ = θ₀ + 1 is Pisot.

sources.excerpt: Powers of Pisot Numbers are also Pisot Numbers. Proof: This follows from the fact that the conjugates of a power of some number are just the powers of the conjugates
sources.match: Exactly the statement; the node supplies the step excluding σ(θ)ⁿ = θⁿ.

nodes.title: Salem numbers through their traces τ + τ⁻¹
nodes.statement: Let τ > 1 be real and α = τ + τ⁻¹. Then τ is a Salem number iff α is an irrational algebraic integer all of whose conjugates other than α are real and lie in (−2, 2). In that case ℚ(α) is a totally real subfield of index 2 in ℚ(τ), α > 2, and deg τ = 2 deg α. Equivalently (Salem): a number field K is ℚ(τ) for a Salem number τ iff K has a totally real subfield ℚ(α) of index 2 with K = ℚ(τ), τ + τ⁻¹ = α, α > 2 an irrational algebraic integer with all other conjugates in (−2, 2).
hypotheses: τ > 1 real (so α > 2 automatically).
Irrationality of α is essential: α = 3 gives the quadratic unit (3 + √5)/2, which is not a Salem number.
proofSteps: (⇒) Every conjugate of α is τ₁ + τ₁⁻¹ for a conjugate τ₁ of τ; τ₁ = τ^{±1} gives α, and |τ₁| = 1 gives τ₁ + τ̄₁ = 2 Re τ₁ ∈ (−2, 2) (τ₁ ≠ ±1). α is an algebraic integer. α is irrational since some conjugate of τ lies on the circle and yields a conjugate of α different from α. ℚ(α) ⊊ ℚ(τ) and τ² − ατ + 1 = 0 give index 2.

(⇐) τ is a root of X² − αX + 1, monic over ℤ[α], so τ is an algebraic integer. Every conjugate τ₁ of τ satisfies τ₁ + τ₁⁻¹ = α₁ for a conjugate α₁ of α: α₁ = α gives τ₁ = τ^{±1}; α₁ ∈ (−2, 2) gives |τ₁| = 1 (the roots of X² − α₁X + 1 are non-real of product 1). Every conjugate α₁ of α arises from some τ₁, and α is irrational, so some α₁ ∈ (−2, 2) exists and gives a conjugate of τ on the circle.
acceptance: Lehmer: α = τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ = 2.0264… is the root > 2 of y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3, whose other roots −1.887, −1.469, −0.585, 0.914 lie in (−2, 2).
Quartic example: α = (3 + √5)/2 with conjugate (3 − √5)/2 = 0.382 ∈ (−2, 2).

sources.excerpt: A number ﬁeld K is of the form Q(τ) for some Salem number τ if and only if K has a totally real subﬁeld Q(α) of index 2, and K = Q(τ) with τ + τ−1 = α, where α > 2 is an irrational algebraic integer, all of whose conjugates ≠ α lie in (−2, 2).
sources.match: The field form; the node's element form is what the proof on p. 3 establishes.

nodes.title: Salem numbers inside ℚ(τ)
nodes.statement: Let τ and τ′ be Salem numbers with τ′ ∈ ℚ(τ). Then ℚ(τ′) = ℚ(τ), and if τ′ > τ then τ′/τ is a Salem number (in ℚ(τ)).
hypotheses: Both τ, τ′ Salem; the statement uses that a Salem number has a non-real conjugate (it fails for the quadratic units, which have none).
proofSteps: Write τ′ = p(α) + τ q(α) with p, q ∈ ℚ[X], α = τ + τ⁻¹ (CA.6/salem-number-iff-trace: [ℚ(τ) : ℚ(α)] = 2).

If k = [ℚ(τ) : ℚ(τ′)] > 1, then k of the values p(αᵢ) + τᵢ q(αᵢ) over the conjugates τᵢ equal τ′ and k equal τ′⁻¹, so one of them with τᵢ non-real is real, forcing q(αᵢ) = 0, hence q(α) = 0 and τ′ = p(α) totally real, a contradiction. So ℚ(τ′) = ℚ(τ).
An automorphism with τ ↦ τ⁻¹ maps τ′ to τ′^{±1}, not to τ′ (else it would fix τ, a polynomial in τ′); so τ′/τ is conjugate to its inverse.

The only conjugate of τ′τ⁻¹ outside the closed disc is τ′τ⁻¹ itself (a conjugate τ′₁τ₁⁻¹ outside needs τ′₁ = τ′, then τ₁ = τ, or τ₁ = τ⁻¹, then τ′₁ = τ′⁻¹ and the value is ττ′⁻¹ < 1); with the pairing, all other conjugates lie on the circle: τ′/τ is a Salem number (CA.6/salem-number-conjugates).
acceptance: τ₁₀² ∈ ℚ(τ₁₀) generates ℚ(τ₁₀) and τ₁₀²/τ₁₀ = τ₁₀ is Salem.

sources.excerpt: Suppose that τ and τ′ are Salem numbers with τ′ ∈ Q(τ). Then Q(τ′) = Q(τ) and, if τ′ > τ, then τ′/τ is also a Salem number in Q(τ).
sources.match: Exactly the statement; the proof on pp. 3-4 is the node's proof steps.

nodes.title: The Salem numbers of a field are the powers of one of them
nodes.statement: If K = ℚ(τ) for a Salem number τ, there is a Salem number τ₁ ∈ K such that the Salem numbers in K are exactly the powers τ₁ⁿ, n ≥ 1.
hypotheses: K generated by a Salem number.
proofSteps: The Salem numbers of K below τ are finitely many: they are algebraic integers of degree ≤ [K : ℚ] all of whose conjugates have modulus ≤ τ (Northcott for the house, DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/finite-algebraic-integers-house-le, or Mathlib's NumberField.Embeddings.finite_of_norm_le in K). Let τ₁ be the smallest.

Powers of τ₁ are Salem numbers in K (CA.6/salem-number-pow). (Equivalently: a Salem number τ′ ≤ τ has M(τ′) = τ′ ≤ τ and degree ≤ [K : ℚ], and Polynomial.finite_mahlerMeasure_le leaves finitely many minimal polynomials.)

For a Salem number τ′ ∈ K choose r with τ₁^r ≤ τ′ < τ₁^{r+1}; if τ₁^r < τ′ then τ′τ₁^{−r} is a Salem number in K (CA.6/salem-number-in-field, applied r times with CA.6/salem-number-pow) smaller than τ₁, a contradiction; so τ′ = τ₁^r.
acceptance: For the quartic example τ = 2.1537…, the Salem numbers of ℚ(τ) are the τⁿ, n ≥ 1, τ being the smallest one (Smyth, p. 13); the reciprocal quadratic unit τ + τ⁻¹ = (3 + √5)/2 ∈ ℚ(τ) is not among them.

sources.locator: Proposition 3(iii) and its proof, p. 4 (arXiv v3)
sources.excerpt: If K = Q(τ) for some Salem number τ, then there is a Salem number τ1 ∈ K such that the set of Salem numbers in K consists of the powers of τ1.
sources.match: Exactly the statement; the finiteness step is the source's 'only ﬁnitely many possibilities for the minimal polynomials'.

nodes.title: λτⁿ is close to integers for a Salem number τ
nodes.statement: For every Salem number τ and every ε > 0 there is a real λ > 0 such that ‖λτⁿ‖ < ε for all n ∈ ℕ, where ‖x‖ = |x − round x| is the distance to the nearest integer. λ can be taken to be an algebraic integer of ℚ(τ).
hypotheses: n ranges over all of ℕ, including 0.
proofSteps: Let K = ℚ(τ), d = [K : ℚ]. By Minkowski's convex body theorem in the Minkowski space of K (NumberField.mixedEmbedding.exists_ne_zero_mem_ringOfIntegers_lt) there is a nonzero λ ∈ 𝓞_K with |w(λ)| < ε′ at every infinite place w except the real place of τ, where the bound is chosen large enough.
Replacing λ by −λ, its value at τ's real embedding is positive (it is nonzero since λ ≠ 0).
σₙ = Tr_{K/ℚ}(λτⁿ) = Σ over the embeddings of λ(τᵢ)τᵢⁿ is an integer (Algebra.isIntegral_trace, ℤ integrally closed).
All terms but λτⁿ have modulus < ε′ (the other conjugates of τ have modulus ≤ 1), so |σₙ − λτⁿ| < (d − 1)ε′ ≤ ε for ε′ = ε/(d − 1).
acceptance: For τ₁₀ and ε = 1/10 some λ ∈ ℤ[τ₁₀] works; with λ = 1 the statement fails (τⁿ mod 1 is dense in (0, 1), Salem's Theorem V, quoted in Smyth's Section 3.4).

nodes.title: Powers of a Pisot number are near integers
nodes.statement: If θ is a Pisot number then ‖θⁿ‖ = |θⁿ − round(θⁿ)| → 0 as n → ∞; more precisely |θⁿ − Tr(θⁿ)| ≤ (d − 1)ρⁿ with d = deg θ, ρ < 1 the largest modulus of a conjugate other than θ, and Tr(θⁿ) ∈ ℤ.
hypotheses: θ a Pisot number; for d = 1 the statement is trivial (θⁿ ∈ ℤ).
proofSteps: sₙ = Σ over the complex roots z of minpoly ℤ θ of zⁿ is an integer (trace of θⁿ, trace_eq_sum_roots, Algebra.isIntegral_trace, ℤ integrally closed; or CA.6/power-sum-frobenius-congruence).
|sₙ − θⁿ| ≤ Σ_{z ≠ θ} |z|ⁿ ≤ (d − 1)ρⁿ → 0.
For n large, (d − 1)ρⁿ < 1/2, so round(θⁿ) = sₙ and ‖θⁿ‖ = |θⁿ − sₙ|.

θ₀¹⁰⁰ is within 2·(0.8689)¹⁰⁰ < 2·10⁻⁶ of the integer Tr(θ₀¹⁰⁰).

nodes.title: M(τ) = ⌈τ⌉ = τ for Pisot and Salem numbers
nodes.statement: Let τ > 1 be a real algebraic integer all of whose other conjugates lie in the closed unit disc (a Pisot or a Salem number, CA.6/pisot-and-salem-numbers). Then M(τ) = τ and ⌈τ⌉ = τ.

Every conjugate has modulus ≤ τ and τ is one of them, so ⌈τ⌉ = τ.

nodes.title: Reciprocal Pisot numbers are quadratic units
nodes.statement: If θ is a Pisot number conjugate to θ⁻¹, then minpoly ℤ θ = X² − aX + 1 for an integer a ≥ 3; so θ = (a + √(a² − 4))/2 ≥ (3 + √5)/2.
hypotheses: θ Pisot and IsConjRoot ℚ θ θ⁻¹.
proofSteps: The conjugates are closed under z ↦ z⁻¹ (CA.6/reciprocal-iff-reverse). A conjugate z ≠ θ has |z| < 1, so z⁻¹ has modulus > 1 and equals θ: z = θ⁻¹.
So the conjugates are θ, θ⁻¹ (distinct, θ > 1): minpoly ℤ θ = X² − aX + 1 with a = θ + θ⁻¹ ∈ ℤ and constant term θθ⁻¹ = 1.

nodes.title: The smallest Pisot number θ₀
nodes.statement: θ₀ = 1.3247179572… is the unique real root of X³ − X − 1 (the plastic number). As a declaration: the supremum of the set of real roots of x³ − x − 1, which is a singleton.
hypotheses: X³ − X − 1 has exactly one real root (its discriminant −23 is negative).
proofSteps: Define θ₀ := sup {x ∈ ℝ : x³ − x − 1 = 0}.
Uniqueness: x ↦ x³ − x − 1 has local extrema at ±1/√3 with negative values, so exactly one real zero, in (1.3247, 1.3248) by evaluation and the intermediate value theorem.
minpoly ℤ θ₀ = X³ − X − 1: the polynomial has no rational root (±1 are not roots), hence is irreducible (degree 3).
θ₀ is Pisot: the two complex roots z, z̄ have |z|² = 1/θ₀ < 1 since the product of the roots is 1 (CA.6/pisot-certificate).
θ₀ is nonreciprocal: the reverse −X³ − X² + 1 is not ±(X³ − X − 1) (CA.6/reciprocal-iff-reverse).

nodes.title: Siegel's theorem: θ₀ is the smallest Pisot number
nodes.statement: Every Pisot number θ satisfies θ ≥ θ₀; θ₀ itself is a Pisot number.
hypotheses: θ Pisot, of any degree.
proofSteps: θ₀ is Pisot (API item isPisot_plasticNumber of CA.6/plastic-number).
If θ is conjugate to θ⁻¹ then θ ≥ (3 + √5)/2 > θ₀ (CA.6/reciprocal-pisot-numbers).
Otherwise θ is a nonzero nonreciprocal algebraic integer, so θ = M(θ) ≥ θ₀ by Smyth's theorem (CA.6/mahler-measure-of-pisot-or-salem, CA.6/smyth-nonreciprocal-lower-bound).
Degree one: θ = n ≥ 2 > θ₀ (covered by the previous step, n being nonreciprocal).
acceptance: θ₀ ≤ φ, θ₀ ≤ 2 and θ₀ ≤ (3 + √5)/2, with equality exactly at θ = θ₀ among the examples.

nodes.title: Lehmer's number τ₁₀
nodes.statement: Lehmer's number τ₁₀ = 1.1762808182… is the largest real root of Lehmer's polynomial L = X¹⁰ + X⁹ − X⁷ − X⁶ − X⁵ − X⁴ − X³ + X + 1. As a declaration: the supremum of the set of real roots of L (which is {τ₁₀⁻¹, τ₁₀}).
hypotheses: L has exactly two real roots, τ₁₀ ∈ (1.17628, 1.17629) and τ₁₀⁻¹ = 0.85013…, and eight roots on the unit circle.
proofSteps: Define τ₁₀ := sup {x ∈ ℝ : L(x) = 0}.
L is reciprocal (reverse L = L), so L(x) = x⁵ Q(x + 1/x) with Q(y) = y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3.
A root y ∈ (−2, 2) of Q gives two roots of L on the unit circle; α₁₀ gives the two real roots τ₁₀^{±1} (solutions of x² − α₁₀x + 1 = 0); these are the ten roots of L.
The real roots of L are therefore τ₁₀ > 1 and τ₁₀⁻¹ < 1, so the supremum is τ₁₀; its enclosure follows from sign evaluations of L at 1.17628 and 1.17629.
acceptance: 2 < τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ < 2.03.

sources.excerpt: The smallest value of M(P) > 1 he could ﬁnd was M(L) = 1.176280818 . . ., where L(z) = z10 + z9 −z7 −z6 −z5 −z4 −z3 + z + 1 is now called 'Lehmer's polynomial'.
sources.match: The polynomial and the numerical value M(L) = τ₁₀.

nodes.title: Lehmer's number is a Salem number
nodes.statement: τ₁₀ is a Salem number and its minimal polynomial is L = X¹⁰ + X⁹ − X⁷ − X⁶ − X⁵ − X⁴ − X³ + X + 1; in particular deg τ₁₀ = 10 and M(τ₁₀) = τ₁₀.
hypotheses: No numerical root finding: the certificate is the list of sign changes of Q(y) = y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3 at the rationals −19/10, −3/2, −1, −1/2, 1/2, 1, 2, 21/10.
proofSteps: α₁₀ = τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ is a root of the monic integer polynomial Q (API item lehmerNumber_add_inv_isRoot); the other four roots of Q lie in (−2, 2) by the sign changes, so every other conjugate of α₁₀ (a root of minpoly ℤ α₁₀, which divides Q) is real in (−2, 2).
α₁₀ ∈ (2, 21/10) is not an integer, hence irrational (an algebraic integer that is rational is an integer).
τ₁₀ is a Salem number by CA.6/salem-number-iff-trace.

minpoly ℤ α₁₀ = Q: Q has no rational root (the candidates ±1, ±3 are not roots) and no quadratic factor over ℤ (Q mod 2 = y⁵ + y⁴ + y³ + y² + 1 has no root in 𝔽₂ and is not divisible by y² + y + 1, the only irreducible quadratic over 𝔽₂), so deg α₁₀ = 5; deg τ₁₀ = 2 deg α₁₀ = 10 (CA.6/salem-number-iff-trace), and minpoly ℤ τ₁₀ divides the degree-10 monic L, so they are equal.
acceptance: deg τ₁₀ = 10, and L is irreducible over ℚ.

nodes.title: Mahler measure versus house
nodes.statement: Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d with r > 0 conjugates of modulus > 1. Then M(α)^{1/d} ≤ M(α)^{1/r} ≤ ⌈α⌉ ≤ M(α).
hypotheses: α integral over ℤ, so M(α) = ∏ max(1, |αᵢ|) over its conjugates.
r > 0 (if r = 0 then M(α) = 1 and the middle term is undefined).
proofSteps: M(α) = ∏_{|αᵢ| > 1} |αᵢ| (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_eq_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_roots with leading coefficient 1).
Each of the r factors is ≤ ⌈α⌉, so M(α) ≤ ⌈α⌉^r.
⌈α⌉ > 1 is one of the factors and the others are ≥ 1, so ⌈α⌉ ≤ M(α).
M(α) ≥ 1 and r ≤ d give M(α)^{1/d} ≤ M(α)^{1/r}.
For α in a number field K, ⌈α⌉ = NumberField.house α (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/house-eq-numberField-house).

sources.excerpt: For α with r > 0 roots of modulus greater than 1 we have the obvious inequality M(α)1/d ≤ M(α)1/r ≤ ⌈α⌉ ≤ M(α) (6)
sources.match: Exactly the statement (for algebraic integers, the survey's standing context in Section 3).

nodes.title: Mahler measure of a unit versus the houses of α and α⁻¹
nodes.statement: Let α ≠ 0 be an algebraic unit (α and α⁻¹ algebraic integers) of degree d. Then M(α) = M(α⁻¹) and M(α) ≤ max(⌈α⌉, ⌈α⁻¹⌉)^{d/2}.
hypotheses: α a unit; α ≠ 0.
proofSteps: The conjugates of α⁻¹ are the αᵢ⁻¹ and ∏|αᵢ| = |N(α)| = 1, so M(α⁻¹) = ∏_{|αᵢ| < 1} |αᵢ|⁻¹ = ∏_{|αᵢ| > 1} |αᵢ| = M(α).
M(α)² = M(α)M(α⁻¹) is a product of at most d factors |αᵢ| (|αᵢ| > 1) and |αᵢ|⁻¹ (|αᵢ| < 1), each at most max(⌈α⌉, ⌈α⁻¹⌉).
acceptance: α = φ: M = φ ≤ max(φ, φ)^{1} = φ (equality).

sources.excerpt: If α is in fact a unit (which is certainly the case if M(α) < 2) then M(α) = M(α−1) so that M(α) ≤ (max(⌈α⌉, ⌈1/α⌉))^{d/2} .
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + h(α)
nodes.statement: For a nonzero algebraic integer α of degree d, ⌈α⌉ ≥ M(α)^{1/d} = exp(h(α)) ≥ 1 + h(α), where h(α) = log M(α)/d is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib's NumberField.absLogHeight₁). Consequently any lower bound M(α) ≥ c₀ > 1 gives ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + log(c₀)/d.
proofSteps: If some conjugate has modulus > 1 use CA.6/house-mahler-measure-comparison; otherwise M(α) = 1 and ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 (NumberField.one_le_house_of_isIntegral).
M(α)^{1/d} = absMulHeight₁ α (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/height-comparisons), so M(α)^{1/d} = exp(h(α)).
exp(t) ≥ 1 + t (Real.add_one_le_exp).

sources.excerpt: Indeed, because ⌈α⌉ ≥ M(α)1/d where d = deg α, we have ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + log M(α)/d = 1 + h(α), (9) so that if M(α) ≥ c0 > 1 then ⌈α⌉ > 1 + log(c0)/d.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Algebraic numbers with M(α) < 2 are units
nodes.statement: If α is a nonzero algebraic number with M(α) < 2, then α and α⁻¹ are algebraic integers.
hypotheses: M(α) is the Mahler measure of the primitive minimal polynomial (DT.0), equal to absMulHeight₁(α)^{deg α}.
proofSteps: The leading coefficient a₀ of the primitive minimal polynomial satisfies a₀ ≤ M(α) < 2, so a₀ = 1 and α is an algebraic integer (API leadingCoeff_le_mahlerMeasure and primitiveMinpoly_eq_minpoly_int of DT.0).
N(α) = ± the product of the conjugates is a nonzero rational integer with |N(α)| ≤ M(α) < 2, so N(α) = ±1.
α⁻¹ = ±∏_{i ≥ 2} αᵢ is a product of algebraic integers (Berrevoets Lemma 2.8).
acceptance: M(τ₁₀) = 1.176 < 2 and τ₁₀ is a unit; M(1/2) = 2 and 1/2 is not an algebraic integer.

sources.excerpt: Let α be an algebraic number and suppose M(α) < 2. Then α is an algebraic unit.

nodes.title: Smyth's rational function F = P(0)P/P* has integer coefficients
nodes.statement: Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic with P(0) = ±1 and P* = X^d P(1/X) its reverse (so P*(0) = 1). Then F = P(0)·P/P* has a Maclaurin expansion with integer coefficients, F(0) = 1, and F is constant iff P is reciprocal (P* = ±P).
hypotheses: P monic, P(0) = ±1. (If |P(0)| ≥ 2 then M(P) ≥ |P(0)| ≥ 2 and Smyth's bound is immediate.)
proofSteps: P*(0) = 1 is a unit of ℤ, so P* is invertible in ℤ⟦X⟧ and F = P(0)·P·(P*)⁻¹ ∈ ℤ⟦X⟧.
If F = c is constant then c = F(0) = 1 and P(0)P = P*, so P* = ±P; conversely P* = ±P = P(0)P (compare constant terms) gives F = 1.
acceptance: P = X³ − X − 1: F = −(X³ − X − 1)/(1 − X² − X³) = 1 + X + … is nonconstant.
P = L (Lehmer): F = 1.

sources.excerpt: The method of proof of (15) was based on the Maclaurin expansion of the rational function F(z) = P(0)P(z)/z^dP(1/z), which has integer coeﬃcients and is nonconstant for P nonreciprocal.
sources.match: Exactly the statement (the survey takes P monic, the minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer; the unit hypothesis P(0) = ±1 is the case that matters, see the hypotheses).

nodes.title: Smyth's theorem: M(α) ≥ θ₀ for nonreciprocal α
nodes.statement: Let α be a nonzero algebraic integer that is not conjugate to α⁻¹. Then M(α) ≥ M(X³ − X − 1) = θ₀ = 1.3247…, and the constant is best possible (equality for α = θ₀).
hypotheses: α ≠ 0: X is nonreciprocal and M(0) = 1 < θ₀; with Mathlib's convention 0⁻¹ = 0, the value 0 counts as conjugate to its inverse and is excluded by the hypothesis anyway.
Reciprocity is IsConjRoot ℚ α α⁻¹ (equivalently minpoly ℤ α reciprocal, CA.6/reciprocal-iff-reverse).
proofSteps: If α is not a unit, |P(0)| ≥ 2 for P = minpoly ℤ α and M(α) ≥ |P(0)| ≥ 2 > θ₀ (Mahler measure ≥ |product of roots|). Assume P(0) = ±1.
F = P(0)P/P* ∈ 1 + Xℤ⟦X⟧ is nonconstant (CA.6/smyth-integer-power-series): F = 1 + a_k X^k + … with a_k ≠ 0.

Factor F = f/g with f, g holomorphic on |z| < 1 and bounded by 1 there: g is the Blaschke product over the roots αᵢ with |αᵢ| > 1 of the factors (z − 1/ᾱᵢ)/(1 − z/αᵢ) (normalised), f = Fg; then f(0) = g(0) = M(P)⁻¹.

Schur's characterisation of the coefficients of power series bounded by 1 on the disc, combined with the integrality of the coefficients of F = f/g, gives M(P) ≥ θ₀. This analytic step is not given by any source read (Smyth 1971, Bull. London Math. Soc. 3, 169-175, not obtained): recorded as a gap.
Sharpness: M(X³ − X − 1) = θ₀ (API item mahlerMeasure_plasticNumber).
acceptance: α = θ₀ gives equality; α = φ (nonreciprocal: reverse(X² − X − 1) = −X² − X + 1) has M = 1.618 ≥ θ₀.
Lehmer's number is reciprocal and has M = 1.176 < θ₀: the hypothesis cannot be dropped.

sources.excerpt: In 1971 Smyth [155] independently improved the constant in (14), showing for α a nonreciprocal algebraic integer M(α) ≥ M(z3 −z −1) = θ0 = 1.3247 . . ., (15)

sources.excerpt: One can write F(z) as a quotient f(z)/g(z) where f and g are both holomorphic and bounded above by 1 in modulus in the disc |z| < 1. Furthermore, f(0) = g(0) = M(P)−1.

nodes.title: f(X)^p ≡ f(X^p) (mod p) for integer polynomials
nodes.statement: Let p be prime and f ∈ ℤ[X₁, …, Xₙ] (any index type). Then f^p − f(X₁^p, …, Xₙ^p) is divisible by p in ℤ[X₁, …, Xₙ]; in Mathlib's terms (p : MvPolynomial σ ℤ) ∣ f^p − expand p f.
hypotheses: p prime.
proofSteps: Map to (ℤ/p)[X]: there expand p f̄ = f̄^p (MvPolynomial.expand_zmod), so f^p − expand p f maps to 0.
A polynomial with integer coefficients mapping to 0 modulo p has all coefficients divisible by p, hence is p times an integer polynomial.
acceptance: f = X + Y, p = 2: (X + Y)² − (X² + Y²) = 2XY.
One variable: (X + 1)³ − (X³ + 1) = 3(X² + X).

nodes.title: Power sums of roots: s_{np} ≡ s_n (mod p)
nodes.statement: Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic with complex roots α₁, …, α_d (with multiplicity) and sₙ = Σ αᵢⁿ. Then every sₙ is a rational integer, and for every prime p and n ≥ 0, s_{np} ≡ sₙ (mod p).
hypotheses: P monic with integer coefficients.
proofSteps: sₙ is a symmetric polynomial with integer coefficients in the roots, hence an integer polynomial in the coefficients of P (Newton's identities, MvPolynomial.psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum, Multiset.prod_X_sub_C_coeff).
Apply CA.6/frobenius-congruence-integer-polynomial to f = X₁ⁿ + ⋯ + X_dⁿ: sₙ^p − s_{np} = p·g(α₁, …, α_d) with g ∈ ℤ[X₁, …, X_d]; since f^p − expand p f is symmetric, so is g, and g(α) is an integer.
Fermat: sₙ^p ≡ sₙ (mod p) (ZMod.pow_card).
acceptance: P = X² − X − 1: s₁ = 1, s₂ = 3, s₄ = 7; p = 2: s₂ ≡ s₁ (mod 2) and s₄ ≡ s₂ (mod 2).
P = X − a: s_{np} = a^{np} ≡ aⁿ (mod p) (Fermat).

sources.excerpt: By Lemma 2.18, there is a gn ∈ Z[T1, . . . , Td] such that σp n −σnp = pgn(α1, . . . , αd). Then gn(α1, . . . , αd) is rational and an algebraic integer, hence it is an element of Z.

nodes.title: Power sums determine a multiset in characteristic zero
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and s, t multisets in K of the same cardinality d. If Σ_{a∈s} a^k = Σ_{b∈t} b^k for k = 1, …, d, then s = t.
hypotheses: Characteristic 0 is needed (Newton's identities divide by k ≤ d).
proofSteps: Newton's identities (MvPolynomial.mul_esymm_eq_sum) express k·e_k as an integer combination of e_j p_{k−j}; dividing by k (char 0), the elementary symmetric functions e₁, …, e_d of s and t coincide.
Hence ∏_{a∈s}(X − a) = ∏_{b∈t}(X − b) (Multiset.prod_X_sub_C_coeff), and s = t as the root multisets of the same polynomial (Polynomial.roots_multiset_prod_X_sub_C).
acceptance: s = {1, 2}, t = {0, 3}: p₁ = 3 = 3 but p₂ = 5 ≠ 9, so they differ.
In characteristic 2, s = {0, 0}, t = {1, 1} have p₁ = p₂ = 0: the characteristic hypothesis is needed.

nodes.title: If α^k and α^l are conjugate (k ≠ l) then α is 0 or a root of unity
nodes.statement: Let α be algebraic over ℚ in a field of characteristic 0 and k ≠ l positive integers with α^k and α^l conjugate over ℚ. Then α = 0 or αⁿ = 1 for some n ≥ 1.
hypotheses: k, l ≥ 1 distinct.
proofSteps: Work in the normal closure L of ℚ(α); choose σ ∈ Gal(L/ℚ) with σ(α^k) = α^l (IsConjRoot.exists_algEquiv).
With N the order of σ: α^{k^N} = α^{l^N}, k^N ≠ l^N, so α = 0 or α^{|k^N − l^N|} = 1.
(Alternative: h(α^k) = k h(α) and conjugates have equal height, so (k − l)h(α) = 0 and Kronecker applies.)
acceptance: α = i, k = 1, l = 3: i and −i are conjugate and i is a root of unity.
α = √2: α² = 2 and α⁴ = 4 are not conjugate.

sources.excerpt: Let α be an algebraic number and suppose there exist distinct k, l ∈ Z>0 such that αk and αl are conjugate. Then α = 0 or α is a root of unity.
sources.match: Exactly the statement (the source follows Dobrowolski 1979).

sources.excerpt: An alternative argument, based on the theory of the Weil height, is to note that α2 = σ(α4) implies that 2h(α) = h(α2) = h(α4) = 4h(α), hence h(α) = 0, and once again α is a root of unity.

nodes.title: Dobrowolski's house bound ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²)
nodes.statement: Let α be a nonzero algebraic integer of degree d that is not a root of unity. Then ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²), e = exp(1). Equivalently: if ⌈α⌉ ≤ 1 + 1/(4ed²) then α = 0 or α is a root of unity.
hypotheses: α algebraic integer; the bound is for the house (maximal modulus of a conjugate).
proofSteps: Choose a prime p with 2ed < p ≤ 4ed (Bertrand, Nat.exists_prime_lt_and_le_two_mul with n = ⌊2ed⌋).
Suppose ⌈α⌉ ≤ 1 + 1/(4ed²). For 1 ≤ n ≤ d: |s_{np}| ≤ d⌈α⌉^{np} ≤ d(1 + 1/(4ed²))^{4ed²} ≤ de and |sₙ| ≤ de (1 + t ≤ eᵗ, Real.add_one_le_exp), so |s_{np} − sₙ| ≤ 2de < p.
With s_{np} ≡ sₙ (mod p) (CA.6/power-sum-frobenius-congruence) this forces s_{np} = sₙ for n = 1, …, d.
So the multisets {αᵢ^p} and {αᵢ} have the same first d power sums and are equal (CA.6/multiset-eq-of-power-sums-eq): α^p is a conjugate of α.
p ≠ 1, so α = 0 or a root of unity (CA.6/conjugate-powers-root-of-unity), a contradiction.
acceptance: d = 2: every quadratic non-torsion algebraic integer has ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(16e) = 1.0230; e.g. ⌈φ⌉ = 1.618.

sources.excerpt: Let α be a non-zero algebraic integer of degree d. Suppose ⌈α⌉ ≤ 1 + 1/(4ed2), where e = 2.718 . . . . Then α is either zero or a root of unity.

sources.excerpt: Hence, |σnp −σn| ≤ |σnp| + |σn| ≤ 2de < p. (7) Combining (6) and (7) we obtain σnp = σn.

nodes.title: N(f_α(α^p)) is divisible by p^d
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, α ∈ K an algebraic integer with minimal polynomial f_α = minpoly ℤ α, and p a prime. Then N_{K/ℚ}(f_α(α^p)) is a rational integer divisible by p^{[K:ℚ]} (for K = ℚ(α): by p^d, d = deg α).
hypotheses: α integral over ℤ.
proofSteps: f_α(X^p) − f_α(X)^p = p·g(X) with g ∈ ℤ[X] (CA.6/frobenius-congruence-integer-polynomial in one variable).
At X = α: f_α(α^p) = p·g(α).
N_{K/ℚ}(p·g(α)) = p^{[K:ℚ]} N_{K/ℚ}(g(α)), and N(g(α)) is an integer (Algebra.isIntegral_norm, ℤ integrally closed).
acceptance: α = 2, p = 3: f_α = X − 2, f_α(8) = 6, divisible by 3.
α = i, p = 2: f_α(i²) = f_α(−1) = 2 and N_{ℚ(i)/ℚ}(2) = 4 is divisible by 2².

nodes.title: A prime p with F(α^p) ≠ 0 in a dyadic range
nodes.statement: Let α be a nonzero algebraic integer of degree d, not a root of unity, with deg(αⁿ) = d for all n ≥ 1. Let F ∈ ℤ[X] be nonzero of degree N with N/d ≥ 13, and x = 3(N/d) log(N/d). Then there is a prime p with x < p ≤ 2x and F(α^p) ≠ 0.
hypotheses: N/d ≥ 13 (the source's justification 'y ≥ 10' is insufficient, ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E703).
α ≠ 0, which the source omits (for α = 0 and F = X^{13} the conclusion fails, ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E716).
proofSteps: For distinct primes p, q the numbers α^p, α^q are not conjugate (CA.6/conjugate-powers-root-of-unity), so their minimal polynomials, of degree d each, are distinct and coprime.
If ζ primes p ∈ (x, 2x] have F(α^p) = 0, the product of the ζ minimal polynomials divides F, so dζ ≤ N.
Rosser–Schoenfeld: π(2x) − π(x) > 3x/(5 log x) for x ≥ 41/2 (requested from AnalyticNumberTheory:AN.2); here x ≥ 3·13·log 13 > 100.
With y = N/d ≥ 13: 3x/(5 log x) = 9y log y/(5 log(3y log y)) > y ⟺ y⁴ > 243 (log y)⁵, true for y ≥ 13 (28561 > 26950 at y = 13, and y⁴/(log y)⁵ increases for log y > 5/4). So π(2x) − π(x) > ζ.
acceptance: y = 13: x = 100.0…, 3x/(5 log x) = 13.03 > 13 = y; at y = 10 the inequality 9.79 > 10 fails.

sources.excerpt: Let α be an algebraic number of degree d, not a root of unity, and suppose deg(αn) = d for all integers n ≥ 1. Let F ∈ Z[X] be a non-zero polynomial of degree N and assume N/d ≥ 13. Define x := 3(N/d) log(N/d).
sources.match: Exactly the hypotheses; the conclusion is 'there exists a prime p such that F(αp) ≠ 0 and x < p ≤ 2x'.

nodes.title: Reduction when a power of α has smaller degree
nodes.statement: Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d with M(α) > 1, and suppose deg(αⁿ) < d for some n ≥ 1. Then there is an algebraic integer β with deg β < d and 1 < M(β) ≤ M(α).
hypotheses: α algebraic integer (the source states the lemma for algebraic numbers, but its computation of M(β) is valid for algebraic integers only, ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E707).
proofSteps: Let f be the monic minimal polynomial of α over ℚ(αⁿ), of degree r = [ℚ(α) : ℚ(αⁿ)] ≥ 2, and β = f(0) ∈ ℚ(αⁿ), an algebraic integer with deg β ≤ deg αⁿ < d.
f divides Xⁿ − αⁿ = ∏(X − ζᵏα), so β = ±ζᵐ α^r for an n-th root of unity ζ; hence |σ(β)| = |σ(α)|^r for every embedding σ of ℚ(α).
Each conjugate of β occurs [ℚ(α) : ℚ(β)] ≥ r times among the σ(β), so M(β) = (∏_σ max(1, |σ(α)|))^{r/[ℚ(α):ℚ(β)]} ≤ M(α).
M(α) > 1 gives some |σ(α)| > 1, so |σ(β)| > 1 and M(β) > 1.
acceptance: α = √2 (degree 2, M(α) = 2): α² = 2 has degree 1; f = X² − 2, r = 2, β = f(0) = −2, and 1 < M(β) = 2 ≤ M(α) = 2.

nodes.title: Dobrowolski's auxiliary polynomial
nodes.statement: Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d, and N, M positive integers with M ≥ 3, N ≥ 10 and dM < N/2. Then there is a nonzero F ∈ ℤ[X] of degree ≤ N with f_α^M ∣ F (α is a zero of multiplicity ≥ M) and max_i |F_i| ≤ N^{2dM²/N} M(α)^{2M}.
hypotheses: α algebraic integer; M(α) = ∏ max(1, |σ_k(α)|).
proofSteps: The conditions F^{(i)}(α)/i! = Σ_j C(j, i) F_j α^{j−i} = 0 for 0 ≤ i ≤ M − 1 are M linear equations over ℚ(α) in the N + 1 integer unknowns F_0, …, F_N, with algebraic-integer coefficients a_ij = C(j, i)α^{j−i} (the row i has the entry a_ii = 1 ≠ 0).

Siegel's lemma over ℚ(α) in product form (requested from DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0) gives a nonzero integer solution with max |F_j| ≤ ((2√2(N+1))^{dM} ∏_k ∏_i max_j |σ_k(a_ij)|)^{1/(N+1−dM)}.
max_j |C(j,i) σ_k(α)^{j−i}| ≤ N^i max(1, |σ_k α|)^N, and ∏_k ∏_{i<M} gives N^{dM²/2} M(α)^{MN}.
2√2(N + 1) ≤ N^{M/2} (N ≥ 10, M ≥ 3) and N − dM ≥ N/2 give the bound N^{2dM²/N} M(α)^{2M}.
The vanishing of F, F′, …, F^{(M−1)} at α gives f_α^M ∣ F in ℚ[X], hence in ℤ[X] as f_α is monic.
acceptance: α = τ₁₀, M = 20, N = 4000: F = (Φ₆ L)^{20} satisfies the bound (‖F‖ = 1.997·10⁹ ≤ 1.058·10¹⁰, Berrevoets Example 4.10).

sources.excerpt: Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d. Let N, M be positive integers satisfying M ≥ 3, N ≥ 10, dM < N/2. Then there exists a non-zero polynomial F ∈ Z[X] with deg F ≤ N, such that α is a zero of F of multiplicity M

nodes.title: Dobrowolski's lower bound for the Mahler measure
nodes.statement: Let α be a nonzero algebraic number of degree d ≥ 2 that is not a root of unity. Then M(α) ≥ 1 + (1/11700)·(log log d / log d)³. Here M(α) is the Mahler measure of the primitive minimal polynomial (DT.0), equal to absMulHeight₁(α)^d; equivalently d·h(α) ≥ log(1 + (1/11700)(log log d/log d)³).
hypotheses: d ≥ 2 (for d = 2 the right-hand side is below 1, since log log 2 < 0, and the statement is immediate).

The constant 1/11700 is the one the source read proves; Dobrowolski's own constant 1/1200 and Voutier's 1/4 (Smyth's survey, (11) and Section 4.2) are proved in papers not read here and are not targets of this node.
proofSteps: Non-integral α: the leading coefficient a₀ ≥ 2 of the primitive minimal polynomial gives M(α) ≥ 2 (DT.0 API leadingCoeff_le_mahlerMeasure) (source gap ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E705). Assume α integral.
d ≤ 20: M(α) ≥ ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²) ≥ 1 + 1/(4e·400) > 1 + (1/11700)(1/e)³ ≥ the bound, since log log x/log x ≤ 1/e (CA.6/dobrowolski-house-bound, CA.6/house-mahler-measure-comparison).

If deg αⁿ < d for some n, pass to β of CA.6/degree-drop-mahler-measure and use strong induction on d: for deg β ≥ 21 the bound is non-increasing in the degree (log log x/log x decreases for x ≥ e^e), for 2 ≤ deg β ≤ 20 use the previous step, for deg β = 1 M(β) = |β| ≥ 2 (source gap ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E706). Assume deg αⁿ = d for all n ≥ 1.
d ≥ 21: M := ⌈7 log d/log log d⌉ (≥ 20), N := dM². CA.6/dobrowolski-auxiliary-polynomial gives F; CA.6/exists-prime-power-not-root gives a prime p ∈ (3M² log M², 6M² log M²] with F(α^p) ≠ 0.
Upper bound: |N(F(α^p))| ≤ ‖F‖^d M(α)^{pN} (each |F(σ_k α^p)| ≤ ‖F‖ max(1, |σ_k α|)^{pN}).
Lower bound: F = f_α^M g with g ∈ ℤ[X], so N(F(α^p)) = N(f_α(α^p))^M N(g(α^p)) is a nonzero integer divisible by p^{dM} (CA.6/norm-minpoly-pow-prime-dvd).

Hence p^M ≤ N^{1+2dM²/N} M(α)^{2M+pN/d}, i.e. (2M + pN/d) log M(α) ≥ M log p − 3 log N, and with 2M + pN/d ≤ 3pN/(2d), 3 log N ≤ 9 log d, M log p ≥ 2M log M ≥ 13 log d, log p/p ≥ 1/(6M²): log M(α) ≥ 4/(117M³) ≥ (1/11700)(log log d/log d)³ (M ≤ 7.368 log d/log log d for d ≥ 21).
Finally M(α) ≥ 1 + log M(α).
acceptance: d = 10 (Lehmer): the bound 1 + (1/11700)(log log 10/log 10)³ = 1.0000041 is below M(τ₁₀) = 1.176.
d = 21: the bound is 1 + (1/11700)(0.3657)³ = 1.0000042; the proof's choice is M = 20, N = 8400.

sources.excerpt: Let α be a non-zero algebraic number of degree d ≥ 2 that is not a root of unity. Then M(α) ≥ 1 + (1/11700)(log log d/ log d)^3.

nodes.title: The polynomial P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m)
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, a monic P ∈ R[X] of degree n and m ∈ ℕ, P_m is the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by x^m on the free R-module R[x]/(P) of rank n (basis 1, x, …, x^{n−1}, AdjoinRoot.powerBasis'). If P = ∏(X − αᵢ) over a field containing the roots, then P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m); in particular P_m ∈ ℤ[X] for P ∈ ℤ[X] monic.
hypotheses: P monic (so R[x]/(P) is free of rank deg P); m ≥ 0 arbitrary.
proofSteps: Define P_m := charpoly of Algebra.leftMulMatrix of x^m in the power basis of AdjoinRoot P.

Monic of degree n (Matrix.charpoly_monic); P_1 = P (charpoly_leftMulMatrix: the charpoly of the generator of a power basis is its minimal polynomial, which for AdjoinRoot of a monic P is P); P_0 = (X − 1)^n.
Base change: the power basis and the matrix commute with ring homomorphisms, so (P.map f)_m = (P_m).map f.

Over a field where P splits, the matrix of x is triangularisable with diagonal αᵢ, so that of x^m has diagonal αᵢ^m: P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m) (equivalently, the eigenvalues of a power are the powers of the eigenvalues).
(P_m)_k = P_{mk} from the root formula over a splitting field and base change injectivity for ℤ ⊂ ℂ.
For P = minpoly K α (L/K finite): P_m = (minpoly K α^m)^{[K(α):K(α^m)]} (the conjugates of α^m are the α_i^m, each repeated [K(α):K(α^m)] times).
Graeffe relation: P_2(X²) = (−1)^n P(X)P(−X).

sources.excerpt: Consider P(X) ∈ Z[X] an integer monic polynomial, with factorization P(X) = ∏n i=1(X −αi) over C. Deﬁne the ancillary sequence of integer polynomials (Pm)m∈N by Pm(X) := ∏n i=1(X −αm i ) ∈ Z[X].
sources.match: Exactly the object; the characteristic-polynomial construction is the intrinsic form that makes P_m ∈ ℤ[X] a definition rather than a claim.

nodes.title: Arnold–Smyth congruence P₄ ≡ P₂ (mod 4)
nodes.statement: For every monic P ∈ ℤ[X], P₄ − P₂ ∈ 4ℤ[X].
hypotheses: P monic with integer coefficients.
proofSteps: Coefficient of X^{n−1}: s₂ = e₁² − 2e₂ and s₄ = e₁⁴ + 2e₂² − 4(e₁²e₂ − e₁e₃ + e₄) (Newton), so s₄ − s₂ ≡ e₁²(e₁² − 1) + 2e₂(e₂ + 1) ≡ 0 (mod 4) for integers eᵢ (e₁²(e₁² − 1) ≡ 0 mod 4 in both parities, e₂(e₂ + 1) is even).

Coefficient of X^{n−k}: it is ± e_k(α₁^m, …, α_n^m) = ± s_m(β) for the k-fold products β = α_{i₁}⋯α_{i_k}, the roots of the k-th symmetric power polynomial ∏_I(X − α_I) ∈ ℤ[X] (fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials); apply the first step to that polynomial.
Hence every coefficient of P₄ − P₂ is divisible by 4.
acceptance: P = X − a: a⁴ ≡ a² (mod 4).
P = X² − X − 1: P₂ = X² − 3X + 1, P₄ = X² − 7X + 1, difference −4X.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.1, (2), and its proof, p. 4 (arXiv v1)
sources.excerpt: Then the following mod 4 congruence holds: (2) P4 ≡ P2 mod 4 Z[X].
sources.match: Exactly the statement (due to Arnold and Smyth); the proof is the symmetric-powers argument.

nodes.title: √(1 + 4Y) has integer coefficients
nodes.statement: There is T ∈ ℤ⟦Y⟧ with constant term 1 and T² = 1 + 4Y; explicitly T = 1 + 2Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k C_k Y^{k+1} with C_k the Catalan numbers, equivalently T = Σ_k C(1/2, k) 4^k Y^k.
hypotheses: Power series over ℤ.
proofSteps: With c(x) = Σ C_k x^k, the Catalan recurrence (catalan_succ) is c = 1 + x c² in ℤ⟦x⟧.
T = 1 − 2x c(x) at x = −Y; T² = 1 − 4x c + 4x²c² = 1 − 4x(c − x c²) = 1 − 4x = 1 + 4Y.

sources.excerpt: It is based on the observation that (3) √1 + 4Y = Σ∞ k=0 (1/2 choose k) 4kY k ∈ Z[[Y ]].
sources.match: Exactly the statement; the Catalan form is the proof of integrality.

nodes.title: Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)
nodes.statement: Let Q ∈ ℤ[X] with Q(0) = 1 and Q a square modulo 4 (Q = U² + 4V with U, V ∈ ℤ[X]). Then there is S ∈ ℤ⟦X⟧ with S(0) = 1 and S² = Q. In particular, for P ∈ ℤ[X] monic with P* = X^n P(1/X), √(P₂*·P₄*) ∈ 1 + Xℤ⟦X⟧.
proofSteps: Normalise U(0) = 1, V(0) = 0: from Q(0) = U(0)² + 4V(0) = 1, U(0) = ±1, V(0) = 0; replace U by −U if needed.
U is a unit of ℤ⟦X⟧ and Y := V/U² ∈ Xℤ⟦X⟧; S := U·T(Y) with T from CA.6/sqrt-one-add-four-integral (substitution of a series without constant term).
S² = U²(1 + 4V/U²) = Q, and S(0) = 1.
For P monic: (P₂P₄)* = P₂*P₄* has constant term 1 and is ≡ (P₂*)² (mod 4) by CA.6/root-power-polynomial-congruence (reversal commutes with reduction mod 4).
acceptance: Q = 1 − 4X = 1² + 4(−X) (Catalan): S = 1 − 2X − 2X² − 4X³ − ….
Q = 1 − 6X + X² = (1 − X)² + 4(−X) (large Schröder numbers): S ∈ ℤ⟦X⟧.

sources.locator: Proposition 2.2 and its proof, p. 4 (arXiv v1)
sources.excerpt: Consider a polynomial Q ∈ Z[X] such that Q(0) = 1 and Q mod 4 is a perfect square in (Z/4)[X]. Then the square radical √Q(X) has an X = 0 Taylor expansion with integer coeﬃcients: √Q(X) ∈ 1 + XZ[[X]].
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: When P₂P₄ is a square (Dimitrov Lemma 2.3)
nodes.statement: Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic irreducible of degree n > 1 with P₂ not a perfect square. Then the following are equivalent: (i) P = Φ_N for an odd N; (ii) P₂ = P₄; (iii) P₂P₄ is a perfect square in ℤ[X]; (iv) P₂P₄ is a square in ℚ(X) (the function √(P₂P₄) is rational).
hypotheses: P irreducible and P₂ not a square; then P₂ is irreducible (P₂ = (minpoly α²)^{[ℚ(α):ℚ(α²)]} with exponent 1 or 2, API rootPowPoly_eq_minpoly_pow), a step the source leaves implicit (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E709).
proofSteps: (i) ⇒ (ii): for N odd, squaring permutes the primitive N-th roots of unity, so P₂ = P₄ = Φ_N.
(ii) ⇒ (iii) ⇒ (iv): P₂P₄ = P₂².
(iv) ⇒ (iii): a monic integer polynomial that is a square in ℚ(X) is the square of a monic polynomial in ℚ[X], which has integer coefficients (Gauss).

(iii) ⇒ (i): P₂ is irreducible and squarefree, so its roots occur in P₄: α² = σ(α)⁴ for some σ in the Galois group; iterating k = ord σ times, α² = α^{2^{k+1}}, so α is a root of unity (or use CA.6/conjugate-powers-root-of-unity with α² and α⁴ conjugate); then P = Φ_N, and P₂ = Φ_N not a square with P₂ = P₄ forces N odd (for N even, squaring halves the level or is 2-to-1).
acceptance: P = Φ₃: P₂ = P₄ = Φ₃.
P = Φ₄ = X² + 1: P₂ = (X + 1)² is a square (excluded by the hypothesis).
P = X² − X − 1: P₂ = X² − 3X + 1, P₄ = X² − 7X + 1, P₂P₄ not a square.

sources.excerpt: Suppose that P(X) ∈ Z[X] is a monic integer irreducible polynomial of deg P > 1, such that P2(X) is not a perfect square. Then the following are equivalent: (i) P is a cyclotomic polynomial of an odd level; (ii) P2 = P4; (iii) P2P4 is a perfect square; (iv) the function √P2P4 is rational.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture
nodes.statement: Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic irreducible of degree n > 1 and not cyclotomic. Then P has a complex root of modulus at least 2^{1/(4n)} = 1 + log 2/(4n) + O(1/n²). Equivalently, a nonzero algebraic integer α of degree n > 1 that is not a root of unity has ⌈α⌉ ≥ 2^{1/(4n)}.
hypotheses: Cyclotomic means P = Φ_N for some N, i.e. its roots are roots of unity.
This settles the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + c/d with c = log 2/4 − ε asymptotically.
proofSteps: Suppose all roots have modulus < 2^{1/(4n)}. Reverse: P* = ∏(1 − αᵢX), P*(0) = 1; P₂*, P₄* are the reverses of P₂, P₄ (CA.6/root-power-polynomial).
f(1/X) := √(P₂*(1/X) P₄*(1/X)) ∈ ℤ⟦1/X⟧ (CA.6/integral-square-root-power-series).

f continues analytically to the complement of the hedgehog K = union of the segments [0, αᵢ²], [0, αᵢ⁴], whose transfinite diameter is ≤ (max|αᵢ|^{8n}/4)^{1/(2n)} < 1 by Dubinin's theorem (gap: transfinite diameter and Dubinin's theorem are planned by no roadmap).
By Bertrandias's rationality theorem (Pólya–Carlson type: an integer power series in 1/X analytic off a compact set of transfinite diameter < 1 is rational; gap) f is rational, so P₂P₄ is a square.
If P₂ is not a square, CA.6/root-power-polynomial-square-cyclotomic makes P cyclotomic, a contradiction.

If P₂ is a square, P₂ = Q² with Q = minpoly α₁², deg Q = n/2, roots αᵢ²; Q is not cyclotomic. If n/2 > 1, induction gives a root of Q of modulus ≥ 2^{1/(2n)}, i.e. |αᵢ| ≥ 2^{1/(4n)}; if n/2 = 1, Q = X − b with |b| ≥ 2 and |αᵢ| = √|b| ≥ 2^{1/8} (the base case the source omits, ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E710).
acceptance: Cyclotomic Φ_N has all roots of modulus 1: the hypothesis cannot be dropped.

nodes.title: The ring of integers as a module over the group ring
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative ring, B a commutative A-algebra and G a group acting on B by ring automorphisms that commute with the action of A (G acts by A-algebra automorphisms). The Galois representation of G on B is the A-linear representation g ↦ (x ↦ g·x), and the group ring A[G] (Mathlib's MonoidAlgebra A G) acts on B on the left by (Σ_g a_g g)·x = Σ_g a_g g(x); this makes B a left A[G]-module whose restriction to A is the given A-module structure. The principal case is a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields with G = Gal(L/K), A = 𝓞_K and B = 𝓞_L, where the action is the restriction of the Galois action on L; the same construction with A = K and B = L gives L as a K[G]-module, and the inclusion 𝓞_L ⊆ L is 𝓞_K[G]-linear. When G is a Galois group for B/A in Mathlib's sense (IsGaloisGroup G A B: faithful action, commuting with A, with invariants the image of A), the norm element N = Σ_g g acts on B with values in A, and for rings of integers it acts as the trace.
hypotheses: A is a commutative ring and B a commutative A-algebra.
G is a group acting on B by ring automorphisms commuting with A: [MulSemiringAction G B] and [SMulCommClass G A B].
The Galois-group hypothesis IsGaloisGroup G A B is needed only for the statements about invariants and the norm element.
The group ring acts on the left; a right action is never used.
proofSteps: Define the representation as Mathlib's Representation.ofDistribMulAction A G B; its value at g is the A-linear map x ↦ g·x.
Take the A[G]-module to be the representation's asModule, with the identification toGroupRingModule : B ≃ₗ[A] ρ.asModule; the module structure is Module.compHom along asAlgebraHom.
Check the evaluation formula on single g a and the scalar tower A → A[G] → B from the definition of asAlgebraHom as MonoidAlgebra.lift.
For invariants use the IsInvariant field of IsGaloisGroup: the fixed points of G in B are the image of A.

For rings of integers, the instance IsGaloisGroup Gal(L/K) 𝓞_K 𝓞_L is found by instance inference at the pin, and trace_eq_sum_automorphisms gives Σ_σ σ(x) = Tr_{L/K}(x); restrict to 𝓞_L through Algebra.algebraMap_intTrace.
acceptance: The underlying A-module of the group-ring module is the A-module B: the scalar tower A → A[G] → B holds.
single g 1 acts as g, and the identity of the group ring acts as the identity.

For number fields the norm element acts as the trace 𝓞_L → 𝓞_K followed by the inclusion; a construction that let G act through a quotient or through a non-faithful action would fail the invariants characterisation.

nodes.title: The rational normal basis map K[G] ≅ L
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of fields with group G. An element θ of L is a normal basis generator if its conjugates (σθ)_{σ∈G} are K-linearly independent, equivalently span L, equivalently form a K-basis of L. For a generator θ the map K[G] → L, x ↦ x·θ, is an isomorphism of left K[G]-modules, sending single σ c to c·σ(θ). Mathlib's IsGalois.normalBasis supplies the canonical generator θ₀ = normalBasis K L 1, and the normal basis map of L/K is the map attached to θ₀. For number fields, A = 𝓞_K and B = 𝓞_L, the map carries the group ring 𝓞_K[G] onto the 𝓞_K-lattice 𝓞_K[G]·θ₀ of L, which in general is not 𝓞_L.
hypotheses: L/K is a finite Galois extension of fields: [FiniteDimensional K L] [IsGalois K L].
The group ring acts on L through the Galois representation of the construction ring-of-integers-as-group-ring-module with A = K and B = L.
proofSteps: Linear independence of the conjugates is IsGenerator; since the index set G has cardinality [L : K] (IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank), independence is equivalent to spanning and to being a basis (basisOfLinearIndependentOfCardEqFinrank).
Mathlib's IsGalois.normalBasis is a basis indexed by G with normalBasis_apply: normalBasis σ = σ(normalBasis 1); hence normalBasis 1 is a generator.
Define equivOfGenerator θ as the composite of the K-linear equivalence K[G] ≃ (G →₀ K) with the representation isomorphism of the basis σ ↦ σθ.
K[G]-linearity: for σ, τ ∈ G, (single σ 1)·(τθ) = (στ)θ, which is the image of single σ 1 * single τ 1; extend by linearity.
acceptance: equiv K L (single σ 1) = σ(normalBasis K L 1).
In a nontrivial extension 1 is never a generator, and over the trivial group every nonzero element is one.
For ℚ(i)/ℚ the element 1 + i is a generator, since its conjugates 1 + i and 1 − i are linearly independent.

nodes.statement: Let L/K be finite Galois with group G and let θ be a normal basis generator. An element β of L is a normal basis generator if and only if β = u·θ for a unit u of K[G]; the unit is unique.
hypotheses: L/K finite Galois; θ a normal basis generator.
proofSteps: By the normal basis map, β = u·θ for a unique u ∈ K[G].
β is a generator exactly when x ↦ x·β = (x u)·θ is bijective, that is when right multiplication by u on K[G] is bijective.
K[G] is finite dimensional over K, so right multiplication by u is bijective exactly when it is injective, exactly when u is a unit.

nodes.title: Normal integral bases
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative ring, B a commutative A-algebra and G a finite Galois group of B/A (IsGaloisGroup G A B). An element α of B generates a normal integral basis if its conjugates (g·α)_{g∈G} form an A-basis of B: they are A-linearly independent and span B. Equivalently the A[G]-linear map A[G] → B, x ↦ x·α, is bijective, so B is free of rank one over A[G] with basis α. B has a normal integral basis over A if some α generates one. For a finite Galois extension of number fields L/K the relevant case is A = 𝓞_K, B = 𝓞_L, G = Gal(L/K); for a finite Galois extension of nonarchimedean local fields it is A = 𝒪_K, B = 𝒪_L.
hypotheses: G is finite and is a Galois group of B/A in Mathlib's sense.
The basis is indexed by G itself, as in Mathlib's IsGalois.normalBasis, not by an arbitrary finite type.
proofSteps: Define IsNIBGenerator α as the conjunction of LinearIndependent A (g ↦ g·α) and span = ⊤, and HasNIB as the existence of such α.
Build the basis with Module.Basis.mk and record basis_apply: basis g = g·α.
The bijectivity characterisation: x ↦ x·α sends single g a to a·gα, so bijectivity is exactly the basis property of (gα)_g.
Change of generator: if α and β generate, the A[G]-linear automorphism of A[G] carrying 1 to the coordinate vector of β is right multiplication by a unit.
Compatibility with the field: for number fields an 𝓞_K-basis of 𝓞_L is a K-basis of L (𝓞_L is a lattice spanning L), so a normal integral basis generator is a normal basis generator of L/K.
acceptance: ζ_p generates a normal integral basis of ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ for an odd prime p.
1 never generates a normal integral basis of a nontrivial extension.
ℚ(i)/ℚ has none, although 1 + i generates a rational normal basis.

nodes.title: The trace of a normal integral basis generator generates for a Galois subextension
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of number fields with group G, let F be an intermediate field with F/K Galois, H = Gal(L/F) and Γ = Gal(F/K) ≅ G/H. If α ∈ 𝓞_L generates a normal integral basis of L/K then Tr_{L/F}(α) ∈ 𝓞_F generates a normal integral basis of F/K.
hypotheses: L/K and F/K finite Galois, K ⊆ F ⊆ L number fields.
The trace is Mathlib's Algebra.intTrace 𝓞_F 𝓞_L.
proofSteps: Write x ∈ 𝓞_F as x = Σ_g c(g) g(α) with unique c(g) ∈ 𝓞_K.
Since h(x) = x for h ∈ H and the coefficients are unique, c(h⁻¹g) = c(g) for h ∈ H.
Choose lifts σ̃ of σ ∈ Γ; regroup the sum as Σ_σ c(σ̃) Σ_{h∈H} hσ̃(α) = Σ_σ c(σ̃) σ(Tr_{L/F}(α)), using that H is normal.
Linear independence of (σ(Tr_{L/F} α))_σ over 𝓞_K follows from that of (gα)_g, since the lifts times H partition G.

nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of number fields with a normal integral basis, and F an intermediate field. Then Tr_{L/F}(𝓞_L) = 𝓞_F; in particular Tr_{L/K}(𝓞_L) = 𝓞_K. In the Galois-group form: if B has a normal integral basis over A for the Galois group G, then Tr_{B/A} : B → A is surjective.
hypotheses: L/K finite Galois; F any intermediate field (F/K need not be Galois: the regrouping runs over the cosets of Gal(L/F) in G).
proofSteps: Tr_{L/F}(𝓞_L) ⊆ 𝓞_F always.
For x ∈ 𝓞_F, the regrouping of the previous lemma writes x = Tr_{L/F}(Σ_σ c(σ̃)σ̃(α)) with Σ_σ c(σ̃)σ̃(α) ∈ 𝓞_L.

nodes.title: Tamely ramified extensions of Dedekind domains
nodes.statement: Let B/A be an extension of commutative rings and P a prime of B lying over p = P ∩ A. B/A is tamely ramified at P if the residue extension (B/P)/(A/p) is separable and the characteristic of A/p does not divide the ramification index e(P|p) (Mathlib's P.ramificationIdx A). B/A is tamely ramified if it is tamely ramified at every nonzero prime of B. When the residue fields are finite (number fields, nonarchimedean local fields) the separability condition holds automatically and the condition is p ∤ e(P|p) for every P, which is the definition of the sources; the separability clause is the convention of Tau Ceti's NumberFieldArithmetic roadmap, so that the predicate is correct in every characteristic.
hypotheses: The ramification index is the unprimed Mathlib P.ramificationIdx A (prime P of B first, base ring A second).
The base prime is P.under A with the LiesOver instance Ideal.over_under.
The residue characteristic is ringChar (A ⧸ P.under A).
proofSteps: Define IsTamelyRamifiedAt P as separability of the residue algebra (Ideal.Quotient.algebraOfLiesOver) together with non-divisibility of the ramification index.
Define IsTamelyRamified as tameness at every nonzero prime of B.
Finite residue fields: a finite field is perfect, so every finite extension of it is separable; this gives the simplified form.

Towers: for A ⊆ B ⊆ C Dedekind, ramification indices multiply (Mathlib's ramificationIdxIn_mul_ramificationIdxIn in the Galois case, and the multiplicativity of e in general), residue separability is transitive, and every prime of B lies under a prime of C; so C/A is tame exactly when C/B and B/A are.
acceptance: ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ is tame for an odd prime p: the only ramified prime is p with e = p − 1.
ℚ(i)/ℚ is not tame: 2 ramifies with e = 2.
An unramified extension (e = 1 everywhere) is tame.

nodes.title: The trace modulo a prime in a Galois extension
nodes.statement: Let B/A be a finite extension of Dedekind domains with a finite Galois group G (IsGaloisGroup G A B), p a nonzero prime of A with pB = (P_1⋯P_g)^e, and x ∈ B. In A/p, Tr_{(B/pB)/(A/p)}(x mod pB) = e·Σ_{i=1}^{g} Tr_{(B/P_i)/(A/p)}(x mod P_i); and by Mathlib this is (Tr_{B/A} x) mod p.
hypotheses: p nonzero maximal; e = p.ramificationIdxIn B, the common ramification index of the primes over p in the Galois case.
proofSteps: The Chinese remainder theorem identifies B/pB with Π_i B/P_i^e.

Each B/P_i^e has the filtration by P_i^j/P_i^e whose successive quotients P_i^j/P_i^{j+1} are one-dimensional B/P_i-spaces; in a basis adapted to the filtration, multiplication by x is block upper triangular with e diagonal blocks equal to multiplication by x mod P_i on B/P_i.
The trace of a block triangular matrix is the sum of the traces of the diagonal blocks.
Mathlib's Algebra.trace_quotient_eq_of_isDedekindDomain identifies the left side with the reduction of Algebra.intTrace A B x.
acceptance: For p unramified (e = 1) the formula is the sum of the residue traces.
For ℤ[i] and p = 2 (e = 2, g = 1) both sides vanish identically in 𝔽_2.

nodes.title: A prime divides the trace ideal exactly when it is not tame
nodes.statement: Let B/A be a finite extension of Dedekind domains with a finite Galois group G, and p a nonzero prime of A. Then Tr_{B/A}(B) ⊆ p if and only if some prime P of B over p is not tamely ramified.
hypotheses: Galois case: all primes over p have the same ramification index.
Tr_{B/A}(B) is an ideal of A.
proofSteps: If some P over p is not tame: either the residue characteristic divides e, and then equation (5) is e·(…) = 0 in A/p for every x; or some residue extension is inseparable, and then all residue extensions are (they are conjugate under G) and every residue trace vanishes (Mathlib's Algebra.trace_eq_zero_of_not_isSeparable). Either way Tr(x) ∈ p for all x.

If every P over p is tame: the residue extension of P_1 is separable, so its trace is nonzero (Algebra.trace_ne_zero); choose β_1 with nonzero residue trace, and by the Chinese remainder theorem β ≡ β_1 mod P_1, β ≡ 0 mod P_i (i ≠ 1). Then Tr(β) ≡ e·Tr(β_1) ≠ 0 mod p since p ∤ e.
acceptance: For ℤ[i]/ℤ and p = 2: Tr(ℤ[i]) = 2ℤ ⊆ (2).
For ℤ[ζ_p]/ℤ, p odd: Tr(ℤ[ζ_p]) = ℤ is contained in no prime.

nodes.statement: If B/A (a finite extension of Dedekind domains with finite Galois group G) has a normal integral basis, then B/A is tamely ramified. In particular a finite Galois extension of number fields or of nonarchimedean local fields with a normal integral basis is tamely ramified.

nodes.title: ℚ(i)/ℚ: a rational normal basis that is not integral
nodes.statement: For the Gaussian field L = ℚ(i) with G = Gal(L/ℚ) = {1, σ}: 1 + i generates a normal basis of L/ℚ, but L/ℚ has no normal integral basis. Concretely, for α = a + bi ∈ ℤ[i] the conjugates a + bi, a − bi have change-of-basis determinant −2ab relative to {1, i}, never ±1; equivalently Tr(ℤ[i]) = 2ℤ ≠ ℤ, and 2 is wildly ramified.
hypotheses: L is the cyclotomic field ℚ(ζ_4) = ℚ(i).
proofSteps: 1 + i: the conjugates 1 + i, 1 − i are linearly independent (determinant −2i ≠ 0).
No normal integral basis: ℚ(i)/ℚ is not tame (tamely-ramified, test tame_test_gaussian_not_tame), so Speiser applies; or directly, Tr(a + bi) = 2a.

nodes.title: Rim's criterion for projectivity over a group ring
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, G a finite group and M a left R[G]-module that is projective as an R-module. If there is an R-linear endomorphism φ of M with Σ_{g∈G} g·φ(g⁻¹·m) = m for all m ∈ M, then M is projective as an R[G]-module.
hypotheses: G finite; M projective over R; the scalar tower R → R[G] → M.
proofSteps: The induced module R[G] ⊗_R M (R[G] acting on the left factor) is R[G]-projective, being the base change of the projective R-module M.
The multiplication map μ : R[G] ⊗_R M → M, x ⊗ m ↦ x·m, is R[G]-linear and surjective.
s(m) = Σ_g g ⊗ φ(g⁻¹m) is R[G]-linear (reindex the sum) and μ ∘ s = id by the hypothesis.
So M is a direct summand of a projective R[G]-module (Module.Projective.of_split).
acceptance: If |G| is a unit in R, φ = |G|⁻¹·id works, so every R-projective module is R[G]-projective (Maschke).
For M = 𝓞_L and φ = multiplication by c with Tr(c) = 1 the hypothesis is Σ_g g(c) = 1.

sources.excerpt: By Rim [8, Prop. 2.3, p. 702] it is enough to show 𝔄 is O_F-projective and there exists an O_F-endomorphism ρ: 𝔄 → 𝔄 such that Σ σρ(σ⁻¹a) = a for all a ∈ 𝔄.

nodes.title: Ullom: tame ramification makes the integers projective over the group ring
nodes.statement: Let B/A be a finite extension of Dedekind domains with finite Galois group G. If B/A is tamely ramified then B is a projective A[G]-module (and projective over A[H] for every subgroup H). In particular, for a tame finite Galois extension of number fields, 𝓞_L is a finitely generated projective 𝓞_K[G]-module.
hypotheses: Galois case; tame.
proofSteps: B is finitely generated and torsion free over the Dedekind domain A, hence A-projective.
Tameness gives c ∈ B with Tr_{B/A}(c) = 1 (tame-iff-trace-surjective); the trace is Σ_g g (ring-of-integers-as-group-ring-module).
Take φ = multiplication by c: Σ_g g(c·g⁻¹(m)) = m·Σ_g g(c) = m.
Apply Rim's criterion.

For ℚ(i)/ℚ the module ℤ[i] is not ℤ[G]-projective (the converse direction, trace-surjective-of-projective).

nodes.title: Projectivity over the group ring forces the trace to be surjective
nodes.statement: Let B/A be a finite extension of Dedekind domains with finite Galois group G. If B is projective as an A[G]-module then Tr_{B/A}(B) = A; hence B/A is tamely ramified.

proofSteps: For the free module A[G], the invariants are A·N with N = Σ_g g, and N·A[G] = A·N: the invariants equal the image of the norm.
The equality of invariants and norm image passes to direct sums and direct summands, so it holds for every projective A[G]-module.
For B: the invariants are A (IsGaloisGroup) and the image of the norm is Tr(B); so Tr(B) = A.
Conclude tameness by tame-iff-trace-surjective.

nodes.title: Unramified local extensions have a normal integral basis
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite unramified Galois extension of nonarchimedean local fields with group G. Then 𝒪_L has a normal integral basis over 𝒪_K; more precisely, any lift α ∈ 𝒪_L of a normal basis generator of the residue extension l/k generates one.
hypotheses: A is a complete discrete valuation ring with finite residue field k of cardinality q and characteristic p (the ring of integers of a nonarchimedean local field K, in the vocabulary of the LocalFieldsRamification roadmap); K = Frac A.
L/K is a finite Galois extension with group G and B is the integral closure of A in L (the valuation ring of L); IsGaloisGroup G A B.
L/K unramified: e = 1.
proofSteps: Unramified Galois: reduction identifies G with Gal(l/k) (LocalFieldsRamification Layer 2, residue correspondence), and p𝒪_L = 𝔓 is the maximal ideal of 𝒪_L.
l/k is a finite Galois extension of finite fields, so it has a normal basis generator ᾱ (Mathlib's normal basis theorem in the finite case).
Let α lift ᾱ and M = 𝒪_K[G]·α ⊆ 𝒪_L. Then M/pM → 𝒪_L/p𝒪_L = l is onto, since its image is k[G]·ᾱ = l.
Hence 𝒪_L = M + p𝒪_L and Nakayama's lemma gives 𝒪_L = M; comparing ranks ([L : K] = |G|), (gα)_g is an 𝒪_K-basis.
acceptance: For K = ℚ_p and L the unramified extension of degree f, a lift of a normal basis generator of 𝔽_{p^f}/𝔽_p generates.
The trivial extension: α = 1.

nodes.title: Totally and tamely ramified local extensions have a normal integral basis
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a totally and tamely ramified Galois extension of nonarchimedean local fields of degree e, with a uniformiser π_L of L satisfying π_L^e = π_K, a uniformiser of K. Then for any units u_0, …, u_{e−1} of 𝒪_K, α = Σ_{j=0}^{e−1} u_j π_L^j generates a normal integral basis of L/K.
hypotheses: A is a complete discrete valuation ring with finite residue field k of cardinality q and characteristic p (the ring of integers of a nonarchimedean local field K, in the vocabulary of the LocalFieldsRamification roadmap); K = Frac A.
L/K is a finite Galois extension with group G and B is the integral closure of A in L (the valuation ring of L); IsGaloisGroup G A B.
L/K totally ramified of degree e = [L : K] with p ∤ e; π_L^e = π_K.
proofSteps: L/K is a cyclic Kummer extension: K contains a primitive e-th root of unity ζ and a generator σ of G acts by σ(π_L) = ζπ_L (LocalFieldsRamification Layer 3, tame totally ramified extensions and their Galois criterion).
𝒪_L = 𝒪_K[π_L] with basis 1, π_L, …, π_L^{e−1} (totally ramified: Eisenstein power basis, LocalFieldsRamification Layer 3).
σ^i(α) = Σ_j u_j ζ^{ij} π_L^j, so the change-of-basis matrix is (u_j ζ^{ij}) with determinant (Π u_k)·det(ζ^{ij}).
det(ζ^{ij}) is a Vandermonde determinant Π_{i<j}(ζ^j − ζ^i) = ζ^m Π_{i<j}(ζ^{j−i} − 1) (Matrix.det_vandermonde).
Each 1 − ζ^k (0 < k < e) divides Π_{k=1}^{e−1}(1 − ζ^k) = e (IsPrimitiveRoot.prod_one_sub_pow_eq_order), a unit since p ∤ e; so the determinant is a unit.
acceptance: The hypothesis p ∤ e is used exactly once, to make e a unit; the statement is false in the wild case (Speiser).

nodes.title: Normalising a uniformiser of a tame local extension
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite tamely ramified Galois extension of nonarchimedean local fields with ramification index e, residue degree f and residue field of K of cardinality q. Then e divides q^f − 1, and there are a uniformiser π_L of L and a (q^f − 1)-st root of unity v in L with π_L^e = v·π_K.
hypotheses: A is a complete discrete valuation ring with finite residue field k of cardinality q and characteristic p (the ring of integers of a nonarchimedean local field K, in the vocabulary of the LocalFieldsRamification roadmap); K = Frac A.
L/K is a finite Galois extension with group G and B is the integral closure of A in L (the valuation ring of L); IsGaloisGroup G A B.
L/K tamely ramified: p ∤ e.
proofSteps: Let L_0 be the maximal unramified subextension; L/L_0 is totally and tamely ramified Galois of degree e with group the inertia group I (LocalFieldsRamification Layers 2 and 3).
By the tame Galois criterion (LocalFieldsRamification Layer 3), I embeds in μ_e(L_0), and μ_e(L_0) injects into the residue field of L_0, which has q^f elements; so e | q^f − 1.
Write π_L^e = u·π_K with u ∈ 𝒪_L^×; let v be the Teichmüller lift of the residue of u (a (q^f − 1)-st root of unity, TauCeti.teichmuller).
v·π_K/π_L^e has residue 1; since p ∤ e, Hensel's lemma gives β ∈ 𝒪_L^× with β^e = v·π_K/π_L^e.
Replace π_L by βπ_L.
acceptance: In the wild case p | e the divisibility e | q^f − 1 fails, since q^f − 1 is prime to p.

nodes.title: The split tame extension above a tame local extension
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite tamely ramified Galois extension of nonarchimedean local fields with ramification index e and residue degree f, and let L′ be the unramified extension of L of degree e. Then L′/K is Galois and tame; its maximal unramified subextension L′_0 has degree ef over K; there is π′ ∈ L′ with π′^e = π_K; K′ = K(π′) is totally and tamely ramified of degree e over K; L′_0 ∩ K′ = K and L′ = L′_0·K′. Writing I = Gal(L′/L′_0) and Γ = Gal(L′/K′), I is normal in G′ = Gal(L′/K), I ∩ Γ = 1 and IΓ = G′.
hypotheses: A is a complete discrete valuation ring with finite residue field k of cardinality q and characteristic p (the ring of integers of a nonarchimedean local field K, in the vocabulary of the LocalFieldsRamification roadmap); K = Frac A.
L/K is a finite Galois extension with group G and B is the integral closure of A in L (the valuation ring of L); IsGaloisGroup G A B.
L/K tamely ramified with invariants e, f.
proofSteps: L′/K is Galois as the compositum of L with the unramified (hence Galois) extension L′_0 of K of degree ef (LocalFieldsRamification Layer 2).
e(L′/K) = e and f(L′/K) = ef by multiplicativity in towers; so L′/K is tame (tamely-ramified, tower stability).

With π_L, v from local-tame-uniformiser: (q^{ef} − 1) = (q^f − 1)(q^{f(e−1)} + … + 1) and the second factor is ≡ e ≡ 0 mod e, so e(q^f − 1) | q^{ef} − 1 and v = u^e for a (q^{ef} − 1)-st root of unity u ∈ L′_0.
π′ = u⁻¹π_L satisfies π′^e = π_K; X^e − π_K is Eisenstein, so K′ = K(π′) is totally ramified of degree e (LocalFieldsRamification Layer 3).
An unramified and a totally ramified extension meet in K, and degrees give L′ = L′_0 K′; Galois theory gives the group-theoretic splitting.

nodes.title: Normal integral bases multiply across a split extension
nodes.statement: Let N/K be a finite Galois extension with group G (of number fields or of nonarchimedean local fields), I a normal subgroup and Γ a subgroup with I ∩ Γ = 1 and IΓ = G; put N_0 = N^I and M = N^Γ. If β ∈ 𝒪_{N_0} generates a normal integral basis of N_0/K (group G/I ≅ Γ) and α ∈ 𝒪_M generates a normal integral basis of N/N_0 (group I), then αβ generates a normal integral basis of N/K.
hypotheses: G = IΓ with I normal and I ∩ Γ = 1, so every g ∈ G is uniquely hγ with h ∈ I, γ ∈ Γ.

nodes.title: Locally free lattices over an order
nodes.statement: Let A be a Dedekind domain with fraction field K and Λ an A-algebra that is finitely generated as an A-module (an A-order in the K-algebra K ⊗ Λ). A left Λ-module M is a locally free Λ-lattice of rank n if M is finitely generated over A and, for every nonzero prime v of A, the completion Â_v ⊗_A M is isomorphic to (Â_v ⊗_A Λ)^n as an Â_v ⊗_A Λ-module: there is an Â_v-linear isomorphism Â_v ⊗ M ≅ Â_v ⊗ Λ^n commuting with the action of every element of Λ. For Λ = A[G] and M = B with its group-ring structure, rank one local freeness says that at every v the completed module has a normal basis: Â_v ⊗ B = Â_v[G]·α_v.
hypotheses: A Dedekind domain, K its fraction field, Â_v = v.adicCompletionIntegers K.
Λ an A-algebra (possibly noncommutative), M a left Λ-module with the scalar tower A → Λ → M.
The rank n is a natural number; rank zero forces M = 0.
proofSteps: Define IsLocallyFreeOfRank as finite generation over A together with, for each HeightOneSpectrum v, an Â_v-linear equivalence commuting with the base changes of the maps DistribSMul.toLinearMap A M λ.
Free lattices: Λ^n is locally free of rank n (the identity equivalence).
Direct sums add ranks; isomorphic modules are simultaneously locally free.
Rank: tensoring the local isomorphism with Frac(Â_v) and comparing dimensions over K gives dim_K(K ⊗ M) = n·dim_K(K ⊗ Λ).
Group ring form: an Â_v[G]-isomorphism Â_v[G] ≅ Â_v ⊗ B is determined by the image b_1 of 1, and b_g = g·b_1.
acceptance: A nonprincipal ideal I of a Dedekind domain A is locally free of rank one over Λ = A, but not free: local freeness does not imply freeness.
ℤ[i] is not locally free of rank one over ℤ[C_2]: at 2 the completed module has no normal basis (local-noether).

nodes.title: Locally free lattices are projective
nodes.statement: Let A be a Dedekind domain and Λ an A-algebra finitely generated as an A-module. A locally free Λ-lattice of rank n is a finitely generated projective Λ-module.
hypotheses: Λ is module-finite over the noetherian ring A, hence left noetherian; M is finitely presented over Λ.
proofSteps: Projectivity of a finitely presented module is the exactness of Hom_Λ(M, −) on surjections.
For a flat commutative A-algebra A′, A′ ⊗ Hom_Λ(M, N) ≅ Hom_{A′⊗Λ}(A′ ⊗ M, A′ ⊗ N) since M is finitely presented.

Exactness of a sequence of A-modules is checked after localisation at every maximal ideal (Mathlib's local properties), and A_(v) → Â_v is faithfully flat (flat local homomorphism of noetherian local rings).
At every v, Â_v ⊗ M ≅ (Â_v ⊗ Λ)^n is free, so Hom out of it is exact; descend.
acceptance: Λ^n is projective.

nodes.title: Lattices are determined by their completions
nodes.statement: Let A be a Dedekind domain, V an A-module, and N ⊆ P two A-submodules of V with P finitely generated. If Â_v ⊗ N → Â_v ⊗ P is surjective for every nonzero prime v of A, then N = P.
hypotheses: A Dedekind domain; P finitely generated over A.
proofSteps: P/N is a finitely generated A-module with Â_v ⊗ (P/N) = 0 for all v (right exactness of the tensor product).
A_(v) → Â_v is faithfully flat, so (P/N)_(v) = 0 for every maximal ideal v.
A module whose localisations at all maximal ideals vanish is zero (Module.eq_zero_of_localization_maximal); hence N = P.

nodes.title: The completed ring of integers is induced from a decomposition group
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of number fields with group G, v a nonzero prime of 𝓞_K and w a prime of 𝓞_L above v with decomposition group G_w, identified with Gal(L_w/K_v). Then, as 𝒪̂_v[G]-modules, 𝒪̂_v ⊗ 𝓞_L ≅ Π_{w′|v} 𝒪_{L_{w′}} ≅ 𝒪̂_v[G] ⊗_{𝒪̂_v[G_w]} 𝒪_{L_w} (induction along G_w ⊆ G, with left modules).
hypotheses: L/K finite Galois; v, w as stated; the completions are the canonical ones of the NumberFieldArithmetic roadmap.
proofSteps: NumberFieldArithmetic Layer 5.7 gives the integral semilocal equivalence 𝒪̂_v ⊗ 𝓞_L ≅ Π_{w′|v} 𝒪_{L_{w′}} with its pure-tensor formula; it is G-equivariant, G permuting the factors.
G acts transitively on the primes over v with stabiliser G_w; NumberFieldArithmetic Layer 5.6 identifies G_w with Gal(L_w/K_v) through decompositionHom.
Choose left coset representatives R of G_w in G; the product is ⊕_{g∈R} g·𝒪_{L_w}, which is the induced module 𝒪̂_v[G] ⊗_{𝒪̂_v[G_w]} 𝒪_{L_w}.
acceptance: For v unramified and split completely, G_w = 1 and the module is 𝒪̂_v[G] ⊗ 𝒪̂_v = 𝒪̂_v[G].
For v inert, G_w = G and the statement is 𝒪̂_v ⊗ 𝓞_L = 𝒪_{L_w}.

nodes.title: Noether's theorem
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of number fields with group G. The following are equivalent: (i) L/K is tamely ramified; (ii) 𝓞_L is a locally free 𝓞_K[G]-lattice of rank one; (iii) 𝓞_L is a projective 𝓞_K[G]-module.
hypotheses: L/K finite Galois.

(ii) ⇒ (iii): locally-free-lattice-is-projective.
(iii) ⇒ (i): trace-surjective-of-projective and tame-iff-trace-surjective.
(i) ⇒ (iii) also holds directly: projective-of-tame.

nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite tamely ramified Galois extension of number fields with group G. Then 𝓞_L, with the action of ℤ[G] through G, is a locally free ℤ[G]-lattice of rank [K : ℚ].

nodes.title: Local freeness is separate from freeness
nodes.statement: Let A be a Dedekind domain with a nonzero nonprincipal ideal I (for example A = ℤ[√−5], I = (2, 1 + √−5)). Then I is a locally free A-lattice of rank one (over the trivial group ring A[1] = A) but is not free. Hence a locally free lattice over an order need not be free, and the class of a locally free lattice in the locally free class group can be nonzero.

proofSteps: Locally free: every completion Â_v is a discrete valuation ring, so Â_v ⊗ I is a nonzero ideal of a DVR (flatness), hence free of rank one.
Not free: a free ideal of rank one is principal; I is finitely generated of rank one, so free would mean I ≅ A, i.e. I principal.

nodes.title: Orders in finite-dimensional algebras
nodes.statement: Let R be a noetherian domain with fraction field F and E a finite-dimensional F-algebra. An R-order in E is an R-subalgebra Λ of E (a subring containing 1 and the image of R) that is an R-lattice in E: finitely generated as an R-module and spanning E over F (Mathlib's Submodule.IsLattice F). Examples: the group ring R[G] in F[G] for a finite group G, the integral closure of R in a finite separable field extension of F, M_n(R) in M_n(F).
hypotheses: R noetherian domain, F = Frac R, E a finite-dimensional F-algebra, not necessarily commutative.
proofSteps: Define IsOrder Λ as Submodule.IsLattice F applied to the underlying R-submodule of Λ.
Every element of an order is integral over R: R[x] ⊆ Λ is a finitely generated R-module.

Conversely (E separable: the trace form of the regular representation is nondegenerate) a subring spanning E whose elements are integral is finitely generated: for an F-basis α_i of E inside Λ and β ∈ Λ, the coordinates of β lie in r⁻¹R with r = det(tr(α_iα_j)) (Cramer), so Λ ⊆ r⁻¹Σ Rα_i.
Group rings: the images of the group elements form an R-basis of R[G] and an F-basis of F[G].
Integral closures: finite over R for separable extensions of the fraction field (Mathlib's IsIntegralClosure.finite) and spanning.
acceptance: ℤ[1/2] ⊆ ℚ is a subring spanning ℚ but not an order: it is not finitely generated.
R itself is an order in F (E = F).

nodes.title: Maximal orders
nodes.statement: Let R be a noetherian domain with fraction field F and E a finite-dimensional F-algebra. An R-order Λ in E is maximal if it is not properly contained in another R-order. The integral closure of an integrally closed R in a finite separable field extension is the unique maximal order there; for a nontrivial finite group G with |G| invertible in F, R[G] is not a maximal order in F[G] when |G| is not a unit in R.
hypotheses: R noetherian domain; E finite-dimensional over F.
